And at this he is indignant and says: "lest", he says, "overpowering us, they go forth out of our land". He does not wish us to go forth out of his land, but wills that we should always "bear the image of the earthly". For if we flee for refuge to his adversary, to Him who has prepared for us the kingdoms of heaven, it is necessary that we leave behind "the image of the earthly" and take up "the image of the heavenly". For this reason, therefore, Pharaoh appoints "taskmasters of works", to teach us his arts, to make us craftsmen of wickedness, to furnish us with a mastery of evils. And because these taskmasters and teachers of wickedness whom Pharaoh has set over us are many, and there is a vast multitude of drivers of this kind, who all exact, command, and extort earthly works, therefore the Lord Jesus, coming, made other masters and teachers, who, fighting against those and subjecting all their "principalities and powers and virtues", defend the sons of Israel from their violence and teach us the Israelite works, and again teach us to see God with the mind, to leave the works of Pharaoh, to go forth out of the land of Egypt, to cast off the Egyptian and barbarous ways, "to put off" the whole "old man with his deeds" "and to put on the new, who is created according to God", to be "renewed" ever "from day to day" unto the image of Him who made us, Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: According to these things, therefore, God is perhaps said also to have hardened the heart of Pharaoh, namely because the material of his heart was such that it received the presence of the Sun of justice not on that side by which it illumines, but on that by which it burns and hardens: on this account, without doubt, that he too was afflicting the life of the Hebrews in hard works, and was making them work with clay and brick. … And as this visible sun binds fast and hardens the material of clay, so the Sun of justice, by these same rays with which he was illumining the people of Israel, was hardening the heart of Pharaoh, in which were clayey thoughts, according to the very qualities of its own motions.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 2

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In Egypt were the children of Israel; they were afflicted in the works of Pharaoh the king with clay and brick, until, groaning, they cried out to the Lord, and He, hearing their groaning, sent to them His word through Moses and led them out of Egypt. And we too, therefore, when we were in Egypt — I mean in the errors of this world and in the darkness of ignorance, working the works of the devil in the desires and pleasures of the flesh — the Lord had mercy on our affliction and sent His Word, His only-begotten Son, to rescue us from the ignorance of error and lead us to the light of the divine law.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This "king, who did not know Joseph," devises many things against the people of God, and is forever seeking new arts of doing harm. But now his cunning surpasses all measure, when through the ministry of the midwives he attempts to destroy the offspring of that people — by the very art through which life is usually preserved. For what does he say? "And the king of the Egyptians said," it says, "to the midwives of the Hebrews, to one of them whose name was Sephora, and the name of the other was Phua, and he said: when you deliver the Hebrew women and they are near the birth, if it be a male, kill him; if a female, let it live." But to these words there is joined in what follows: "but the midwives feared God, and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, and they let the males live." If the things that are written were to be taken according to the narrative of the history, then what Scripture says — that "the midwives did not do according to what the king of Egypt commanded them" — would seem unable to stand. For the midwives are not found to have failed to let the females live, whom the king of Egypt commanded to be let live. For thus he says: "if indeed it is a male, kill him; if a female, let it live." And if "the midwives did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded," then surely, just as they "let the males live" against the king's command, so too they ought to have killed the females, that this also might be against the king's command. For to have let the females live was to have done according to Pharaoh's command. These things for the moment I say on account of those who are friends of the letter, and do not think the law to be spiritual and to be understood spiritually. But we, who have learned that all the things that are written were written not as accounts of antiquities, but for our instruction and profit, perceive that these things which are read even now come to pass, not only in this world, which is figuratively called Egypt, but also in each one of us. Let us inquire, then, how the king of Egypt, who is "the prince of this world," does not wish the males to live, but wishes the females to live. If you remember, we have often shown in our discussions that in the females the flesh and the affection of the flesh is signified, but the male is the rational sense and intellectual spirit. The rational sense, therefore, which can have a taste for heavenly things, which can understand God and "seek the things that are above" — this Pharaoh, king and prince of Egypt, hates; this he desires to be slain and destroyed. But he desires that whatever things are of the flesh should live, and the things that pertain to bodily matter — these he desires not only to live, but even to be increased and cultivated. For he wishes that all should have a taste for carnal things, should desire temporal things, should seek "the things that are upon the earth," that no one "lift up his eyes to heaven," that no one inquire whence he came here, that no one call to mind his homeland, paradise. When, therefore, you see men leading their life in pleasures and delights, awash in luxury, giving their labor to feasts, wine, banquets, beds, and unchaste acts — know that in these the king of Egypt is slaying the males and letting the females live. But if you see some rare person, "one out of a thousand," turning to God, lifting his eyes upward, seeking the things that are perpetual and eternal, contemplating not the things "that are seen, but the things that are not seen," hating delights, loving continence, fleeing luxury, cultivating virtue — this one, as a male, as a man, Pharaoh desires to be slain, persecutes, harries, and fights against with a thousand devices. He hates such men, he does not allow them to live in Egypt. Hence, then, it is that in this world the servants of God and all who seek God are held in disdain and contempt. Hence they are exposed to insults, hence they are filled with reproaches, hence hatreds and persecutions are stirred up against them — because Pharaoh hates them, hates males of this kind, he who loves the females. This one also sets about corrupting the midwives, and through them accomplishing what he desires; whose very names are indicated to us by the foresight of the Holy Spirit, who willed these things to be written. "Sephora" it says, "the one" — which is interpreted sparrow (passer) — and "Phua," which among us can be called either ruddy (rubens) or modest. Through these, then, he seeks to have the males slain and the females alone let live.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But what does Scripture say? "The midwives feared God," it says, "and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them." Certain men before us have said that these midwives hold the pattern of rational learning. For midwives are, as it were, in the middle, and tend both the males and the females at their birth. This learning, then, of common rational knowledge reaches to nearly every faculty, instructs all, tends all. If anyone in it be of manly spirit and wish to seek heavenly things and to pursue divine things, he will come, as though healed and warmed by learning of this kind, better prepared for the understanding of divine things. For there is one, as it were the sparrow, which teaches the loftier things and, with the rational wings of doctrine, summons souls to fly on high. The other, which is ruddy or modest, is moral, orders behavior, teaches modesty, instills honesty. To me, however, since Scripture says of these that "because they feared God, they did not do the command of the king of Egypt," these two midwives seem to preserve the figure of both testaments: "Sephora," which is interpreted sparrow, may be compared to the law, which "is spiritual"; but "Phua," which is ruddy or modest, indicates the Gospels, which are ruddy with the blood of Christ and throughout the whole world glow red with the gore of his passion. By these, then, as by midwives, the souls that are born in the church are healed, because from the reading of the Scriptures all the medicine of learning is bestowed upon them. Yet Pharaoh attempts through these things to slay the males of the church, when he suggests heretical notions and perverse doctrines to any who are studious in the divine Scriptures. But the foundation of God stands immovable. For "the midwives fear God," that is, they teach the fear of God, because "the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." Thus, finally, I think there is fitted still more suitably that which is written in the later passage, where it says: "because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses." This saying can have no coherence according to the letter. For what order of reasoning is it, that it should say: "because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses"? — as though a house should come to be for the reason that God is feared. If this is taken as it is written, it will seem to have not only no coherence, but also very great emptiness. But if you see how the Scriptures of the new and old testament, teaching the fear of God, make houses for the church and fill the whole circle of the earth with houses of prayer, then what is written will seem to be written reasonably. Thus, then, these midwives, because they fear God and teach the fear of God, do not carry out the command of the king of Egypt, but let their males live. Nor yet is it said that they obeyed the command of the king so as to let the females live. I dare confidently to say, according to the sense of Scripture: these midwives do not let the females live. For neither are vices taught in the churches, nor is luxury proclaimed, nor are sins nourished — for this is what Pharaoh wishes, when he commands the females to be let live — but virtue alone is cultivated, and virtue alone is nourished. But let us refer these things also to each one of us. And you too, if you fear God, do not carry out the command of the king of Egypt. For he commands you to live in delights, to love the present age, to covet present things. But you, if you fear God and exhibit the office of a midwife toward your soul, if you desire to confer salvation upon it, do not do these things, but let live the male that is in you, tend and cherish your inner man, and through good acts and understandings win for it eternal life.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But after this, when Pharaoh saw that through the midwives he could not slay the males of Israel: "he commanded," it says, "all the people, saying: every male whatsoever that shall be born to the Hebrews, cast into the river, and every female let live." See what "the prince of this world" commands his own, that they may seize our infants, that they may cast them into the river, and, lying in wait for the very first birth of our own, may straightway, as soon as they have touched the first breasts of the church, rush upon them, tear them away, persecute them, and overwhelm them with the waves and billows of this age. "See what you hear"; the wisdom of God through Solomon says: "understand intelligently the things that are set before you." See, as soon as you are born — nay rather, as soon as you are reborn — what threatens you. This is that which you read in the Gospel, that Jesus, as soon as he came up from baptism, "was led by the Spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil." This, then, is what in this passage too Pharaoh commanded his people: to fall upon the Hebrew infants, as soon as they were born, to tear them away, to drown them in the waters. This is perhaps also what is said through the prophet: "for the waters have entered even to my soul. I am sunk fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance." But for this reason Christ overcame and conquered, that he might open for you the way of conquering. For this reason, by fasting, he conquered, that you too might know that "a kind of demons of this sort" is to be overcome "by fastings and prayers." For this reason also he despised all the kingdoms of the world and their glory when they were offered to him, that you too, despising the glory of the world, might be able to overcome the tempter. The Egyptians, therefore, to whom Pharaoh gave commands, let only the females live, they hate the males; for they hate the virtues, and nourish only vices and pleasures. And now, therefore, the Egyptians lie in wait, in case perchance some male be born to the Hebrews, so that they may straightway persecute and kill him, unless they take heed, unless they watch and hide the male seed. Finally, Scripture relates that "one of the tribe of Levi, who begot a male and saw that the infant was comely, hid him for three months." See whether it is not for this reason that we are commanded not to perform our good acts in public, not to "do our righteousness before men," but rather, "with the door shut, to pray to the Father in secret," and that "what our right hand does, our left hand should not know." For unless it be in secret, it will be torn away by the Egyptians, it will be assailed, cast into the river, drowned in the waves and billows. Therefore, if I give alms, because it is a work of God, I beget a male. But if I do it so that it may become known to men, and I seek praise from men and do not hide it, my alms has been snatched away by the Egyptians and drowned in the river, and with such great labor and such great zeal I have begotten a male for the Egyptians. Therefore, O people of God, who hear these things, do not think, as we have already often said, that the tales of the ancients are being recited to you, but that you are being taught through these things, so that you may recognize the order of life, the discipline of morals, the contests of faith and virtue.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Seeing," then, these of the tribe of Levi "that the infant was comely, they concealed him for three months. And when they could no longer conceal him, his mother took," it says, "an ark and daubed it with bitumen and placed the infant in it and set it in the marsh beside the river. And his sister watched from afar, to see what would happen to him. But the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself in the river, and she heard the infant crying, and she sent," it says, "and took him up, and the daughter of Pharaoh said that this is of the infants of the Hebrews." After this it is then related how his sister spoke, that she might call the mother of the boy to nurse him. "And the daughter of Pharaoh said to her," it says, "keep this infant for me, and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages. And when she had nursed him, as he grew stronger, she brought him to the daughter of Pharaoh, and he became to her a son, and she named his name Moses, saying: because I took him up out of the water." Each of these things is filled with immense mysteries and demands a great length of time, and if we should spend the space of a whole day upon them, it would perhaps scarcely suffice. Yet briefly some things must be knocked upon by us for the edification of the church. I think the daughter of Pharaoh can be seen as the church, which is gathered from the nations, which, although she has an impious and iniquitous father, yet to her it is said through the prophet: "hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the house of your father, because the king has desired your beauty." This, then, is she who goes out from her father's house and comes to the waters, that she may be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father's house. Finally, straightway she takes up "the bowels of mercy" and has compassion on the infant. This church, therefore, coming from the nations, finds Moses lying in the marsh, cast off by his own and exposed, gives him to be nursed, he is nursed among his own, there he passes his infancy. But when "he has grown stronger," then he is brought to her and adopted as a son. That Moses is called the law has already often been treated in many places. Coming, therefore, to the waters of baptism, the church received also the law — the law, however, which was shut up within an "ark," daubed with pitch and "bitumen." An "ark" is a kind of covering woven from twigs or from papyrus, or even formed from the bark of trees, within which the infant, once placed in it, appeared exposed. The law, therefore, lay shut up within coverings of this kind and daubed with pitch and "bitumen"; hedged about by the base and foul senses of the Jews, it lay in squalor, until the church should come from the nations and take it up out of the muddy and marshy places and receive it within the halls of wisdom and the royal roofs. This law, nevertheless, passes its infancy among its own. For among those who do not know how to understand it spiritually, it is a little one and an infant, having the food of sucklings; but when it comes to the church, when it enters the house of the church, Moses is stronger and more robust. For once the veil of the letter is removed, "perfect" and "solid food" is found in the reading of it. Yet what is it that she, among whom the law was both born and nursed, receives the wages of her nursing from the daughter of Pharaoh? What is it that the synagogue receives from the church? I think it can be understood as that which the same Moses writes, saying: "I will lead you into jealousy over that which is no nation, over a foolish nation I will provoke you to wrath." The synagogue, then, receives this as its wages from the church, that it no longer worship idols. For seeing those who are of the nations so converted to God that they no longer know idols, and venerate no one except the one God, she herself is ashamed any longer to worship idols. This benefit, therefore, the synagogue receives from the church, in that she was seen to have nursed the law as a little one. But we too, even if we have had Pharaoh for a father, even if "the prince of this world" begot us in evil works, when we come to the waters, let us take up to ourselves the law of God, and let not the base and obscure covering of its letter be squalid to us; the things that are little and of sucklings in it let us yield up, but the things that are perfect and robust let us take, and let us place these within the royal roofs of our heart. Let us have a great and robust Moses; let us think nothing about him that is little, nothing lowly, but wholly magnificent, wholly excellent, wholly comely. For everything is great, whatever is spiritual, whatever is of sublime understanding. And let us pray to our Lord Jesus Christ, that he himself may reveal and show to us how "great" Moses is and how sublime he is. For he himself "reveals" to whom he wills "through the Holy Spirit." "To Him be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In Exodus something of this kind is written: "and it came to pass after many days, the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned, and their cry went up to God". As long as Pharaoh lived, the "children of Israel" did "not groan", and, placed under punishments, they did not even have the free faculty of "groaning"; for the king was alive, who commanded them to make "bricks and straw". As long as Pharaoh lived, they did "not groan to God"; when Pharaoh died, then they had the strength to lift up their faces wet with weeping. The wicked king lives in our breast as long as Pharaoh the devil lives. Then we labor at "bricks" and "straw", then we swallow our tears in silence and do the first works of iniquity; but when he has died, at the visitation of the Lord our God, then we "groan to the Lord".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Moses, when he had seen the bush burning and not consumed, marveling at the sight said: "I will pass over and behold this sight." Certainly he too was not signifying that he would traverse some span of earth, nor climb mountains nor go apart into the steep places of the valleys. The vision was close to him, in his mouth and in his eyes. But he says: "I will pass over," to show that, admonished by the heavenly vision, he ought to ascend to a higher life and to cross over from those things in which he was to better things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Great, then, is the vision, when God is seen with a pure heart. Great is the vision when with a pure heart the Word of God, and the Wisdom of God, who is His Christ, is acknowledged. Great is the vision, to acknowledge and to believe in the Holy Spirit. Great, then, is this vision — the knowledge of the Trinity. Nevertheless, even Moses was then seeing in Exodus the great vision, and he who was seen in the bush in the fire is called an angel, and he calls it a great vision. For he understood who it was in the angel. For immediately thereupon He says to God: "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob". See, then, how great this vision is — although this very thing also is great, to know that God makes "His angels spirits, and His ministers a burning fire". And now indeed to Moses, still pasturing the flocks of Jethro his father-in-law, and stepping or passing over from these, this vision is great, in which an angel is said to appear to him. But if he shall also have passed over the Red Sea, and the pillar of cloud has covered him, and he has adored the sacraments of the future baptism, then he will be able to see a still greater vision. For he will enter into the darkness and the whirlwind, where God Himself is said to be, where it is written that Moses alone drew near to God, but the others stood afar off. And Moses advances so far through these great visions, that he says to God: "If I have found", he says, "grace before Thee, manifest Thyself to me, that I may evidently see Thee". And then he hears from God: "I will set thee in the cleft of the rock" — and the rock was Christ — that through a very small opening thou mayest see My hinder parts, that is, that thou mayest acknowledge those things which in the last times shall be fulfilled through the assumption of the flesh: "But My face thou shalt not be able to see".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Observe that he has named a certain power of the soul feet, with which we as it were make our way, walking toward him who said "I am the way", and which must be shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace. And I think that the symbols of these sandals are the "sandals" recorded in Exodus, which those who ate the Passover and were ready for the journey were required to have. For thus he says, "You shall eat it: your loins girded and your sandals on your feet and your staffs in your hands, and you shall eat it with haste; it is the Lord's Passover". For it belongs to readiness both to eat "with haste" and to eat shod, so that, being strengthened by the food, they may be able to journey.

Therefore let him who is journeying be shod, but let him who has arrived at the holy land unloose his sandals; for "Loose", he says, "the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground".

For this reason let him who is not an apostle be shod as to the feet in readiness of the gospel of peace; but let the apostle no longer "take up sandals for the road", since he has already been perfected and is in the place where, both standing and walking, he is in "holy ground", living in Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Abraham sets forth, as it were, moral philosophy, through obedience. For so great was his obedience and observance of the commandments that, when he heard: "Go forth from your land, and from your kindred, and from the house of your father," he did not delay, but did it at once … For hearing that he should sacrifice his son, not even then does he doubt, but he obeys the precept: and, to give to posterity an example of the obedience which is moral philosophy, he did not spare even his only son. Isaac also holds to natural philosophy, since he both digs wells and searches out the depths of things. But Jacob too holds the inspective place, inasmuch as he was named Israel on account of the contemplation of divine things, and saw the camps of heaven, and beheld the house of God and the ways of the angels — that is, the ladder stretched out from earth to heaven.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: God has been recorded indeed to be the God "of Abraham, and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." He indeed who wishes the light to belong to none other than men (because it is said, "The life was the light of men") will think, according to this analogy, that the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob is the God of no one except these three fathers alone. But he is at least also the God of Elijah, and, as Judith says, the God of her father Simeon, and he is God of the Hebrews. Wherefore, according to the analogy, if nothing prevents him from being the God of others also, nothing prevents the light of men from also being the light of other creatures besides men.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2.143

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If the God of the universe, having been made familiar to the saints, becomes their God, the being named the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, by how much more will it be possible for the Holy Spirit, having been made familiar to the prophets, to be called their spirit, that the Spirit might thus be said to be the spirit of Elijah and the spirit of Isaiah?
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.68

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: That the activity of the Father and the Son is to be found both in saints and in sinners is clear from the fact that all rational beings are partakers of the word of God, that is, of reason, and so have implanted within them some seeds, as it were, of wisdom and righteousness, which is Christ. And all things that exist derive their share of being from him who truly exists, who said through Moses, "I am that I am"; which participation in God the Father extends to all, both righteous and sinners, rational and irrational creatures and absolutely everything that exists.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It is difficult to see what this sign can symbolize for us. But since we must not stop seeking and must deliver to the reader what occurs to us as an interpretation, we will say that in many passages the hand is a symbol of deeds. Now the bosom of Moses has two meanings. The first, in accordance with the sense of the letter, makes the deed of the doer like snow, as it says in the Hebrew, and leprous. The second, however, in accordance with the spiritual law, shows that the conduct is pure and that it is restored to the will of the nature of the Word.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 32.268

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And of old indeed Moses said: "but I am ἄλογος (without speech or reason)" — which, though the Latin has rendered it otherwise, can nevertheless be more properly translated: "without speech or reason" —, and after he said this, he received reason or speech, which he had confessed that he did not before possess. But the people of Israel in Egypt, before it received the law, was in a certain way "mute", without speech and reason; then it received speech, of which Moses was an image. This people, therefore, does not now confess what it then confessed in Moses, namely that it is "mute" and ἄλογος, but by nods and silence indicates that it does not have speech and does not have reason. Does it not seem to you to be a confession of foolishness, when none of them can render a reason for the legal precepts and the prophetic oracle?
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 5

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But I will bring forward to you yet another thing, which you cannot contradict. In Exodus, where we in the books of the Church have it written that Moses answered the Lord and said: "Provide, Lord, another whom you may send. For I am of a thin voice and slow of tongue," you in the Hebrew copies have: "but I am uncircumcised in lips." Behold, you have circumcision of the lips according to your copies, which you say are truer. If, then, according to you Moses says he is still unworthy, because he is not circumcised in lips, it is certain that he thereby indicates this, that he is worthier and holier who is circumcised in lips. Apply, then, the sickle also to your lips and cut away the coverings of your mouth, since such an understanding in the divine letters pleases you. But if you recall the circumcision of the lips to allegory, and likewise call the circumcision of the ears allegorical and figurative, how do you not also seek an allegory in the circumcision of the foreskin?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: So long as Moses was in Egypt and "was being instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians", he was not "of a thin voice" nor "slow of tongue", nor did he profess himself to be lacking in eloquence. For, as far as the Egyptians were concerned, he was both of a sonorous voice and of incomparable eloquence. But when he began to hear the voice of God and to receive the divine utterances, then he perceived his own voice to be feeble and thin, and he understood his tongue to be slow and hampered; then he pronounces himself mute, when he began to recognize that true Word which "was in the beginning with God". But that what we are saying may more readily be grasped, let us make use of a comparison of this kind. If a rational man, however unskilled and untaught, be compared with dumb animals, he will seem eloquent in comparison with those which are devoid both of reason and of voice; but if he be set beside learned and eloquent men, men most approved in all wisdom, he will seem inarticulate and mute. And if someone should contemplate the divine Word itself and look upon the divine wisdom itself, then, however great his learning and however great his wisdom, he will profess himself before God a mute animal, far more than the beasts are before us. This surely was what the blessed David also, gazing upon it and weighing himself in such a manner against the divine wisdom, was saying: "I became as a beast of burden before you". According to this, therefore, Moses too, the greatest of the prophets, says to God in the present reading that he is "of a thin voice" "and slow of tongue", and that he is not eloquent. For all men, in comparison with the divine word, are to be reckoned not only inarticulate, but even mute.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Thus I understand also that which God says: "Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God?" There is an eye of the body, with which we behold these earthly things, an eye according to the sense of the flesh, of which the Scripture says: "walking vainly, puffed up by the sense of the flesh". To this we have another, contrary and better, that savors of divine things; and because it was blind in us, Jesus came to make it see, that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might be made blind.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 16

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Because, therefore, he had advanced so far in understanding as to recognize his own self—in which lies the greatest part of wisdom—the divine favor rewards him. Hear with what rich and magnificent gifts. "I," he says, "will open your mouth, and will instruct you in what you ought to speak". Blessed are those whose mouth God opens, that they may speak. To the prophets God opens the mouth and fills it with his own utterance, as he says in the present passage: "I will open your mouth and will instruct you in what you ought to speak". But through David also God says: "Enlarge your mouth, and I will fill it". Likewise Paul too says: "that speech may be given me in the opening of my mouth". The mouth, therefore, of those who speak the words of God, God opens. But I fear that there may be some whose mouth, on the contrary, the devil opens. For whoever speaks a lie, it is certain that the devil has opened his mouth, that he might speak the lie. Whoever gives false testimony, whoever utters buffooneries, whoever brings forth filthy things and the rest of this kind out of his mouth—the devil has opened their mouth. I fear that the devil opens also the mouth "of whisperers and detractors", and also of those who "utter idle words, of which an account is to be rendered in the day of judgment". And indeed, as for those who "speak iniquity on high", "who deny that my Lord Jesus Christ has come in the flesh", or "who blaspheme the Holy Spirit", to whom "it shall be forgiven neither in the present nor in the age to come"—who doubts that the devil opens their mouth? Do you wish me to show you this also from the Scriptures, how the devil opens the mouth to men of this kind, who speak against Christ? See what is written of Judas, how it is related that "Satan entered into him", and that "the devil put it into his heart to betray him". He, then, opened his mouth, that "he might confer with the chief priests and Pharisees how he might betray him" for money received. Whence it seems to me to be no small grace to discern the mouth which the devil opens. It is not without the grace of the Holy Spirit to distinguish a mouth of this kind and its words; and therefore in the distribution of spiritual graces this too is added, that to some is given "the discernment of spirits". It is therefore a spiritual grace by which the spirit is discerned, as also elsewhere the Apostle says: "test the spirits, whether they be of God". But as God opens the mouth of the saints, so I think that God opens also the ears of the saints to hear the divine words. For thus says the prophet Isaiah: "The Lord will open my ear, that I may know when the word ought to be spoken". So too the Lord opens the eyes, as "the Lord opened the eyes of Hagar, and she saw a well of living water". But Elisha the prophet also says: "Open, Lord, the eyes of the servant, that he may see that there are more with us than with the adversaries. And the Lord opened," he says, "the eyes of the servant, and behold, the whole mountain was full of horsemen and chariots and heavenly aids". For "the angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him, and will deliver them". God therefore opens, as we have said, both the mouth and the ears and the eyes, that we may either speak or discern or hear the things that are God's. But that also I do not take idly, which the prophet says: "the instruction," he says, "of the Lord opened my ear". This seems to me to pertain to us, that is, in common to the whole Church of God. For if we are engaged in "the instruction of the Lord", "the instruction of the Lord" opens the ear for us also. But the ear which is opened through "the instruction of the Lord" is not always open, but at one time open, at another closed. Hear the lawgiver saying: "you shall not receive a vain report". If, then, at any time vain things are spoken, if at any time empty, foolish, base, profane, wicked things are brought forth, he who knows "the instruction of the Lord" closes his ears and turns away his hearing and says: "but I, like a deaf man, was not hearing, and like a mute man who has not opened his mouth". But if the things that are spoken pertain to the profit of the soul, if the discourse is about God, if it teaches morals, invites to virtues, cuts away vices, the ears ought to lie open to utterances of this kind—and not only the ears, but also the heart and the mind, and the whole gate of the soul is to be thrown open to hearing of this kind. Yet with the utmost moderation of precept the law expressed itself, so as to say: "you shall not receive a vain report"; it did not say: you shall not hear a vain report, but "you shall not receive". For we frequently hear vain things. What Marcion speaks are vain things; what Valentinus speaks are vain things; and all who speak against God the creator—vain are the things they speak. But nevertheless we frequently hear them, that we may be able to answer against them, lest perchance they steal upon any of the simpler of our brethren through the ornament of speech. We hear these things, then, but we do not receive them. For they were spoken from that mouth which the devil opened. And therefore we must pray that the Lord may deign to open our mouth, that we may be able both to refute those who contradict and to stop up the mouth which the devil opens. So much for what is written: "I will open your mouth, and will instruct you in what you ought to speak".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But not to Moses only is it promised that his mouth shall be opened by the Lord, but to Aaron also. For it is said concerning him too: "I will open your mouth and his mouth, and will instruct you in what you are to do".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now many have been troubled by the story of Pharaoh, in dealing with whom God says several times, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart." For if he is hardened by God and through being hardened sins, he is not himself responsible for the sin; and if this is so, Pharaoh has no free will. And someone will say that in the same way those who are lost have no free will and will not be lost on their own account. Also the saying in Ezekiel, "I will take away their stony hearts and will put in them hearts of flesh, that they may walk in my statutes and keep my judgments," might lead one to suppose that it was God who gave the power to walk in the commandments and to keep the judgments, by his removing the hindrance, the stony heart, and implanting something better, the heart of flesh.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Why too does he blame Pharaoh, saying, "You will not let my people go; behold, I will smite all the firstborn in Egypt, even your firstborn," and all the rest that is recorded as being said by God through Moses to Pharaoh? It is incumbent on him who believes that the Scriptures are true and that God is just, if he is a thoughtful man, to take pains to show how God, in using such expressions as these, can be clearly conceived to be just.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And is there anything more profound to say of Israel, not of nature but of grace, of whom it was written, "Israel is my firstborn son," when Israel was in dispersion? You yourself will also understand that these are the scattered children of God for whom Jesus was to die in order to gather them together into one.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 28.185

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We must also inquire who that being was of whom it is said in Exodus that he wished to kill Moses because he was setting out for Egypt. And afterwards, who is it that is called the "destroying angel," and who also is he who in Leviticus is described as Apopompeus, that is, the Averter, of whom the Scripture speaks thus: "One lot for the Lord, and one lot for Apopompeus"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For Aaron also "met" Moses, and he went out of Egypt. But "he met" him where, in what kind of place? For it matters where "he meets" him—Moses, that is, whose mouth is to be opened by God. "He met him," he says, "in the mountain of God". You see that his mouth is deservedly opened, who is able to "meet in the mountain of God". Peter and James and John ascended the mountain of God, that they might be counted worthy to see Jesus transfigured and to see Moses with him and Elijah in glory. And you too, therefore, unless you ascend to "the mountain of God" and there "meet" Moses—that is, unless you ascend to the lofty sense of the law, unless you win your way up to the summit of spiritual understanding—your mouth is not opened by the Lord. If you stand in the lowly place of the letter and bind the text of the history to Jewish narratives, you have not met Moses "in the mountain of God", nor has God "opened your mouth" nor "instructed you in what you ought to speak". Unless, then, "Aaron had met Moses in the mountain", unless he had seen his lofty and arduous sense, unless he had discerned his exalted understanding, Moses would never have spoken to him the words of God, nor handed over to him the power of signs and wonders, nor associated him as a partaker of so great a mystery.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But since it is a long matter to speak of each thing in order, let us see what "Moses and Aaron", "having gone in" to Pharaoh, say: "Thus says the Lord: let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness". Moses does not will that the people, while placed in Egypt, should serve the Lord, but that it should go out into the desert and there serve the Lord. This is without doubt what he shows: that so long as anyone remains in the dark deeds of the world and is engaged in the obscurity of affairs, he cannot "serve the Lord"; for he cannot "serve two masters", he cannot "serve the Lord and mammon". We must, therefore, go out of Egypt; the world must be forsaken, if we wish to "serve the Lord". But it must be forsaken, I say, not in place, but in mind; not by setting out on a journey, but by advancing in faith. Hear John saying these same things: "little children, do not love the world nor the things that are in the world; for all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But Pharaoh resists; "the ruler of these darknesses" does not wish to release you; he does not wish you to be drawn away from his darkness and led to the light of knowledge. And hear what he says: "who is he," he says, "whose voice I should hear? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go". You hear what "the prince of this world" answers: he says that he does not know God. Do you see what raw pride does? So long as "he is not in the labors of men and is not scourged with men", for that reason pride held him fast. Then, a little later, you will see how much he profits under the scourges, how much better he is made when beaten. He who now says: "I do not know the Lord", afterward, when he has felt the force of the blows, is going to say: "pray the Lord for me"; and not only this, but even, when his own magicians testify, he will confess that "it is the finger of God" in the power of the signs. Let no one, then, be so untaught in divine discipline as to think the divine scourges a ruin, as to believe the blows of the Lord a punishing destruction. Behold Pharaoh too, most hardened; yet he profits when beaten. Before the blows he does not know the Lord; when beaten, he asks that the Lord be entreated for him. It is an advance under punishments to recognize this very thing—why you have deserved the punishment. "I do not know," then, he says, "the Lord, and I do not let Israel go". But see in the Gospels how, when beaten, he amends this saying. For it is written that the demons cried out to the Lord and said: "why have you come before the time to torment us? we know you, who you are: you are the Son of the living God". When they have felt the torments, they know the Lord. Before the scourges he says: "I do not know the Lord, and I do not let Israel go"; but he will both let Israel go, and not only let it go, but will himself urge it to go out. For there is no "fellowship of light with darkness"; no "part of the faithful with the unfaithful".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And yet what does he say? Let us see how or how far he bids us set out from Egypt: "we will go," he says, "a journey of three days into the wilderness, and there we will sacrifice to the Lord our God". What is "the way of three days" which we must travel, that, going out from Egypt, we may be able to arrive at the place in which we ought to sacrifice? I understand that way to be he who said: "I am the way, the truth, and the life". This way must be traveled by us in three days. For whoever "shall confess with his mouth the Lord Jesus and shall believe in his heart that God raised him from the dead" on the third day, "shall be saved". This, then, is the "three days' way" by which one arrives at the place where one may sacrifice to the Lord and render "the sacrifice of praise". This, as far as pertains to the mystical understanding. But if we seek also the moral sense, which is most useful to us, we set out "a three days' journey" from Egypt if we so preserve ourselves from every defilement of soul, body, and spirit that, as the Apostle said, "our spirit whole, and soul, and body, may be kept in the day of Jesus Christ". We set out "a three days' journey" from Egypt if, taking away rational, natural, and moral wisdom from worldly things, we turn it to the divine ordinances; we set out "a three days' journey" from Egypt if, purifying in ourselves words, deeds, and thoughts—for these are the three by which men can sin—we are made "pure in heart", that we may be able to "see God". But do you wish to see that such are the things which the Holy Spirit indicates in the Scriptures? This Pharaoh, who is the prince of Egypt, when he sees himself more vehemently pressed to let the people of God go, in the second place desires to obtain this, "that they should not go far off", that they should not set out the whole three days, and he says: "do not go far off". He does not want the people of God to be made "far" from himself; he wants it, if not in deed, at least to sin in word; if not in word, at least to offend in thought. He does not want them to set out from him the whole three days. He wants to have at least one of his days in us; in others two, in others he possesses the whole three days. But blessed are those who withdraw from him the entire three days, and he possesses no day of his own in them. Do not think, then, that Moses led the people out of Egypt only at that time: now too Moses, whom we have with us—"for we have Moses and the prophets"—that is, the law of God, wishes to lead you out of Egypt; if you hear it, it wishes to make you "far" from Pharaoh; it desires to rescue you from the work of mud and straw, if only you hear the law of God and understand it spiritually. It does not want you to remain in the deeds of the flesh and of darkness, but to go out to the wilderness, to come to a place empty of the disturbances and waves of the world, to come to the quiet of silence. For "the words of wisdom are learned in silence and quiet". When, therefore, you come to this place of quiet, there you will be able "to sacrifice to the Lord", there to recognize the law of God and the power of the divine voice. For this reason, then, Moses desires to cast you out from the midst of tossing affairs and from the midst of clamoring peoples. For this reason he desires you to go out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of ignorance, that you may hear the law of God and receive the light of knowledge.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But what does he yet add in his answers? "Why," he says, "O Moses and Aaron, do you turn my people away from their works? Depart, each one of you to your work". So long as the people is with him and works "mud" and "brick", so long as it is occupied in "straw", he does not think it perverted, but that it walks in the right path. But if it should say: I wish to go "the way of three days" and "to serve the Lord", he says that the people is perverted by Moses and Aaron. This indeed "was said to the ancients". But even today, if Moses and Aaron—that is, the prophetic and the priestly word—should rouse the soul to the service of God, invite it to go out of the world, to renounce all that it possesses, to give heed to the divine law and follow the word of God, immediately you will hear it said by those who are of one mind with Pharaoh and his friends: 'see how men are seduced and perverted—what young men, that they may not toil, may not do military service, may not do anything that would profit them, forsaking necessary and useful things pursue trifles and idleness. What is it to serve God? They do not wish to labor and seek occasions for slothful idleness.' These were the words of Pharaoh then, and these his friends and intimates speak now too.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The matter is carried on not by words only; blows follow too—he orders the scribes of the Hebrews to be scourged, straw not to be given, the work to be exacted; these things the fathers endured, in the figure of whom the people of God also, which is in the Church, often suffers as well. For you will find, if you consider them, that those who have wholly handed themselves over to "the prince of this world" act with prosperous successes, that everything, as they themselves think, turns out happily for them; but that to the servants of God often not even these humble and small things of human sustenance turn out well. For these things I think seem to be the straw that is furnished by Pharaoh. It often happens, then, that those who fear God lack even this cheap sustenance, like straw; often too they endure the persecutions of tyrants, they bear tortures and savage torments, so that some, worn out, say to Pharaoh: 'Why do you afflict your people?' For some, overcome by the blows, fall away from the faith and confess themselves to be the people of Pharaoh. "For not all who are of Israel are Israelites; nor because they are the seed are they all sons as well".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: These, then, who are doubtful and are worn out in tribulations, even speak against Moses and Aaron and say: 'from the day you go in and go out to Pharaoh, you have made our odor abominable before him.' These men speak truly, though perhaps they know not what they say, just as that Caiaphas too spoke truly that "it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people", but he knew not what he was saying. For, as the Apostle says, we are the "good odor" of Christ; but, he says, "to some an odor from life unto life, but to others an odor from death unto death". So the prophetic word too is a "sweet odor" to those who believe, but to the doubtful and unbelieving, and to those who confess themselves to be the people of Pharaoh, it becomes an abominable odor.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But Moses himself too says to the Lord: "from the time I spoke with Pharaoh, he has afflicted your people". For it is certain that, before the word of God is heard, before the divine preaching is made known, there is no tribulation, there is no temptation, because, unless the trumpet sound, battle is not joined; but when the trumpet of preaching has given the signal of war, there affliction follows, there all the fighting of tribulations rises up. From the time Moses and Aaron began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God is afflicted. From the time the word of God is brought into your soul, of necessity a struggle is stirred up within you, of the virtues against the vices; but before the word came which would rebuke, the vices endured within you in peace; but when the word of God began to make the distinction of each, then a great disturbance rises up and war is born without treaty. "For when can iniquity accord with justice", unchastity with sobriety, falsehood with truth? And therefore let us not be greatly disturbed if our "odor" seems to be abominable to Pharaoh; for virtue is a thing of abomination to the vices. Nay rather, as he says in what follows, that Moses stood "before Pharaoh", let us too stand "against Pharaoh" and not be bent nor bowed, but let us stand "girt about our loins in truth and our feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace". For thus the Apostle exhorts us, saying: "stand, therefore, and do not again cleave to the yoke of servitude". And again he says: "in which we stand, and glory in the hope of the glory of God". But we stand confidently if we beseech the Lord to "set our feet upon a rock", lest that befall us which the same prophet says: "but my feet were almost moved, and my steps were almost poured out". Let us stand, then, "before Pharaoh", that is, let us resist him in the struggle, as the Apostle Peter too says: "resist him, strong in faith". But Paul likewise says: "stand in faith and act manfully". For if we stand bravely, that too follows which Paul prays for his disciples, saying: "God will crush Satan under your feet speedily". For the more constantly and bravely we stand, the weaker and more feeble will Pharaoh be; but if we begin to be either weak or doubtful, he will become stronger and more constant against us. And truly that is fulfilled in us of which Moses gave a figure: for when he himself "lifted up his hands", Amalek was overcome; but if, as though they were weary, he "let them down" and laid low his feeble arms, "Amalek prevailed". So, then, let us too, in the power of the cross of Christ, lift up our arms and "raise up" in prayer "holy hands in every place without wrath and disputation", that we may deserve the help of the Lord. For this same thing the Apostle James too exhorts, saying: "but resist the devil, and he will flee from you". Let us act, then, with all faith, that Satan may not only "flee from us", but also "be crushed under our feet", just as Pharaoh too was sunk in the sea and extinguished in the deep of the abyss. But we, if we withdraw from the Egypt of the vices, will escape the waves of the world as though by a solid road, through Jesus Christ our Lord, "to whom is the glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For though there were three sons of Korah whose names we find in the book of Exodus—Aser, which is, by interpretation, "instruction," and the second Elkana, which is translated "possession of God," and the third Abiasaph, which in the Greek tongue might be rendered "congregation of the father"—yet the prophecies were not divided but were both spoken and written by one spirit and one voice and one soul, which worked in true harmony. And the three speak as one, "As the hart pants after the springs of the water, so pants my soul after you, O God."
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 14.1

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I think therefore, so far as I am able to perceive, that Moses coming to Egypt and bearing the rod with which he chastises and beats Egypt with ten plagues — this Moses is the law of God, which has been given to this world, that it may correct and amend it with ten plagues, that is, with the ten commandments which are contained in the Decalogue; but the rod, through which all these things are wrought, through which Egypt is subdued and Pharaoh is overcome, is the cross of Christ, through which this world is conquered and "the prince of this world" with his principalities and powers is triumphed over. And that the rod, when cast down, becomes a dragon or serpent and devours the serpents of the Egyptian magicians, who had done "likewise" — that the serpent is put for wisdom or prudence the Gospel word indicates, when it says: "be prudent as serpents", and elsewhere: "the serpent was more prudent than all the animals and beasts that were in paradise". The cross of Christ, therefore, whose preaching seemed "foolishness", which Moses, that is the law, contains, as the Lord said: "for he wrote of me" — this cross, I say, of which Moses wrote, after it was cast down upon the earth, that is, after it came to the belief and faith of men, was turned into wisdom, and into so great a wisdom that it should devour all the wisdom of the Egyptians, that is, of this world. For behold how "God made foolish the wisdom of this world", after he manifested "Christ, who was crucified, to be the power of God and the wisdom of God", and now the whole world has been caught by him who said: "catching the wise in their own craftiness".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that the waters of the river are turned into blood is fitted suitably enough. First indeed, so that that river, to which they had handed over the little ones of the Hebrews by cruel slaughter, might render to the authors of the crime a cup of blood, and that by drinking they might feel the gore of the polluted flood, which they had stained with parricidal killing. Then next, so that nothing might be lacking to the allegorical laws also, the waters are turned into blood and its own blood is given to Egypt to drink. The waters of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers; because these have deceived all who are little ones in perception and children in understanding, when the cross of Christ showed the light of truth to this world, they are required to pay the penalties of their slaying and the guilt of blood. For thus also the Lord himself says that: "all the blood which has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of Abel the just unto the blood of Zachariah, shall be required of this generation".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But by the second plague, in which the frogs are brought forth, I judge that the songs of the poets are figuratively indicated, who, by a certain empty and inflated modulation, like the sounds and songs of frogs, have brought upon this world the fables of deception. For that animal is useful for nothing else except that it renders the sound of its voice with wicked and importunate clamors.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: One should also observe that the term prayer,which often differs in meaning from "invocation," is here employed in the case of one who promises in a vow to do certain things if God grants him certain other things. But the term is also used in the ordinary way. For example, we found this to be so in Exodus after the description of the plague of the frogs, which was the second of the ten plagues: … "But Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: 'Pray to the Lord on my account to take away the frogs from me and my people; and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the Lord.' " When Pharaoh employs the word prayer the habitual meaning of "prayer" is conveyed in addition to the above meaning. If anyone finds this difficult to see, it becomes clear in what follows, namely: "And Moses said to Pharaoh: 'Set me a time when I shall pray for you, and for your servants, and for your people, that the frogs may be driven away from you and from your house and from your people, and may remain only in the river.' "We noted, however, that in the case of the sciniphs, the third plague, Pharaoh does not ask that prayer be made, nor does Moses pray. And in the case of the flies, the fourth plague, he says, "Pray therefore for me to the Lord." And then Moses said, "I will go out from you and will pray to the Lord. And the flies shall depart from Pharaoh, and from his servants, and from his people tomorrow." And a little further on we read: "So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to God." Again in the case of the fifth and also of the sixth plague Pharaoh did not ask that prayer be made, nor did Moses pray. In the seventh plague "Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron, saying to them, 'I have sinned this time. The Lord is just, but I and my people are wicked. Pray to the Lord, that the thunderings of God and the hail and the fire may cease.' " And a little further on we read: "And Moses went from Pharaoh out of the city and stretched forth his hands to the Lord; and the thunders … ceased." We shall discuss more suitably at another time why it is not said as on the previous occasions that "he prayed" but rather that "he stretched forth his hands to the Lord." And in the case of the eighth plague Pharaoh says, "And pray to the Lord your God, that he take away from me this death. And Moses going forth from the presence of Pharaoh, prayed to the Lord."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this the gnats are brought forth. This animal is indeed suspended by its wings, flitting through the air, but it is so subtle and minute that it escapes the sight of the eye unless one sees sharply; yet when it has settled on the body, it bores in with a most bitter sting, so that the one whom a man is not able to see flying, he feels stinging. This kind of animal therefore I think most fittingly compared to the art of dialectic, which bores through souls with minute and subtle stings of words and circumvents them with such craftiness that the deceived man neither sees nor understands whence he is deceived.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And in the fourth place I would compare the dog-fly to the sect of the Cynics, who, among the rest of the wicked doings of their deception, even proclaim pleasure and lust to be the highest good. Since therefore through each of these the world was previously deceived, the word and law of God, coming, convicts it with corrections of this kind, so that from the quality of the punishments it may recognize the qualities of its own error.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This Pharaoh, who is the prince of Egypt, when he sees himself more vehemently pressed to let the people of God go, in the second place desires to obtain this, "that they should not go far off", that they should not set out the whole three days, and he says: "do not go far off". He does not want the people of God to be made "far" from himself; he wants it, if not in deed, at least to sin in word; if not in word, at least to offend in thought. He does not want them to set out from him the whole three days. He wants to have at least one of his days in us; in others two, in others he possesses the whole three days. But blessed are those who withdraw from him the entire three days, and he possesses no day of his own in them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that in the fifth place Egypt is beaten by the slaying of the animals or cattle, in this there is convicted the madness and folly of mortals, who, like irrational cattle, imposed the worship and the name of God upon the figures not only of men but also of cattle, stamped upon wood and stones, venerating Ammon-Jupiter in a ram and Anubis in a dog, worshipping Apis also in a bull, and the rest of the monstrous gods which Egypt marvels at, so that in the very things in which they believed a divine worship to reside, in these they might see pitiable torments.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these, sores and blisters with burning are brought forth in the sixth blow. And it seems to me that in the sores there is convicted deceitful and festering malice, in the blisters swelling and inflated pride, in the burning the madness of anger and fury. Thus far the torments are tempered to the world through the figures of its own errors.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But after these blows come from on high "voices", it says — of thunder without doubt — "and hail and fire running about in the hail". See the temperateness of the divine correction: it does not beat in silence, but gives voices and sends teaching from heaven, through which the chastised one may be able to recognize his own fault. It gives also hail, through which the still tender growths of the vices may be laid waste. It gives also fire, knowing that there are "thorns and thistles" which that fire ought to feed upon, concerning which the Lord says: "I came to send fire upon the earth"; for through this the incentives of pleasure and lust are consumed.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: See whether it is for this reason that God hardens the heart of Pharaoh, so that at a moment when he was not hardened he could say, "The Lord is just: I and my people are wicked." His heart has to be hardened further, and he has to suffer more, that he may not, because he has been freed of his hardheartedness too quickly, think too lightly of that hardheartedness and so may have to have his heart hardened over and over again.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And the briefly recorded fact that the heart of Pharaoh experienced a kind of softening when he said, "But you shall not proceed far; you shall go a three days' journey and leave your wives behind," and whatever else he spoke when yielding before the marvelous works makes it clear that these signs had some effect even on him, though they did not entirely accomplish their object. Yet not even this would have happened if the idea held by most people about the words, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart," rightly represented what was wrought by him, that is, by God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that mention is made of locusts in the eighth place, I think that through this kind of plague the inconstancy of the human race, ever at variance with itself and discordant, is confuted. For the locust, though it has no king, as Scripture says: "leads forth its army arrayed in one battle-line"; but men, though made rational by God, have been able neither to govern themselves in ordered fashion nor to bear patiently the guidance of God their king.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
We say, lest perhaps also the "palpable darkness" in Egypt was made in this manner for "three days", not from an eclipse of the sun, but either because dark clouds ran together into one, or because the air there then became thicker over the Egyptians only — for "to all the sons of Israel", as the scripture testifies, "there was light in all the places in which they were dwelling".

For it is also impossible in an eclipse of the sun, which happens from the coming together of the moon to the sun, for darkness to be made for "three" continuous "days"; and it would be believed that there was some other cause of the darkness in Egypt, if the sun had even been named, or as though darkened at that time. But now the scripture of Exodus says nothing else except that "Moses stretched out his hand to heaven, and there was darkness and gloom and the rest over the whole land of Egypt for three days; and no one saw his brother, nor did anyone rise from his bed for three days".

And just as, when Moses stretched out his hand "to heaven", "darkness was made over the Egyptians", who held the servants of God in servitude, an image of the future darkness which was to seize the Egyptians, similarly also when Christ at the sixth hour stretched out his hands on the cross to heaven over the people who had cried out: "take this man from the earth", and "crucify, crucify him", darkness was made, and they were deprived of all light. Likewise under Moses "there was darkness and gloom over the whole land of Egypt for three days; and no one saw his brother, nor did anyone rise from his bed for three days; but to all the sons of Israel there was light in all the places in which they were dwelling". But under Christ darkness fell over the whole earth of Judea for three hours, but there was light over all the rest of the earth. Which everywhere illumines the whole Church of God in Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The ninth plague is darkness, whether so that the blindness of their mind may be convicted, or so that they may understand that the reasons of the divine dispensation and providence are most obscure. For "God has made darkness his hiding-place", which they, desiring boldly and rashly to search out, and asserting one thing from another, have been rolled down into the thick and "palpable darkness" of errors.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Moses, when he had come to the place that God showed him, is not permitted to ascend, but before that it is said to him: "loose the strap of the sandal from your feet." To Abraham none of these things is said, nor to Isaac, but they ascend and do not put off their sandals. In which perhaps this is the reason: that Moses, although he was "great," yet was coming from Egypt, and there were certain bonds of mortality knotted to his feet. But Abraham and Isaac have none of these things, but come to the place.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: At the last the destruction of the firstborn is brought on, in which there is perhaps something above our understanding, namely what seems to have been committed by the Egyptians against "the church of the firstborn, which is enrolled in heaven". Whence too the destroying angel is sent to a ministry of this kind, to spare only those who shall be found to have both doorposts marked with the blood of the lamb. Meanwhile the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed, whether we say they are the "principalities and powers" and "the rulers of the darkness of this world", whom Christ at his coming is said to have "led forth", that is, to have led captive "and to have triumphed over on the wood of the cross"; or whether we say they are the authors and inventors of the false religions which have been in this world, which the truth of Christ has extinguished and destroyed together with their authors. This much as regards the mystical sense.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In Matthew it is not written: "he was beginning"; but here, because he was about to ascend from baptism, "he was beginning" is read, Scripture relating: "and this same Jesus was beginning". For when he was baptized and took up the mystery of the second birth, so that you too might destroy your former nativity and be born in the second regeneration, then he is said "to have begun". And just as the people of the Jews, when they were in Egypt, did not have a beginning of months, but when they had gone out of Egypt, then it is said to them: "this month, the beginning of months, shall be the first for you among the months of the year", so he who is not yet baptized is not narrated "to have begun". For let us not suppose that it was added in vain to that which is said, "this same was Jesus", what follows: "beginning".
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 28

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But now we shall pass to the text itself, word by word, so that the meaning inherent in the historical events may be shown more rationally. The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: "This month is for you the beginning of months, the first for you among the months of the year."

God says to Moses and Aaron, as they come out of Egypt, that this is the beginning of months and the first among the months of the year. As regards the historical sense, then, this is indeed the first month, and the Jews celebrate this feast every year on the fourteenth day of the first month, when they sacrifice a lamb in their houses according to the Law given to them through Moses. Yet since Christ came "not to abolish the Law and the Prophets, but to bring them to fulfillment," He has shown us what the true Passover is, the true passage out of Egypt.

It is the beginning of months for the one who effects this passage precisely when the month of the passage out of Egypt comes, so that for him there may be the beginning of another birth, when a new manner of life begins for the one who definitively abandons the darkness and sets out on the way toward the light. I refer specifically to the sacrament granted through water to those who have placed their hope in Christ. This water is called "the laver of regeneration." Regeneration: what else does it mean but the beginning of a second birth?

It is truly necessary to live according to a perfect manner of life and love, so that one, though still continuing to live in the present world, may be able to hear the words: "This month is the beginning of months for you." For this prescription is not given by God to the whole people, but only to Moses and Aaron; for it is not written, "And God said to the people, This month is for you the beginning of months," but it is written: "The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: This month is for you the beginning of months." Only then does He add: "Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel: On the tenth day of this month let each one take a lamb."

For if He had added, "Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel: This month is for you the beginning of months," God would have spoken indistinctly both to Moses and Aaron and to the whole people. But since it is said to Moses and Aaron, "This month is for you the beginning of months," and then the command is given to convey to the people not this order, but that on the tenth day of the month they take a lamb in the houses of each family, it is clear that that was the beginning of the month not for the whole people, but only for Moses and Aaron, to whom the command is given.

For it is necessary to have renounced completely the creation and this world, in order to understand that one has become almost another person than what he was, so that he may be able to hear: "this month is for you the beginning of months, the first for you among the months of the year." That the perfect believer indeed has the beginning of another birth and becomes another person than what he was before, the Apostle teaches us when he says: "Our old man has been crucified with Christ," and again: "If we have died together with Christ, together with Him we shall also live"; of himself he says simply: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me."

These, though still living in the world, are able to hear that this is the first month and that it is for them the beginning of months. Let us reflect on the fact that the perfect believer, having become another person than what he was, receives from God promises and blessings. It is not Abram who receives the promises, but Abraham; and it is not Jacob who receives the blessings, but Israel. The first disciple of the Savior is Peter and not Simon; James and John, apostles, are sent forth having become Boanerges, which means "sons of thunder." If we observe attentively the whole of Scripture taken in its totality, we shall find in it that designations of this kind are noted because those who have been made perfect have other names: they are no longer what they were, but have become other persons than those they were previously.

And so it became for them the beginning of months. It is fitting to ask […] He could have said, "This is for you the beginning of the months and of the year," or, "This is the first month of the year for you"; instead, as though there were a distinction to be drawn, He says that the month is a beginning, and that it is the first. Strictly speaking, one speaks of the first only when there is nothing else that precedes; whereas the word "beginning" takes on its meaning in relation to the things of which it is the starting-point, even if they come at the end. What is first, this is also a beginning; but what is a beginning is not also first. Now then, since the beginning does not possess the absolute beginning, whereas the first does in fact possess the beginning as well, Scripture defines this month as the beginning of months and the first of the months of the year for them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But let us now proceed to what follows in the pericope: "Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel: On the tenth day of this month let each one take a lamb for every family, let each one take a lamb per house."

He does not say, "Let them sacrifice a lamb on the tenth of the month," but "Let them take a lamb." They are commanded to sacrifice this lamb on the fourteenth day of the month, and it is in this way that the Hebrews celebrate the Passover. They must, then, take the lamb in every house and in every family beginning from the tenth day, feed it still on the eleventh, the twelfth, and the thirteenth day, and finally consecrate it with a prayer: "This lamb is offered in sacrifice for this and this reason," without neglecting the eighteen names. On the fourteenth day, between the two evenings, the lamb is immolated, so that five are the days that intervene from the choosing of the lamb until its immolation. All of this takes place according to what is perceptible to the senses.

[…] Christ is the true lamb because He, who is second after the Father, is taken during the second monad, that is, I mean the number ten.

Just as, according to that prescription, the lamb is not immolated at the same time as its choosing on the tenth day of the month, but on the fourteenth, so that five days pass, in the same way whoever takes the true lamb, that is, Christ, does not sacrifice Him and feed upon Him at once, for five days pass after His choosing.

For whoever sets himself to listen to Christ and believes in Him, this one chooses Christ, but he does not sacrifice Him and feed upon Him before five days have passed. For, since the senses of man are five, unless Christ be present in each one of them, He could not be offered in sacrifice and, roasted, eaten. When He should make clay with His saliva, anoint our eyes with it, and make us see distinctly; when He should open the ears of the heart so that we might be able to hear with these ears; when we should smell His fragrance, recognizing that His name is the fragrance of ointment poured out; if by taste we should learn that the Lord is good, and by touch should handle Him, as John too says: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, seen with our own eyes, and our hands have touched, that is, the Logos of life," then we should be able both to sacrifice the lamb and to eat it, and so to come out of Egypt […].

That which was according to the typology of the mystical realities reveals also a spiritual understanding, of which we shall speak hereafter. The biblical saying too which affirms: "See, thou shalt make all things according to the typology of the tent that was shown thee on the mountain" gives to understand that the legislation is a shadow and a typology […].

We too, if the perfect and true light did not rise for us and we did not see that the higher part of our soul is well illumined, could not offer the true lamb in sacrifice and feed upon it.

[…] And indeed, when He tells the disciples to have the people arranged upon the grass, He gives this exhortation: "make them sit down in groups of guests," and thus prepares a banquet for them. For He serves them the food, after having gathered the multitude of those who eat His bread, not in undifferentiated groups but like with like. And the passage that immediately follows is akin, indeed identical, to the explanation already given.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"If they were too few in one house to be sufficient for eating a lamb, he shall take to himself his neighbor, the one nearest. And each shall measure, upon a lamb, what is sufficient for him, reckoning the number of persons. Let the lamb be for you perfect, male, and a year old. You shall take it from among lambs and kids" […].

Each one must associate to himself the neighbor nearest to his house, so that the guests may be sufficient for the lamb, that is, the number of persons is counted for one lamb.

"A perfect lamb, male, a year old." For Christ is perfect because He is lacking in nothing and, in Himself, is in nothing imperfect. Male refers to His strength and His courage.
