He is called "a year old" because a year indicates a perfect number, inasmuch as in the space of twelve months the sun returns to its seat.

Those who eat do not feed in the same way but differently, each according to his capacity, since not all can partake of Him as a lamb, but some, and perhaps the greater number, feed upon Him as a kid. The perfect, with great effort, now without sins, feed upon the lambs, because "Christ is the lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world," while those who still lie under the weight of sin will take from the kids, because, according to the Law, it is affirmed that a goat is offered for sins.

Perhaps the Gospel too knows the same distinction, when the Savior feeds those who followed Him with loaves that are not alike but different. For to some of them He breaks five of wheat, to others seven of barley, so that those who are not able to partake of the purer bread, the bread of wheat, of Christ, because they still live in a beast-like way and are not yet rational, may feed upon the bread of barley.

And because these are the more numerous, the loaves of barley are seven: this is the number of idleness, according to which the greater part of people live, sluggish and unoccupied until the rising of the day. The loaves of wheat are five, just as the senses are, which spiritual men do not allow to suffer hunger. These continually nourish the senses with spiritual bread, and therefore enjoy the possession of them, as it is also written in the Bible: "They shall neither hunger nor thirst, nor shall their eyes be overcome by sleep."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
To the advantage of these last salvation has come, thanks to His blood, the blood of Christ, the perfect lamb; for "as a lamb He was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb silent before its shearer, so He opens not His mouth. Who shall tell of His generation? For His life is taken away from the earth, and for the iniquities of His people He was led to death. And I will give the poor in exchange for His death and the rich in exchange for His tomb, because He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth." For His death was not caused by sin, but He Himself "bears our sins and is afflicted for us; by the blows He suffered we were healed."

As those of old were prefigured in a male lamb, so are we in a man like a lamb; as they were in a perfect lamb, so are we in the fullness of the will of the Father; as they were in a lamb of one year, so are we in the completion of the ages — for as a year is the completion of the months, so is He the completion of the Law and the Prophets —; as they were in a lamb without defect, so are we in a lamb without sin; as they were in the first month, so are we in the beginning of all creation, because "in Him all things were created"; as they were in the ten, so are we in the fullness of the monarchy. The "until the fourteenth day," of the second week, signifies the rest of two weeks, which went from the first creation, which is hidden, to the second, which is visible.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month. The whole assembly of the children of Israel shall slaughter it at sunset, and they shall take some of its blood and place it upon the two doorposts and upon the lintel of every dwelling in which they shall eat of the lambs, among them" […].

We are given the command to sacrifice the lamb at sunset because in the last hour the true lamb, our own, the Savior, came into the world […].

We sacrifice and anoint with the blood our own houses — by which I mean our bodies. This anointing is precisely our faith in Him, through which we believe that the power of the destroyer is brought to nothing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"The whole multitude of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening." The whole multitude of the children of the man who sees God, that is, of the power of God; at evening, that is, at the end of the times.

"And they shall anoint with its blood the lintels and both the doorposts of the doors." The lintels: that which is above the head of all the lambs; the doorposts of the doors: their edges, through which they enter and go out among them — some enter into them, others go out from them — in which are contained those who dwell among them.

The sacrifice takes place in Egypt, where Pharaoh reigns, a land turned toward the things of the earth and blinded by darkness, which is ignorance. Those live in the gross ignorance of their blindness who are subject to the lordship of him who is king in Egypt; and this man, who has fixed his dwelling there, is under the dominion of the deceptive opinion of his own arrogance, as it is written: "Who then is the Lord? I do not know Him. I will not let Israel go." This declaration accords with this other one: "I will set my throne above the clouds, I will ascend to heaven, I will be equal to the Most High."

Those who listen to the prophet fulfill this commandment, since they are as strangers in the presence of Pharaoh, inasmuch as they have fallen under his tyranny in a time of famine, in that they have received from their fathers the most ancient oath that their offspring would be strangers, as was said to father Abraham.

The offering of this sacrifice is made by them in ignorance, because "they do not know what they do" — and for this reason it is forgiven them — namely, that "it is expedient that one man should die for the people." It is not permitted that a prophet die outside Jerusalem, that is, outside the company of those who strive to live in peace and in justice.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Christians every day eat the flesh of the Lamb, that is, they daily take the flesh of the word. "For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed." And because the law of the Passover is such that it should be eaten in the evening, therefore the Lord suffered in the evening of the world, so that you may always eat of the flesh of the word, because you are always in the evening, until the morning comes. And if in this evening you are watchful and lead your life "in weeping and fastings" and in every labor of righteousness, you too will be able to say: "Weeping shall tarry until the evening, and joy until the morning." For you will rejoice in the morning, that is, in the age to come, if in this age you gather "the fruit of righteousness" in weeping and labor.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And we must eat the meat roasted with fire with unleavened bread. For the Word of God is not only flesh. He says, indeed, "I am the bread of life," and "This is the bread which comes down from heaven that one may eat of it and not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eat of this bread he shall live forever."36We must not, however, fail to remark that all food is loosely said to be bread, as it is written in the case of Moses in Deuteronomy: "He did not eat bread for forty days, and he did not drink water," instead of saying he partook of neither dry nor wet nourishment.
Now I have noted this because it is also said in the Gospel according to John, "And also the bread which I shall give for the life of the world is my flesh."
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.99-101

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Finally, the unleavened bread too is commanded to be eaten with bitter herbs; nor is it possible to reach the land of promise unless we pass through bitter things. For just as physicians insert certain bitter ingredients into their medicines with a view to the safety and health of the sick, so too, with a view to our safety, the physician of our souls has willed us to suffer the bitter things of this life in various trials, knowing that the end of this bitterness gains for our soul the sweetness of salvation; just as, on the contrary, the end of the sweetness which is in bodily pleasure, as the example of that rich man has taught, yields a bitter end in the hell of punishments.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But we eat the flesh of the lamb and the unleavened bread with bitter herbs either by being grieved with a godly grief because of repentance for our sins, a grief which produces in us a repentance unto salvation which brings no regret, or by seeking and being nurtured from the visions of the truth which we discover because of our trials.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.102

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: One must not therefore eat the flesh of the lamb raw, as the slaves of the letter do in the manner of animals which are irrational and quite savage. In relation to men who are truly rational through their desire to understand the spiritual aspects of the world, the former [slaves of the letter] share the company of wild beasts.We must strive, however, in transforming the rawness of Scripture into boiled food, not to transform what has been written into what is flaccid, watery and limp. This is what they do who "have itching ears and" turn them away "from the truth" and transform the anagogical meanings so far as they are concerned to the carelessness and wateriness of their manner of life.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.103-4

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Once we have been anointed — that is, once we have believed in Christ — then we are given the command to approach the food of Christ, as the words that follow clearly show: "They eat the flesh roasted with fire this night, and they feed upon the unleavened bread set on bitter herbs. You shall not eat of a lamb raw or boiled in water, but roasted with fire, the head with the feet and the entrails."

[…] If Christ is the lamb, and if Christ is the Logos, what is the flesh of the divine words if not the divine Scriptures? It is upon these very Scriptures that we ought fittingly to feed, when they are neither raw nor boiled. If some make a superficial use of these words, they would be feeding upon the flesh of the Savior raw; and, precisely because they partake of His flesh raw, they would procure for themselves not life but death, inasmuch as they eat of His flesh like wild beasts and not like men — for "the letter kills, but the spirit gives life," as the Apostle teaches. If the Spirit is granted to us as a gift by God, "God is a consuming fire," and the Spirit Himself is fire. And so the Apostle, fully persuaded of this, exhorts us to be "fervently kindled with the Spirit."

Rightly is the Holy Spirit called fire; and we, receiving Him, duly enter into familiarity with the flesh of Christ — by which I mean the divine Scriptures — so that, once we have cooked them at the fire of the Spirit, we may feed upon them, precisely because they have been roasted with this fire. For the words of Scripture are so transformed by this fire that we shall behold the sweetness of their nourishment, without cooking them together with some inferior water.

In conclusion, we are commanded not to cook the flesh of the Savior — that is, the words of the Scriptures — in such water, not to mingle with these words some other matter that would soak them and soften them through boiling. On the contrary, we are commanded to partake of them only after they have been cooked with fire — that is, with the divine Spirit — and not to feed upon them when they are raw or boiled with water. The Jews partake of them when they are raw, because they rest upon the mere literal interpretation of the Scriptures. For if, through the Spirit, they came to know wherein the true circumcision consists, and — would that it were so! — also the true meaning of the Sabbath, and "if they work while it is day, before the night comes, when no one can any longer work," only then would they eat the Scripture cooked with fire by the Spirit […].

Some partake of His head, others of the hands, others of the breast, some of the entrails, others of the thighs, and some even of the feet, where there is not much flesh, because each one shares in the lamb according to his own capacity. And thus we are able to take a fitting portion of the true lamb, if we partake of the divine Logos. There are those who partake of the head, and preferably of each part of the head — of the ears, for example, so that "having ears they may hear" His words; those who taste of the eyes will see distinctly, "so that their feet do not stumble"; those who feed upon the hands are the industrious, whose hands are neither slack nor cramped in giving, cleaving tenaciously to the teaching of the Lord before His wrath blazes forth.

Others, leaning upon the breast of the Lord, will through this food come to know also who are the betrayers of Christ. Those who feed upon the entrails will behold even "the depths of God"; for the entrails are furnished with intricate folds and set in motion the complexity of the vital functions for the benefit of the body. Such likewise is the one who has been initiated into the mysteries — or rather, he will behold the profound meaning of the Incarnation, hidden and as it were situated in the midst, if we take the head to be the divinity. Those who partake of the thighs keep guard over their flesh, following wherever Christ goes. Those who share in the feet, without any hesitation, run with zeal "toward the prize of the heavenly calling of Christ." The head might also be faith, and the feet the works, without which faith is dead.

The food of those who eat the Passover is varied, and yet all share the same purpose: he who feeds upon the head shares it with the one who eats the feet, because "the head cannot say to the feet: I have no need of you." Many are the parts that are eaten, but the body of Christ is one alone. Yet, so far as is possible, let us strive to preserve the harmony of the parts, that we may never be accused of rending Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us therefore compare the divine Scripture itself with itself, and let us follow the path of solution which it shall have opened to us. For we find in the sacrifice of the Passover, which is commanded to be immolated "in the evening", a command similarly given that "nothing remain of the flesh until the morning". This is not idle, that the divine word does not wish us to eat yesterday's flesh, but always fresh and new — those especially who immolate to God the sacrifice of the Passover or "the sacrifice of praise"; it commands them to eat new and fresh flesh of that very day, and forbids yesterday's.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"You shall not leave any part of the lamb until morning, nor shall you break a bone of it: what remains you shall burn in the morning."

Just as the mysteries of the Passover celebrated in the Old Testament have been done away with by the truth of the New Testament, so the mysteries of the New, which we are to celebrate in like manner, will not be necessary in the resurrection; for this is the meaning of the "morning," when nothing shall be left over and whatever remains shall be burned […].

[…] "Imperfectly we know, imperfectly we prophesy," as the Apostle himself teaches, "but when perfection comes, that which is imperfect shall be abolished" — which corresponds to the burning up completely in the morning. For the night signifies the present world, and the day the world to come. This too the Apostle attests when he says: "The night is far advanced, the day is at hand."

Truly few are they who, possessing senses long exercised "to distinguish the beautiful from the evil," able to nourish themselves on solid food, will also be able to leave nothing of the flesh until morning, according to the Scripture — perhaps one in a thousand, or two out of ten thousand; and among these were the blessed apostles.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
He who has crossed beyond the borders set by God on account of the disobedience in Adam is the Lord, He who has blunted the sting of death and cast down its power, and has given to the spirits imprisoned in Hades the possibility of leaping forth outside, through the proclamation of the good news; in other terms, He has offered a way of ascent to heaven through His ascension, when gates and portals were lifted up at His entrance: "Princes, lift up your portals, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter in."

And since the command was heard a second time by the powers that guarded the gates, at their reply, "Who is He?", they heard this answer: "The Lord strong and mighty in battle, the Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory" — Lord of the glory of the Father, in whom the Father is glorified. He "reconciled the world to Himself, not reckoning the transgressions against Him, canceling the bond that was against Him, which was hostile to Him, and He took it out of the way." This was accomplished in Christ when He says: "It was God reconciling the world to Himself in Christ." And the reconciliation consists in this: "Like an innocent lamb led to the sacrifice, without knowing it."

For they contrived a wicked plan against Him, knowing that "it is necessary that the Son of Man suffer many sufferings, die, and on the third day rise again." And since the disciples, on hearing it, were in a certain way grieved, He added: "That I go away comes about for your benefit: if the grain of wheat does not die, it remains alone, but if it dies, it bears much fruit" — words that correspond to these others: "Behold, I and the children whom God has given Me." Since, then, "the children have blood and flesh in common, He likewise was associated with them, in order to reduce to nothing, through His death, him who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and to set free those who, through fear of death, were subject to slavery all their life long."

The true lamb, that is, Christ, has freed us from the slavery of the ruler of the darkness of this world — the lamb of whom the lamb slaughtered in Egypt was the type, in that time the savior of the Hebrews from the ancient dominion of the prince of Egypt, defined as darkness, the reckless Pharaoh, who scatters the works accomplished in the light of virtue, by reason of his mighty domination — that is, the manner of thinking of those who live in the darkness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Before undertaking a word-by-word explanation of the Passover, it is fitting to offer a few brief remarks on the simple term "Passover." For most of the brethren, perhaps all of them, accept an etymology of the word "Passover" according to which the feast would take its name of "Passover" from the passion of the Savior.

In truth, the feast here set before us is properly named in Hebrew not "Passover" but "phas," of which the translation is "passage" (for the three letters of "phas," together with the more forceful rough breathing among the Hebrews, make up the name of this feast). Since, then, it was on the occasion of this feast that the people of Israel came out of Egypt, it is consequently called "phas," that is, "passage."

Because it is not possible to pronounce the Hebrew word with Greek phonetics — the Greeks being unable to say "phas" with the reinforcement of the rough breathing, which is harder in Hebrew — the term was Hellenized. Among the prophets it is said "phasek," and then, more completely Hellenized, it came to be called "Pascha."

If, then, one of our own should meet with Hebrews and quite incautiously tell them that the etymology of "Passover" derives from the passion of the Savior, he would be covered with ridicule by them, since he would be wholly in the dark as to the meaning of the term — granted that the perfect interpret the word "Passover" exactly as the Hebrews do.

What has been said so far about the word simply in itself is already sufficient for our instruction concerning the meaning of the term "phas" and for our edification, so that we do not hastily employ the Hebrew tongue without first knowing the Hebrew meaning of the words. Now we shall pass to the explanation of the text itself, it being established that the meaning of "Passover" is passage.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
By the following rules the Scripture prescribes also that those who eat the Passover be clothed in such a manner: "Thus shall you eat the Passover: your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands. And you shall eat the meal in haste. It is the Passover of the Lord."

We shall be instructed by other words of Scripture as to why the loins are to be girded. The Apostle, in his explanation of the offspring that comes from the loins of Abraham, who was blessed by Melchizedek, says: "And Levi, who himself receives tithes, paid the tithe, because he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek went to meet him." In another passage he affirms: "though he came from the loins of Abraham"; and in the book of Job it is said, concerning the devil: "His strength is in his loins and in the navel of his belly."

For the devil has power to harass and to lay men low above all by force of this appetite, since the loin is to be interpreted as the male sexual organ and, by a decent expression, the navel of the belly as the female, so that it may appear plainly that it is chiefly through this urge that the devil holds dominion over both male and female.

Once the Scripture has indicated that the loins stand for sexual relations, we are on the right path to understand why, when it speaks of the Passover, it requires that we eat it with our loins girded, gathered together by families. We are given the command, when we eat the Passover, to be pure from sexual acts — since this is the meaning of the girdle about the loins — for it teaches us to place a covering around the organ that produces the seminal fluid, and it orders us to restrain the stirrings of sexual union, when we partake of the flesh of Christ […].

He who prepares himself for the contest, and observes those who submit to continence for the sake of a perishable combat in order to win a temporary victory, aspires by his own exertion to gain an incorruptible victory. If, then, a man girds his loins in this manner, he will be able to leave no remnant of the flesh until morning. Perhaps with this same intention John the Baptist too, as a perfect man, wore "a girdle of leather about his loins," because he wished to make evident that he had mortified every sexual appetite of his: for the leather signifies mortality, since mortality had wholly penetrated his nature. He who eats the Passover and is married will gird his own loins. "Blessed are those who, though having a wife, live as though they had none," says the Apostle.

The Scripture says that those who eat the Passover are to keep their sandals on, a directive that to some might seem to contradict the oracle given to Moses. For when Moses was walking upon holy ground, he was given the command to take off his shoes. How is it, then, that although the Passover too is holy, those who eat of it are prescribed to put on their sandals? But these passages of Scripture are not in opposition, for they express different ideas.

When a man walks upon holy ground, he receives the command to have nothing with him that is in a condition of death, because he had nothing of himself in this state to conceal; whereas when he eats the Passover, he is given the command to eat in haste so as to be ready, as the Apostle also teaches when he says: "Having your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel." So that, when the day comes, he may go out without hindrance, he is given the command to have his sandals already on his feet; and in this precept he shows a meaning still more evident concerning the condition of the flesh at the resurrection, for it comes out of Egypt together with us: "For we must mortify the members that are upon the earth — fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry" and what follows, and so come out of Egypt.

To see the likeness between the Law and the Gospel, let us compare what is said according to the Law with what is said according to the Gospel. Moses, who prepares to lead the people out of Egypt in order to bring them into the holy land in obedience to the command of God, receives the order to have no sandals; while to the apostles sent to lead out of the spiritual Egypt the people coming from the pagan nations, the command is given "to carry no staff on the road, nor wallet, nor to have sandals on their feet."

Thus, as there those who eat the Passover in haste are commanded to have their sandals on their feet, so likewise in the Gospel to those who are now able to sacrifice and eat the Passover, as has been explained, the Apostle commands that, "having girded their loins with truth and put on the breastplate of righteousness and taken the helmet of salvation," they have their sandals on their feet in readiness for the Gospel, and that they hold also the staff in their hands because they share in discipline, since the staff is precisely the symbol of discipline. For we have read in the book of Proverbs that "he who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him corrects him with care."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Although they were under the Law, they did not carry out its prescriptions, but, acting against the Law, they turned aside from the salvation that comes by the natural law […] Rather, those have consented to celebrate the Passover according to the Law who are zealous for the faith and hold in check the thoughts of the body, who with sandals ready for the preparation of a journey that brings good, and with staves in their hands, henceforth pass their life in fear, which is for them salvation: "If you do not eat My flesh and drink My blood, you have no part with Me."

This the true lamb says, the lamb who truly "takes away the sin of the world" and who, alone, dies for the salvation of the whole people, according to the high priest of that year, who spoke without knowing what he was saying. For the sacrifice was made ready for the salvation of those who dwell as strangers because of their childish love for the earth, which by feeding them had become their nurse.

Having this nurse, they treated her as if she were their mother, since they did not know the true one, reared bodily in the licentiousness of the flesh in this transient world, made the sweeter by the pleasure they tasted, while ignorance of their paternal world held them under the yoke. These are called Hebrews. And so it is that Scripture declares: "The God of the Hebrews has called us." At the passage of the passing world into the abiding aeon of the Father, the conversion of the sons comes about through the perfect fulfillment of the word "Passover," which means precisely passage. For they pass through the naming of the mystery and take part in it, and thus they obtain salvation for themselves, inasmuch as they are not destroyed together with the firstborn sons of the Egyptians, "from Pharaoh who sits upon his throne, to the maidservant who is beside the mill" — that is, those who live, in ignorance, in the pride stirred up by riches and power, and do not know Him who "raises up rulers out of the dung and sets them upon royal thrones."

They were held in subjection in their ignorance, shut within their own borders, one by fate, another by chance, another by the tyranny of the prince, since, on account of food conformed to that of the time of their infancy, they had been reared forgetful of their natural mother and of their true Father, who said: "I have set My gaze upon the sufferings of My people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry, and I have come down to deliver them from the taskmasters of the works, to deliver them from the slavery inflicted by Pharaoh and from the hand of the Egyptians, to lead them toward the land of the fathers, which I swore to Abraham and to Isaac to give them for an inheritance" — which He accomplished in the fullness of the times when He came to remove sin by means of His flesh, doing away with the enmity.

By His coming He "brought the glad tidings to us who were far off and to those who were near," ransoming us from the dominion of darkness and transferring us into His light. In keeping with this, He has brought us out of Egypt and away from its princes, whom He nailed to the cross, when He made of them a public spectacle, in His triumph. Therefore: "Behold, I come — it is written in the scroll of the book concerning Me — O God, to do Thy will," having first said: "Sacrifice and offering Thou hast not willed, but a body Thou hast prepared for Me; Thou hast not been pleased with holocaust for sin." Through this offering of Himself is obtained the purification of the world gone astray, until it shall come to its conversion. He "makes peace with all things through the blood of His cross," having done away with the enmity, which is the wrath for the destruction of the disobedient.

For if these had disposed themselves with fervor to obey the legislation, according to what has been said, celebrating it with a bunch of hyssop — that is, with the fragrance of thoughts directed toward conversion — the true Passover would have been accomplished for them, Christ, who says: "I sanctify Myself for these, and not for these only, but for all who believe in Me." It was not in faith that they set themselves to celebrate this rite, but in unbelief, without knowing the Scriptures that the prophets had announced: "If you have not believed, you will not understand. I have not come to do My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me," and His will consisted in being delivered up on behalf of all who believe. Had those been zealous to lead Him to the sacrifice for their own sanctification, the commandment would have been fulfilled for them: "Eat the lamb in haste; it is the Passover of the Lord" — that is, it is the passage of the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Observe that he has named a certain power of the soul feet, with which we as it were make our way, walking toward him who said "I am the way", and which must be shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace. And I think that the symbols of these sandals are the "sandals" recorded in Exodus, which those who ate the Passover and were ready for the journey were required to have. For thus he says, "You shall eat it: your loins girded and your sandals on your feet and your staffs in your hands, and you shall eat it with haste; it is the Lord's Passover". For it belongs to readiness both to eat "with haste" and to eat shod, so that, being strengthened by the food, they may be able to journey.

Therefore let him who is journeying be shod, but let him who has arrived at the holy land unloose his sandals; for "Loose", he says, "the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground".

For this reason let him who is not an apostle be shod as to the feet in readiness of the gospel of peace; but let the apostle no longer "take up sandals for the road", since he has already been perfected and is in the place where, both standing and walking, he is in "holy ground", living in Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We must also inquire who that being was of whom it is said in Exodus that he wished to kill Moses because he was setting out for Egypt. And afterwards, who is it that is called the "destroying angel"? And who also is he who in Leviticus is described as Apopompeus, that is, the Averter, of whom the Scripture speaks thus: "One lot for the Lord, and one lot for Apopompeus"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And who else could be the destroyer in Exodus, which Moses wrote, except the one who is the cause of destruction to those who obey him and who do not resist and struggle against his wickedness?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth," the Apostle Paul, handed down to the Church which he gathered from among the Gentiles how it ought to attend to the books of the Law, which it had received from others and which had formerly been unknown to it and altogether foreign, lest, in taking up institutions foreign to it and being ignorant of the rule of those institutions, it should tremble amid an alien instrument. Therefore he himself, in a number of passages, hands down examples of the understanding, so that we too may observe things similar in the rest, lest perchance, on account of the likeness of the reading and of the instrument of the Jews, we should believe that we have been made their disciples. This, then, is what he wishes to distinguish between the disciples of Christ and the disciples of the synagogue: that the Law which they, by understanding it badly, did not receive Christ, we, by understanding it spiritually, may show to have been rightly given for the instruction of the Church. The Jews, then, understand only this: that "the children of Israel departed" from Egypt, and that their first departure was "from Rameses," and that departing thence they came "to Succoth," and that "departing from Succoth" they came "to Othon" by Epauleum near the sea; then, further, that there the cloud went before them and that "the rock" followed, from which they drank water, and that they also passed through the Red Sea and came into the desert of Sinai. But let us see what rule of understanding concerning these things Paul the Apostle has handed down to us. Writing to the Corinthians, he says in a certain place thus: "For we know that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ." You see how much Paul's tradition differs from the historical reading: what the Jews think a crossing of the sea, Paul calls baptism; what they reckon a cloud, Paul sets down as the Holy Spirit; and he wishes that to be understood as like this which the Lord commanded in the Gospels, saying: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdoms of heaven." And again the manna, which the Jews reckon food for the belly and satiety for the gullet, Paul names "spiritual food." And not only Paul, but the Lord Himself in the Gospel says concerning the same thing: "your fathers ate manna in the desert, and they died. But whoever shall eat of the bread which I give him shall not die for ever." And after this He says: "I am the bread which came down from heaven." Then, further, concerning "the rock that followed" Paul openly declares and says: "and the rock was Christ." What, then, must we do, who have received from Paul, the teacher of the Church, institutions of understanding of this kind? Does it not seem just that we should keep the rule of this kind handed down to us by a like example in the rest? Or shall we, as certain people wish, forsaking these things which so great and such an Apostle handed down, turn back again to "Jewish fables"? For my part, if I should expound these things otherwise than as they seem to Paul, I think this is to give a hand to the enemies of Christ, and this is what the prophet says: "Woe to him who gives his neighbor to drink with turbulent overthrow!" Having therefore received from the blessed Apostle Paul the seeds of spiritual understanding, let us cultivate them, insofar as the Lord shall deign to enlighten us through your prayers.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Raising themselves up," it says, "the children of Israel came from Rameses to Succoth, and departing from Succoth they came to Othon." If there is anyone who is preparing to depart from Egypt, if there is anyone who desires to leave behind the dark deeds of this world and the darkness of errors, first of all he must depart "from Rameses." Now "Rameses" is interpreted the commotion of the moth. If, therefore, you wish to come to this, that the Lord may be your leader and go before you "in the pillar of the cloud" and that the rock may follow you, which may furnish you "spiritual food" and no less "spiritual drink," depart and go out "from Rameses," "and do not lay up treasure there, where the moth destroys and where thieves dig through and steal." This is what the Lord openly says in the Gospels: "if you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." This, then, is to depart "from Rameses" and to follow Christ. But let us see what also is the place of encampment to which one comes "from Rameses." "They came," it says, "to Succoth." The interpreters of names hand down that "Succoth" is understood among the Hebrews as tabernacles. When, therefore, forsaking Egypt, you have shaken off from yourself the moths of all corruption and have cast away the incitements of vices, you will dwell in tabernacles. For we dwell in tabernacles, out of which "we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon." And the dwelling in tabernacles indicates that he who hastens to God is unencumbered and without any impediments.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We partake of the flesh of Christ, that is, of the divine Scriptures, […] we strive to follow in the footsteps of the true lamb, for the Apostle declares that Christ is the lamb of our Passover when he says: "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed." His flesh, His bones, and His blood, as has already been shown, are the divine Scriptures: if we eat them, we possess Christ, inasmuch as His bones have become words, and the thoughts that arise from the words, flesh. If we approach them as is fitting, we contemplate what is to come "in an enigma and as through a mirror," for His blood is the evangelical faith of the new covenant, as the Apostle testifies when he says: "profaning the blood of the covenant." Anointed with this blood, that is, with faith, we shall escape the destroyer.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The males which were holy from the fact that they had opened their mother's womb were offered before the altar of the Lord: "every male," it says, "that opens the womb", sounds something sacred. For whatever male you may say has been poured forth from the womb, he does not open his mother's womb as the Lord Jesus does, because in all women it is not the birth of the infant, but the intercourse of the man, that unlocks the womb. But the womb of the Lord's mother was unlocked at that time at which the birth also was brought forth, because before the birth of Christ no male at all touched that holy womb, to be venerated with all reverence.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But one must not stand still even in this; the departure must be pressed on, the camp must be moved even "from Succoth," and one must hasten to come "to Othon." Now they say that "Othon" is turned into our language as signs to them. And rightly so, for here you will hear it said that: "God went before them, by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire"; you do not find this done at Rameses nor at Succoth, which are called the second camp for those departing, but it is the third camp in which divine signs come to pass. Recall what was read above, when Moses said to Pharaoh: "we will go a journey of three days into the desert, and we will sacrifice to the Lord our God." This, then, was the three days' space to which Moses hastened and which Pharaoh opposed; for he said: "do not go farther." Pharaoh did not permit the children of Israel to arrive at the place of signs, he did not permit them to advance so far as to be able to enjoy the mysteries of the third day. For hear what the prophet says: "God will raise us up after two days, and on the third day we shall rise again and shall live in his sight." The first day for us is the passion of the Savior, and the second, on which he descended into hell, but the third is the day of the resurrection. And therefore on the third day "God went before them, by day in a pillar of cloud, by night in a pillar of fire." But if, according to those things which we said above, the Apostle rightly teaches us that the mysteries of baptism are contained in these words, it is necessary that "those who are baptized in Christ should be baptized in his death, and be buried together with him," and rise again with him on the third day from the dead, whom also, according to that which the Apostle says: "he raised up together with himself, and made to sit together in the heavenly places." When, therefore, the mystery of the third day has been received by you, God will begin to lead you forth and Himself to show you the way of salvation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what is said to Moses after these things, what way is enjoined to be chosen. "From Othon," it says, "turn back and make your journey between Epauleum and Magdolum, which is over against Beelsephon." Now these are interpreted thus: "Epauleum" indeed a winding ascent, "Magdolum" a tower, "Beelsephon" the ascent of a watchtower, or having a watchtower. You perhaps believed that the way which God shows was level and soft and had absolutely no difficulty or labor: it is an ascent, and a winding ascent. For the way by which one strives toward the virtues is not downhill, but one ascends, and ascends narrowly and with difficulty. Hear also the Lord in the Gospel saying how "strait and narrow is the way that leads to life." See, then, how greatly the Gospel agrees with the Law. In the Law the way of virtue is shown to be a winding ascent; in the Gospels it is called "the strait and narrow way that leads to life." Cannot even the blind openly see this, that one and the same Spirit wrote the Law and the Gospels? It is, then, a journey which they travel, a winding ascent and the ascent of a watchtower, or having a watchtower; the ascent pertains to deeds, the watchtower to faith. He shows, therefore, that both in deeds and in faith there is much difficulty and much labor. For many temptations arise, many stumbling-blocks for those who wish to do the things that are of God. Then, further, in faith you will find many winding things, very many questions, many objections of heretics, many contradictions of unbelievers. This journey, then, must be made by those who follow God; but there is also a tower on this journey. What is that tower? That one, surely, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: "which of you, wishing to build a tower, will not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has the means to complete it?" This, then, is the tower, the steep and lofty seat of the virtues. But see what Pharaoh says, beholding these things: 'they are wandering astray,' he says, 'these people.' In Pharaoh's judgment, he who follows God is said to wander astray; because, as we said, the way of wisdom is winding, having many bends, many difficulties, very many turnings. In short, when you confess one God, and by the same confession affirm the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit to be one God, how winding, how difficult, how inextricable this seems to be to unbelievers! Then, further, when you say that "the Lord of majesty" was crucified and that he is the Son of Man "who came down from heaven," how winding these things seem and how difficult! He who hears, if he does not hear with faith, says that these people are wandering astray; but be you fixed and do not doubt concerning faith of this kind, knowing that God has shown you this way of faith. For He Himself said: "taking up the camp from Othon, pitch it between Epauleum and Magdolum over against Beelsephon." Fleeing therefore from Egypt, you come to these places, you come to these ascents of works and of faith, you come to the building of the tower, you come also to the sea, and the waves meet you. For the journey of life is not made without the waves of temptations; as the Apostle also says: "all who wish to live piously in Christ shall suffer persecution." But Job likewise declares that: "our life upon the earth is a temptation." This, then, is to have come to the sea.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And you too, therefore, if you withdraw from the Egyptians and flee from the power of demons, see how great the helps are that are divinely prepared for you, see how great the helpers are whom you employ. Only let it be that you remain strong in faith, and that neither the cavalry and the terror of the chariots of the Egyptians strike you with dread, nor that you cry out against the Law of God, against Moses, and say, as certain of them said: "as though there were no graves in Egypt, so you have led us out, that we might die in this desert. It were better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this desert." These are the words of a soul fainting in temptation. But who is so blessed that he so disburdens himself of the weight of temptations that no thought of uncertainty creeps into his mind? See what is said by the Lord to that great foundation of the Church and most solid rock, upon which Christ founded the Church: "O you of little faith," He says, "why did you doubt?" Yet nevertheless, in that they say: "it were better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness," these are the words of temptation and of frailty; otherwise it is false; for it is far better "to die in the wilderness" than "to serve the Egyptians." For he who dies in the wilderness, by this very fact that he has been separated from the Egyptians and has departed from "the rulers of the darkness" and from the power of Satan, has had some advance, even if he was not able to arrive at completeness. For it is better to die on the way while seeking the perfect life than not even to set out to seek perfection. Whence also the opinion of those seems to be mistaken who, while they set forth the way of virtue as too steep, and while they enumerate its many difficulties and many dangers and falls, judge that it is not even to be entered upon or begun. But it is much better for me even to die on this journey, if so it must be, than, remaining among the Egyptians, to be slain and overwhelmed by the salt and bitter waves.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if the mental voice of those who pray should not be extremely loud, though it is not weak, and should they not raise a cry and shout, God still hears those who pray thus. For it is he who says to Moses, "Why do you cry out to me?" when he had not cried out audibly (for this is not recorded in Exodus), but through prayer he had cried out loudly in that voice which is heard by God alone.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.101

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But meanwhile Moses cries out to the Lord. How does he cry out? No voice of his crying is heard, and yet God says to him: "why do you cry out to me?" I would like to know how the saints cry out to God without a voice. The Apostle teaches that: "God gave the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father!" And he adds: "the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings." And again: "but he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he asks for the saints according to God." Thus, then, when the Holy Spirit intercedes with God, through the silence of the saints a cry is heard.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if, following Moses—that is, the Law of God—you make this journey, the Egyptian indeed pursues and hounds you, but see what happens: "the angel of the Lord," it says, "who went before the camp of Israel, raised himself up and went behind them. And the pillar of cloud also lifted itself from before their face, and stood behind them, and entered between the camp of the Egyptians and of the Israelites." This "pillar of cloud" is made a wall for the people of God, but upon the Egyptians it imposes obscurity and darkness. For the pillar of fire is not transferred to the Egyptians, that they may see the light, but they remain in darkness, because "they loved darkness rather than light."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: How troublesome a trial it is to pass through the midst of the sea, to see the waves rising up in a heap, to hear the roar and crash of the raging billows; but nevertheless, if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, the waters will become for you a wall on the right hand and on the left, and you will find a path through dry ground in the midst of the sea. But that heavenly journey too, which we have said the soul makes, may perhaps have some waters as well; it may be that there too waves are found; for there is a certain portion of waters above the heaven and a certain portion beneath the heaven, and we for the present endure the waves and billows of these waters that are beneath the heaven.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And what after this? Moses is commanded to strike the sea with his rod, so that it may split apart and give way to the people of God as they enter, and so that the obedient service of the elements may serve the divine will, and that the waters, which were feared, being made "a wall on the right hand and on the left" for the servants of God, may not only know no ruin, but may even present a defense. The wave, therefore, is forced into a heap, and the surge, checked upon itself, is curved. The liquid takes on solidity, and the floor of the sea is dried into dust. Understand the goodness of God the Creator; if you obey His will, if you follow His Law, He compels the very elements to serve you even against their own nature. I have heard it handed down by the elders that in that parting of the sea individual divisions of the waters were made for each and every tribe of the children of Israel, and that a way was opened in the sea proper to each tribe, and that this is shown from that which is written in the Psalms: "who divided the Red Sea into divisions." By which it is taught that many divisions were made, not one. But also by that which is said: "there is Benjamin the younger in amazement, the princes of Judah their leaders, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali," no less does a proper entrance seem to be enumerated for each tribe. These things, observed by the elders in the divine Scriptures, I have thought it a religious duty not to pass over in silence. What, then, are we taught through these things? We have already said above what the Apostle's meaning is in these matters. This he names "a baptism accomplished in Moses in the cloud and in the sea," so that you too, who are baptized in Christ, in water and in the Holy Spirit, may know that the Egyptians indeed pursue after you and wish to recall you to their servitude—namely "the rulers" of this "world" and the "spiritual wickednesses," to which formerly you were enslaved. These indeed try to pursue, but you go down into the water and come out unharmed, and, the filth of your sins being washed away, you ascend "a new man" ready "to sing a new song." But the Egyptians, pursuing after you, are drowned in the abyss, even though they seem to beg Jesus not to send them meanwhile into the abyss.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But we can also derive another understanding from these things. If you flee Egypt, if you leave the darkness of ignorance and follow the Law of God, Moses, and the sea meets you, and the wave of those who contradict runs against you, do you strike the struggling waves with the rod of Moses—that is, with the word of the Law and the vigilance of the Scriptures—and by disputing open for yourself a way through the adversaries; the waves will give way at once, and the conquered surges will yield place to the victors, and while those who a little before were opposing you marvel and are astonished and are fixed in stupor, you, along the lawful lines of disputations, will cut the straight way of faith and will make such progress by the word of teaching that your hearers, whom you have instructed by the rod of the Law, may themselves now rise up against the Egyptians like the waves of the sea, and not only assail them, but also overcome and extinguish them. For he extinguishes the Egyptian who does not do "the works of darkness"; he extinguishes the Egyptian who lives not carnally but spiritually; he extinguishes the Egyptian who either drives away from his heart filthy and impure thoughts or does not receive them at all, as the Apostle also says: "taking up the shield of faith, that we may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one." In this way, then, we can even today "see the Egyptians dead and lying on the shore," and their chariots and horses submerged. We can even see Pharaoh himself submerged, if we live with such faith that "God may crush Satan under our feet swiftly" through Jesus Christ our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: As a perfect bride, therefore, of a perfect man, she has received the words of perfect doctrine. The first song, then, Moses and the children of Israel sang to God when they saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore, and when they saw the strong hand and the exalted arm of the Lord, and they believed God and his servant Moses. Then they sang, saying: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified." But I judge that no one can come to that perfect and mystical song, and to that perfection of the bride which is contained in this Scripture, unless he first walk through the dry ground in the midst of the sea … And by Moses I mean the Law and the Gospels and all the divine Scriptures; for then he will rightly sing and say: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified."
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We read that many songs were made in the divine Scriptures, yet the first of them all is this song, which the people of God sang after their victory, when the Egyptians and Pharaoh had been drowned. For it is the custom of the saints, whenever an adversary is conquered, to offer God a hymn of thanksgiving, as those who know that the victory was won not by their own power but by the grace of God. And as they sing the hymn, they take up timbrels also in their hands, as is related of Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron. And you too, therefore, if you cross the Red Sea, if you see the Egyptians drowned and Pharaoh extinguished and cast down into the depth of the abyss, you can sing a hymn to God, you can send forth the voice of thanksgiving and say: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified; the horse and the rider he has cast into the sea." But you will say these things better and more worthily if you have a timbrel in your hand — that is, if you have "crucified your flesh with its vices and desires," and if you have "mortified your members which are upon the earth." And yet let us see what he says: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified"; as though it were not enough to say "he has been glorified," so he added "he has been gloriously glorified." For my part, so far as I can conjecture, it seems to me that to be glorified is one thing, and to be gloriously glorified is another. For my Lord Jesus Christ, when he took flesh from the Virgin for our salvation, was indeed glorified, because "he came to seek what had perished," yet he was not "gloriously glorified." For it is said of him: "We saw him, and he had no form nor beauty, and his countenance was ignoble beyond the sons of men." He was glorified also when he came to the cross and endured death. Do you wish to know that he was glorified? He himself said: "Father, the hour has come, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you." The passion of the cross, then, was also a glory to him; but this glory was not glorious, but lowly. Finally it is said of him: "He humbled himself even unto death, even the death of the cross," concerning which too the prophet had foretold: "Let us condemn him with a most shameful death." And Isaiah also says of him: "In his humiliation his judgment was taken away." In all these things, therefore, the Lord was glorified, but, so to speak, humbly, not "gloriously glorified." But because "it behooved Christ to suffer these things and so to enter into his glory," "when he shall come in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels," "when he shall come in his majesty" "to judge the earth," when he shall also "slay the true Pharaoh, that is, the devil, with the spirit of his mouth," when therefore he shall shine forth in "the majesty of his Father" and, after the coming in humility, shall show us a second coming in glory — then not only is the Lord glorified, but he is also "gloriously glorified," when "all so honor the Son as they honor the Father."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The horse and the rider he has cast into the sea; he has become for me a helper and protector unto salvation." The men who pursue us are horses, and, so to speak, all who are born in the flesh are figuratively horses. But these have their riders. There are horses which the Lord mounts, and they go about the whole earth, concerning which it is said: "And your cavalry is salvation." But there are horses which have as their riders the devil and his angels. Judas was a horse, but so long as he had the Lord as his rider, he belonged to the cavalry of salvation. For along with the other Apostles he was sent and bestowed salvation on the sick and health on the ailing; but when he laid himself down beneath the devil — for "after the morsel Satan entered into him" — Satan became his rider, and, led by his reins, he began to ride against our Lord and Savior. All, therefore, who persecute the saints are neighing horses, but they have riders by whom they are driven, the evil angels, and for that reason they are fierce. If, therefore, you should ever see your persecutor raging too savagely, know that he is being goaded by his rider the demon, and for that reason he is savage, for that reason he is truculent. The Lord, therefore, "has cast the horse and the rider into the sea, and he has become for me unto salvation."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "This is my God, and I will honor him; the God of my father, and I will exalt him." This one, then, is both "my" "God" and the God "of my father." Our Father, who made us and begot us, is Christ, and he himself says: "I go to my Father and your Father, my God and your God." If, therefore, I recognize that God is "my" "God," I will glorify him; but if I also recognize this, in what way he is the "God" of Christ "my father," I will exalt him: for it is a loftier understanding, in what way Christ, in order to bind fast and safeguard the truth of the one God, calls him his God whom by nature he calls Father.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The Lord who crushes wars, the Lord is his name." I would not have you think that the Lord "crushes" only visible battles, but he "crushes" also those which are for us "not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and against the rulers of the darkness of this world." For "the Lord is his name": and there is no creature of which he is not Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The chariots of Pharaoh and his army he has cast into the sea, the chosen riders, the three officers he has sunk in the Red Sea." Pharaoh, as one more powerful in wickedness and holding the kingdom of iniquity, drives "chariots." It is not enough for him to mount one horse; he drives many at once, he compels many at once with the blows of the twisted lash. Whomever you see more shameful in luxury, more savage in cruelty, more foul in avarice, more disgraceful in impiety, know that these belong to the chariots of Pharaoh; upon these he sits, these he yokes to his chariot, on these he is borne and flies about, and through the open fields of crimes he drives them with loosened reins. There are others, "chosen riders" — chosen, without doubt, for wickedness. But we have already spoken above about the riders; now let us also see who the "three officers" are. It seems to me that "three officers" are so called because there is a threefold way of sinning for men; for one sins either in deed or in word or in thought. And therefore "three officers" are said to be assigned to each and every one, who besiege these three ways of sinning within us and are always on the watch and lie in ambush, so that the one may draw an evil word out of the wretched man, or another may wring out an unjust deed, or another may snatch up a wicked thought. Finally, where the seed of the word of God falls and perishes, the place is described as threefold; one is said to be "beside the way," which is trodden down by men; another "among thorns," another "on rocky ground." And on the contrary the "good ground" is said to bring forth threefold fruit, either "a hundredfold" or "sixtyfold" or "thirtyfold." For there is also a threefold way of acting well; for nonetheless something good is done either by deed or by thought or by word. This same thing the Apostle also signifies when he says: "But he who builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones," indicating a threefold way of good things. He adds nonetheless a threefold way of evil things also, when he says: "wood, hay, stubble." These "three officers," then, are the wicked angels of Pharaoh's army, who stand in ways of this kind, watching each one of us to drive us through these into sin; whom the Lord will sink in the Red Sea and hand over to the fiery waves on the day of judgment and cover with a sea of punishments, if you, following God, withdraw yourself from their power.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "They went down into the deep like a stone." Why did "they go down into the deep like a stone"? Because they were not such "stones as those from which sons of Abraham could be raised up," but such as loved the deep and cherished the liquid element — that is, who seized the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Whence it is said of them: "They were sunk like lead in the mightiest water." Sinners are heavy. Finally, iniquity too is shown "to sit upon a talent of lead," as the prophet Zechariah says: "I saw," he says, "a woman sitting upon a talent of lead, and I said: what is this? And he answered: iniquity." Thence it is, therefore, that the wicked "were sunk into the deep, like lead in the mightiest water." But the saints are not sunk; rather they walk upon the waters, because they are light and are not weighed down by the burden of sin. Finally the Lord and Savior "walked upon the waters"; for he it is who truly knows no sin. His disciple Peter also "walked," although he trembled a little; for he was not so great and of such kind as to have nothing at all of the nature of lead mixed within him. He had some, though little. On account of which the Lord says to him: "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?" Therefore he who is saved is saved through fire, so that, if perchance he should have anything of the nature of lead mixed in, the fire may boil it away and dissolve it, so that all may be made good gold — because "the gold of that land" is said "to be good," which the saints are to possess, and "as the furnace tests gold," so temptation tests just men. All must come, then, to the fire; all must come to the smelting-furnace; "for the Lord sits and smelts and purges the sons of Judah." But when one comes there, if anyone has brought many good works and but a little of iniquity, that little is dissolved by the fire "like lead" and is purged, and the whole remains pure gold. And if anyone has brought there more lead, he is burned more, so that he may be boiled longer, so that, even if there be but a little gold, it may nevertheless remain purified. But if anyone comes there wholly of lead, there will befall him that which is written: he will be sunk "into the deep, like lead in the mightiest water." But it is a long matter, if we should wish to expound in order; it is enough to touch on a few points briefly.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Who," he says, "is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you? Glorious among the saints, wonderful in majesties, working prodigies." When he says "who is like you among the gods?", he does not compare God to the idols of the nations, nor to the demons who falsely claim for themselves the name of gods, but he calls those gods who are called gods through the grace and participation of God. Concerning whom Scripture also says elsewhere: "I said: you are gods," and again: "God stood in the assembly of the gods." But these, although they are capable of God and seem to be granted this name through grace, yet none is found like to God either in power or in nature. And although John the Apostle says: "little children, we do not yet know what we shall be; but if he shall be revealed to us" — speaking, of course, of the Lord — "we shall be like him," yet this likeness is referred not to nature but to grace. For example, as if we should say that a picture is like him whose image is seen expressed in the picture: as far as pertains to the grace of sight, it is called like; as far as pertains to substance, it is far unlike. For that is the form of flesh and the beauty of a living body, this is a tinting of colors and wax laid upon boards devoid of feeling. None, therefore, "among the gods is like the Lord"; for none is invisible, none incorporeal, none immutable, none without beginning and without end, none the creator of all things, save the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "You stretched out your right hand, the earth devoured them." The earth indeed devours the impious even today. Or does it not seem to you that the earth devours him who always thinks of earth, who always has earthly deeds, who speaks of earth, disputes about earth, desires earth, and places all his hope in earth? — who does not look to heaven, who does not think of things to come, who does not fear the judgment of God nor desire his blessed promises, but always thinks of things present, and sighs after things earthly? When you see such a man, say that "the earth has devoured him." But also if you see anyone given over to the luxury of the flesh and the pleasures of the body, in whom the mind avails nothing, but the lust of the flesh has taken possession of the whole, say also of this one that "the earth has devoured him." It still moves me that he says: "you stretched out your right hand, and the earth devoured them," as though this were the cause of their being devoured by the earth, that "the Lord stretched out his right hand." If you consider how the Lord, exalted upon the cross, "all the day stretched out his hands to a people that did not believe and that contradicted him," and how the death of the crime committed crushed the unbelieving people who cried out: "Crucify, crucify him!" — you will evidently find how "he stretched out his right hand and the earth devoured them." And yet one must not utterly despair. For it is possible that, if perchance he who has been devoured should come to his senses, he may again be vomited forth, as Jonah was. But I think that all of us too, once devoured by the earth, were held in the inner recesses of hell; and therefore our Lord descended not only as far as the lands, but even as far as "the lower parts of the earth"; and there he found us devoured and "sitting under the shadow of death," and leading us thence he prepares for us no longer a place of earth, lest we be devoured again, but a place of the kingdom of heaven.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "You have led forth this your people in your righteousness, whom you have set free. You have comforted them by your power in your holy rest." The Lord leads forth "in righteousness" his people whom "he set free through the laver of regeneration," and he comforts them also through the consolation of the Holy Spirit in "his power and in his rest." For the hope of things to come brings rest to those who labor; just as, for those set in the contest, the hope of the crown soothes the pain of wounds.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The nations heard and were angry; pangs seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Then the leaders of Edom hastened, and the princes of the Moabites; trembling took hold of them. All the inhabitants of Canaan melted away." As far as pertains to the history, it is established that none of these nations was present at the marvels which were done; how, then, will they seem to be terrified with trembling, or to have "hastened," as he says, or the "Philistines" and "Moabites" and "Edom" and the rest of the nations which he enumerates, to be "angry"? But if we return to the spiritual understanding, you will find that "Philistia" — that is, falling peoples — and "Edom," which is interpreted earthly, tremble, and the princes of all these run about and are afraid, gripped by pangs, when they see their kingdoms, which are in hell, penetrated by him "who descended into the lower parts of the earth," that he might rescue those who were possessed by death. Hence "fear and trembling seized them," because they felt "the greatness of his arm." Hence too "all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away," who are interpreted as changeable and moveable, when they see their kingdoms moved, "the strong one bound and his vessels plundered." "Let" therefore "fear and trembling at the greatness of your arm come upon them." What do the demons fear, what do they tremble at? Without doubt the cross of Christ, in which "they were triumphed over, in which their principalities and powers were stripped." "Fear," then, "and trembling shall fall upon them," when they see the sign of the cross faithfully fixed in us, and "the greatness of the arm" of him which the Lord stretched out upon the cross, as he says: "All the day I stretched out my hands to a people that did not believe and that contradicted me." They will not, then, fear you otherwise, nor will "your trembling come upon them otherwise," unless they see in you the cross of Christ, unless you too can say: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I will yet set down one testimony concerning stones, since indeed in the canticle of Exodus it is written: "let them be turned into stones, until your people pass over, O Lord, until this your people pass over, whom you have possessed". And so God is asked that for a little while the Gentiles be turned into stones—for the Greek word sounds this more pointedly, "ἀπολιθούντωσαν" (let them be petrified)—"until the people" of the Jews "pass over". There is no doubt that, after those have passed over, the Gentiles will cease to be stony and, in place of a hard heart, will receive in Christ a human and rational nature: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 22

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Let them become like stone, until your people pass over, O Lord, until this your people pass over, whom you have acquired." "To become like stone" is not to be by nature a stone; for it would not become that which it was not. This we say on account of those who say that Pharaoh or the Egyptians were of an evil nature and were not led into these things by the freedom of the will; and also on account of those who accuse God the creator as savage, because he turns men into stones. Let these, therefore, before they blaspheme, consider with the utmost weighing the things that are written. For he did not say "let them become like stone" and fall silent, but he set a time and decreed a measure of the condemnation. For he says: "until your people pass over," namely so that after the passing of the people they may not be "like stones." In which it seems to me that something of prophecy lies hidden. For I see that the former people, who were before us, became "like a stone," hard and unbelieving; yet not so far as to remain in the nature of a stone, but "until this people pass over, the people whom he has acquired": for "blindness in part happened in Israel" — that Israel according to the flesh — "until the fullness of the nations should enter in." For when "the fullness of the nations shall have entered in," then also "all Israel," which through the hardness of unbelief had become "like a stone," "shall be saved." And do you wish to see how it "shall be saved"? "God is able," he says, "from these stones to raise up sons of Abraham." Now, therefore, they remain stones, "until your people pass over, O Lord, this your people whom you have acquired." But if the Lord himself is the creator of all things, it must be seen how here he is said to have "acquired" those which there is no doubt are his own — for it is said also in the other song, that of Deuteronomy: "Is not this same one your God, who made you and created you and acquired you?" —; for each one seems to acquire that which was not his own. Hence finally the heretics too say of the Savior that those whom he "acquired" were not his own; for, a price being given, he purchased men whom the creator had made. And it is certain, they say, that each one buys that which is not his own; for the Apostle says: "you were bought with a price." But hear what the prophet says: "By your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I dismissed your mother." You see, then, that we are indeed all the creature of God, but each one is sold by his own sins and for his own iniquities departs from his own creator. We are, therefore, God's, according as we were created by him; but we became slaves of the devil, according as we were sold by our sins. But Christ, coming, "redeemed us," while we were serving that lord to whom we had sold our very selves by sinning. And so he seems to have received back as his own those whom he had created, but to have acquired as aliens those who by sinning had sought for themselves an alien lord. But perhaps it is rightly said that Christ redeemed us, who gave his own blood as our price — but what did the devil give of such a kind, that he might purchase us? Therefore, if it seems good, give heed. Murder is the devil's money; for "he is a murderer from the beginning." You have committed murder: you have received the devil's money. Adultery is the devil's money; for on it is the devil's "image and superscription." You have committed adultery: you have received a coin from the devil. Theft, false testimony, rapacity, violence — all these are the devil's wealth and the devil's treasure; for such money proceeds from his mint. With this money, therefore, he buys those whom he buys, and makes his slaves all who receive from his wealth of this kind even the least amount. But I fear lest even some of those who are in the church, some of those standing by, while we do not know, the devil secretly purchases; lest to some of our own also he presses this money which we enumerated above, and makes them his own again, and again writes for them the tablets of servitude and the bonds of sin, and mingles among the servants of God those whom he has made his own slaves by the price of sin. For it is his custom, since he is "the enemy man," "to mingle tares with the wheat." And yet, if perchance anyone deceived by the devil has received money of this kind, let him not utterly despair; for "the Lord is merciful and compassionate," and "does not will the death" of his creature, "but that it be converted and live." By repenting, by weeping, by making satisfaction, let him blot out what has been committed. For the prophet says: "when, being converted, you shall groan, you shall be saved." We have proceeded a little more widely, in wishing to expound how God is said "to acquire" the things which are his own, and Christ to "redeem with his precious blood" those whom the devil had bought with the cheap price of sin.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"Leading them in, you planted them on the mountain of your inheritance." God does not will to plant us in Egypt, nor in low and lowly places, but he wills to plant "on the mountain of his inheritance" those whom he plants. Then, besides, that he added "leading them in, you planted them" — does it not seem to you as though he were speaking of children, who are led in to schools, led in to letters, led in to all learning? Understand, therefore, through these words, if only you have "ears to hear," how God plants — lest perhaps, when you hear that he leads in and plants, you should think that he is setting fig trees or other shrubs of this kind in the ground. Hear also elsewhere how God plants. The prophet says: "You transferred a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations and planted it. You made a way passable before it, you planted its roots, and it filled the earth. Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God." Do you now notice how God plants and where he plants? He does not plant in the valleys, but on the mountains, in high and lofty places. For those whom he leads out of Egypt, whom he brings from the world to faith, he does not will to place again in lowly places, but he wills their manner of life to be lofty. He wills us to dwell on the mountains; but even on these very mountains nonetheless he does not will us to creep along the ground, nor does he will his vine to have its fruits cast down further upon the ground, but he wills its shoots to be led upward, to be set on high, to become layered branches — and layered branches not upon any lowly trees whatever, but upon the high and loftiest cedars of God. "The cedars of God" I take to be the prophets and the Apostles, to whom if we, the vine which God "transferred out of Egypt," be joined, and through their branches our shoots be spread abroad, and, resting upon them, we become as it were certain layered branches bound together by mutual bonds of charity, we shall without doubt bring forth very much fruit. For "every tree that does not bear fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire."

"In your prepared habitation, which you have prepared, O Lord." See the goodness of the merciful Lord: he does not will to lead you into labor, he does not will that you should make yourself a dwelling; already he leads you to a "prepared habitation." Hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: "Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor."

"The sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have prepared." The tabernacle of God or the temple is called a "sanctuary" from this, that it sanctifies those who approach. This he says was "not made by the hand of man," but by the hand of God. What then? On your account God both plants and builds, becomes a farmer, becomes a builder, lest anything be lacking to you. Hear Paul also saying: "You are God's tillage, God's building." What, then, is this "sanctuary," which was "not made by the hand of men," but prepared by the hands of God? Hear Wisdom saying that she "built herself a house." But I think this is more rightly to be understood of the incarnation of the Lord. "For it was not made by the hand of men," that is, not by human work is the temple of the flesh built in the Virgin; but, as Daniel had foretold, "a stone cut out without hands grew, and became a great mountain." This is the "sanctuary" of the flesh assumed and "without hands," that is, apart from the work of men, "cut out" from the mountain of human nature and the substance of the flesh.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "O Lord, who reign unto the age and unto the age and still."
