But if she be joined to a lawful husband, to that husband to whom Paul joins and unites souls in marriage, as he himself says: "for I have determined to present you as a chaste virgin to one husband, to Christ", and concerning whom it is written in the Gospels that "a certain king made a marriage for his son"—into the marriage, then, of this husband when the soul has given herself, and has obtained by lot a lawful matrimony with him, even if she was once a sinner, even if she played the harlot, yet if she has handed herself over to this husband, he suffers her to sin no further. He cannot bear that the soul which has obtained a husband by lot should again dally with adulterers: his jealousy is aroused over her, he defends the chastity of the marriage. And "God" is called "jealous" because he does not suffer the soul made his own to mingle with demons. Otherwise, if he see her violating the rights of the marriage and seeking occasions for sin, then, as it is written, he gives her "a bill of divorce" and dismisses her, saying: "where is the bill of divorce of your mother, by which I dismissed her?" To which he adds also and says: "behold, for your sins you have been sold, and for your iniquities I have dismissed your mother". He who speaks these things is "jealous" and, moved with jealousy, says these things; for after the acknowledgment of himself, after the illumination of the divine word, after the grace of baptism, after the confession of faith, and the marriage confirmed by sacraments so many and so great, he does not wish us to sin any further, he does not suffer the soul, of which he is himself called either the bridegroom or the husband, to sport with demons, to fornicate with unclean spirits, to wallow in vices and uncleannesses; and if perhaps it sometime unhappily happen, at least that she may be converted and return and repent. For this is a new kind of his goodness, that even after adultery he receives the soul, provided she returns and repents from the heart; as he himself also says through the prophet: "if a woman go out from her husband and sleep with another man, shall she return again to her husband? Shall she not be defiled with defilement? But you have fornicated with many shepherds, and yet you were returning to me". Likewise elsewhere he says: "and after you had fornicated in all these things, I said: return to me; and not even so did you return, says the Lord". This "jealous God", then—if he requires and desires your soul to cleave to him, if he keeps you from sin, if he rebukes, if he chastises, if he is indignant, if he is angry and, as it were, uses a certain jealousy toward you—recognize that there is for you hope of salvation. But if, chastised, you do not come to your senses, if, rebuked, you are not amended, if, scourged, you despise it, know that, if you have so far advanced in sinning, his jealousy will depart from you, and that will be said to you which through the prophet Ezekiel is said to Jerusalem: "therefore my jealousy shall depart from you, and I will be angry over you no more". See the mercy and the loving-kindness of the good God. When he wishes to have mercy, he says that he is indignant and angry, as through Jeremiah he says: "with grief and with scourge you shall be chastised, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you". If you understand these things, it is the voice of a God who has mercy, where he is angry, where he is jealous, where he applies griefs and scourges. "For he scourges every son whom he receives". But do you wish to hear the terrible voice of an indignant God? Hear what he says through the prophet: when he had enumerated the many wicked things which the people had committed, he adds also these: "and for this reason" he says "I will not visit upon your daughters when they fornicate, nor upon your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery". This is the terrible thing, this the extremity: when we are no longer rebuked for our sins, when we are no longer corrected when we transgress. For then, when we have exceeded the measure of sinning, the "jealous God" turns his jealousy away from us, as he said above: "for my jealousy shall be taken away from you, and I will be angry over you no more". So much concerning that which was said: "a jealous God".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us now see also what follows, how the "sins of the fathers" are said to be repaid "upon the sons unto the third and fourth generation". For in this saying the heretics are wont to jeer at us, that it is not the saying of a good God, who says that one is punished for the sins of another. But even according to their own reasoning, who say that the God who commanded these things in the law is, though not good, yet just, not even they can show how, according to their own sense of justice, it seems to accord that one should be punished when another sins. It remains, therefore, that we beseech the Lord to show us how these precepts accord with a just and good God. We have often said already that the divine Scriptures speak not everything to the outer man, but very much to the inner. Our inner man, therefore, is said either to have God as father, if he lives according to God and does the things that are God's, or the devil, if he be in sins and does his wills; as the Savior evidently shows in the Gospels, when he says: "you are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and stood not in the truth". Just as, then, the seed of God is said to remain in us, when, keeping the word of God, we do not sin in ourselves, as John says: "but he who is of God does not sin, because the seed of God remains in him", so also, when we are persuaded by the devil to sin, we receive his seed. But when we even fulfill in deed what he has counseled, then indeed he has also begotten us; for we are born his sons through sin. But since it scarcely almost happens that we who sin should sin without a helper, but we always require either ministers or helpers of sin—for example's sake, if someone contrives adultery, he cannot accomplish this alone, but there must needs be also an adulteress as partner and companion of the sin; and moreover, even if not several, yet there must needs be some man or some woman in the services and companionship of the sin; all of whom, begotten as it were one from another according to the order of persuasion, "from their father the devil" draw the progeny of a harmful birth. And, to come to the things that are written, the "Lord of majesty", Jesus Christ our Savior, was crucified. The author of this crime and the father of the wickedness is without doubt the devil. For thus it is written: "but when the devil had entered into the heart of Judas Iscariot, that he should betray him". The father of the sin, then, is the devil. He, in this wickedness, first begets a son, Judas; but Judas alone could not accomplish this. What, then, is written? "Judas went" it says "to the scribes and Pharisees and to the chief priests, saying to them: What will you give me, and I will betray him to you?" There is born, then, from Judas a third and fourth generation of sin. And you will be able to detect this order in each single sin as well. Now, therefore, let us see, according to this progeny of which we have spoken, how God "repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons and unto the third and fourth generation", and does not repay upon the fathers themselves; for he said nothing about the fathers. The devil, then, who has already exceeded the measure of sinning—as the prophet says, "as a garment congealed in blood shall not be clean", so he too shall not be clean in this age, nor is he rebuked for his sin, nor scourged; for all things are reserved for him unto the future. Hence he himself too, knowing that a set time of punishments is appointed for him, said to the Savior: "why have you come to torment us before the time?" While, therefore, this world stands, the devil, who is the father of those who sin, does not receive his sins; but they are repaid upon the sons, that is, upon those whom he begot through sin. For men, set in the flesh, are rebuked by the Lord, are beaten, are scourged. For "the Lord does not wish the death of the sinner, but that he should return and live". And therefore the "kind and merciful Lord" repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons, so that—since the fathers, that is, "the devil and his angels", and the rest, "the princes of the world and rulers of these darknesses" (for these too are made fathers of sin, just as the devil is)—since, I say, these fathers are unworthy to be rebuked in the present age, but in the future receive what they deserve, their sons, that is, those whom they have persuaded to sin and who nonetheless have been enlisted by them into the partnership and companionship of sin, these receive what they have done, so that they may pass more purified to the age to come and no longer be made companions of the devil in punishment. Because, therefore, God is merciful and "wishes all men to be saved", for this reason he says: "I will visit their misdeeds with a rod of iron and their sins with scourges. But my mercy I will not take away from them". The Lord, then, visits and requires the souls which this most evil father has begotten by persuasion to sin, and says to each one of them: "hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the house of your father". He visits you, then, after sin, and admonishes you, and with scourge and rod he visits you for the sin which the devil your father put upon you, that he may repay it to you "into your bosom", that is, while you dwell in the body. And thus it is fulfilled that the "sins of the fathers" are repaid "into the bosoms of the sons, unto the third and fourth generation". For "God" is "jealous" and does not wish the soul which he has betrothed to himself in faith to remain in the defilement of sin, but wishes her quickly to be purged, wishes her swiftly to cast off all her uncleannesses, if perhaps anything has stolen upon her. But if she remain in sins and say: we will not hear the voice of the Lord, but doing we will do our own wills and will burn offerings "to the queen of heaven", as is reproached through the prophet: then she too is reserved for that sentence of wisdom which says: "since indeed I called and you would not hear, but mocked my words; therefore I too will laugh at your destruction", or for that which is set before them in the Gospel, the Lord saying: "depart from me into eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels". I desire that, while I am in this age, the Lord may visit my sins and here repay them to me, so that there he may say also concerning me, Abraham, as he said concerning poor Lazarus to the rich man: "remember, son, that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now here he is at rest, but you are tormented". For this reason, therefore, when we are rebuked, when we are chastised by the Lord, we ought not to be ungrateful, but let us understand that we are rebuked in the present age for this, that in the future we may obtain rest, as the Apostle also says: "but when we are chastised by the Lord, we are rebuked, lest we be condemned with this world". Finally, for this reason too the blessed Job willingly received all torments and said: "if we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not also endure evil things?" "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so has it been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord". But he also repays "mercy unto thousands to those who love him". For those who love do not need rebuke, nor indeed do they sin, as the Lord too says: "he who loves me keeps my commandments". And therefore "perfect love casts out fear". On this account, then, for those who love, mercy alone is set; for "blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy upon them" in Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Although making a variety of suppositions about him, we all know something of God but do not all know what he is, for few indeed and fewer (if I may say so) than few are they who grasp his holiness in all things. Thus we are rightly taught to pray that our concept of God may be hallowed among us. Thus we shall see his holiness in creating, in providing, in judging, in choosing and abandoning, in accepting and rejecting, in rewarding and punishing each one according to his merits.In these activities and others like them is found, so I may say, the stamp of the personal character of God, that which in my opinion is called in Scripture the "name of God." So in Exodus: "You shall not take the name of your God in vain."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And God said, "Honor your father and your mother," teaching that the child should pay the honor which is due to his parents. Of this honor to parents one part was to share with them the necessaries of life, such as food and clothing, and if there was any other thing in which it was possible for them to show favor toward their own parents.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 11.9

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And again, who would deny that the command which says, "Honor your father and your mother, that it may be well with you," is useful quite apart from any spiritual interpretation and that it ought certainly to be observed, especially when we remember that the apostle Paul has quoted it in the same words?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
The saying is taken from Exodus, running thus: "Honour your father and your mother, that it may be well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth which the Lord your God gives you." And here, in setting out the wording, the Apostle has left out the "your" (after 'mother'), and instead of "and that you may be long-lived" he has made it and you shall be long-lived, and he has left out, after upon the earth, the "which the Lord your God gives you."

But it is the fifth commandment of the Decalogue; therefore it must be asked how one ought to understand the which is the first commandment, since the first commandment is stated to be "You shall have no other gods besides me." Now some have read which is the first commandment with a promise in this way, as though the commandments before it did not contain a promise; for they think that upon this one there lies for the first time the promise "that it may be well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth which the Lord your God gives you."

But these seem not to have observed that a promise is set down also upon the second commandment; for it says, "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything, whatever is in the heaven above and whatever is on the earth below and whatever is in the waters beneath the earth; you shall not bow down to them, nor shall you serve them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, requiting the sins of fathers upon children unto the third and fourth generation to those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and to those who keep my commandments." For note that it is a promise, the "showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and to those who keep my commandments."

Perhaps, then, since the Decalogue is spoken of as the first legislation to the people after their coming out of Egypt, each of the ten commandments is first, being spoken among the first of those that follow.

He, however, who wishes to hold fast to the rendering of which is the first commandment with a promise will say that the promise "that you may be long-lived upon the earth which the Lord your God gives you" is proper to the commandment "Honour your father and your mother," but not proper to the "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything" or "showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and to those who keep my commandments."

But again, on the other hand, he who expounds the whole Decalogue as containing first commandments will resist this too; for he will say that being long-lived upon the earth which the Lord God gives to the saints is granted not on account of the "Honour your father and your mother" commandment alone but also on account of countless others; and such a one will need to gather together the commandments to which is attached the "that you may be long-lived upon the earth, which the Lord your God gives you."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"But if two men should be fighting and strike a pregnant woman, and her infant should come forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss, as much as the woman's husband shall impose, and he shall pay with honor. But if it be fully formed, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise." First of all, in these matters, I think we must inquire under what heading of the law statutes of this kind are reckoned. For it is not, as it seems to the simpler sort, that everything which is enacted is called "law"; rather, some things are indeed called law, some testimonies, others commandments and acts of righteousness, and some are called judgments. This the eighteenth Psalm teaches more plainly, gathering them together in one place, when it says: "the law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to little ones. The acts of righteousness of the Lord are upright, gladdening hearts; the precept of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is chaste, enduring unto the age of the age; the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves." Since, then, these diversities exist among the things enacted in the law, the passage now in hand is written under the heading of acts of righteousness or justifications. For thus it says above: "and these are the acts of righteousness which you shall set openly before them." But it is not for the present occasion to set forth the differences of each of these, for we are called upon to explain the things which have been read. It should indeed be known that some portion of these matters, of which we must treat, is set down in the Gospel according to Matthew, the Lord speaking in this manner: "you have heard that it was said: eye for eye, tooth for tooth. But I say to you, do not resist evil. But if anyone strike you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also." But perhaps one who reads the Scriptures more attentively may say that the words we have recalled as written in the Gospel are not taken from this passage of Exodus, but rather from Deuteronomy, where nonetheless certain things are recorded as written in this manner: "but if," it says, "an unjust witness should stand, bearing testimony against a man concerning impiety, both men who are in controversy shall be set before the Lord and before the priests and before the judges, whoever they may be in those days, and the judges shall examine diligently and investigate. And behold, they shall find that the unjust witness has testified unjustly, that he has risen up against his brother; and you shall do to him as he himself attempted to do to his brother, and you shall remove the malignant one from your midst, that the rest, hearing, may have fear, and may not go on further to do according to this evil word among you. Your eye shall not spare over him: life for life, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot." Similar things indeed seem to be said in both places; yet it is not plainly shown from which passage in particular the words set down in the Gospel seem to be taken, where he said: "you have heard that it was said: eye for eye, tooth for tooth."

Nevertheless, our discourse must now be turned to the things written in Exodus, where two men are fighting and strike a pregnant woman, and strike her in such a way that the infant comes forth from her either "already formed" or "not yet formed." First indeed let us consider concerning the one who has come forth "not yet formed": how is it that one of those who are fighting is commanded to be struck with a monetary loss, when by Scripture the guilt of the quarrel is referred not to one, but to both? What too is the meaning of the fact that the woman's husband "imposes" or lays it upon him and not upon them, and that he "shall pay" and not rather that they shall pay "with honor"? And what is this honor? But if the infant has come forth already formed, the pregnant woman having been struck by the fighting men, we easily understand that life is given for life, that is, that what was committed is avenged by death. But the things that follow are worth explaining: "eye for eye, tooth for tooth." For it does not seem possible that we should understand of the infant, which the struck woman has miscarried, even if it came forth formed, that it lost an eye in the womb, struck by the heel of a fighting man, for which he ought to be deprived of an eye by the judges. But grant that even this be so, since it is reported as already formed—what shall we say also about the tooth? Did it have teeth in the mother's womb, which the striker's blow could knock out? But if we refer these things to her who has miscarried, how again will it fit that a miscarrying woman should lose an eye or suffer pains in her teeth? But grant that she is said to be struck in the eye or in the tooth, and that from this the cause of casting out the infant arose; grant that she received a bruise, grant that she received a wound—what shall we say too about "burn for burn"? Could a woman standing by while men were fighting be burned, so that "burn for burn" be paid? Yet each of these particulars seems to me not to admit of an easy solution even in the passages of Deuteronomy, where similar things are recorded as written. For let us suppose there too that "an unjust witness has risen up" speaking false testimony against a man concerning impiety. Let both be brought to judgment, let the judges inquire diligently, let them detect that that accuser or witness has spoken falsely: how shall the judge, who ought not to spare the false witness and to condemn the life of the guilty party for the life of an innocent one—how, I say, shall he also be able to take out "eye for eye"? As though indeed the one who was being unjustly accused was to have been injured in his eye by the accuser, or in tooth or hand or foot. But these things have been said by us because we wish to show that in both passages the things written cannot easily be expounded. For it was fitting for us first to examine according to the history the things that are read, and thus, since "the law is spiritual," to seek the spiritual understanding in them.

But, as far as concerns the present, even that portion of allegory itself, which is always accustomed to lie more broadly open, is here forced into a narrow compass. Nevertheless, as far as we are able, we shall attempt to explain what seems to us in this passage. We have frequently said that in the Scriptures the members of the soul are named by the same words and the same functions by which the members of the body are used or called. For example, as when it is said: "you see the speck in your brother's eye, and behold, in your eye a beam lies beneath." For it is certain that he does not speak of the eye of the body, in which a beam lies, but of the eye of the soul. And when he says: "he who has ears to hear, let him hear," and: "how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good tidings of peace," and many things similar to these. Now we have set these things down beforehand for this reason, that the likeness in the names of the members may not disturb us. Let these two men, then, who are fighting, be two men disputing and inquiring with one another about the doctrines or questions of the law, and, to speak in the words of the Apostle, quarreling "about battles of words." Whence the same Apostle also, knowing that quarrels of this kind arise among brethren, gives command and says: "do not contend with words, for it is useful for nothing, unto the subversion of the hearers," and elsewhere: "but avoid the questions of the law, knowing that they beget quarrels. But the servant of God ought not to quarrel." Because, therefore, these men who quarrel over questions quarrel "unto the subversion of the hearers," for this reason they strike a pregnant woman and cast out her infant, whether already formed or not yet formed. The pregnant woman is said to be the soul which has recently conceived the word of God. Now concerning such a conception we read it written also in another place: "from fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb, and we have given birth." Those, therefore, who conceive and immediately give birth—these are to be reckoned not as women, but as men, and perfect men. Hear, finally, also the prophet saying: "if the earth has given birth in one day, and a nation has been born at once." This is the generation of the perfect, which is born immediately, on the same day, as soon as it has been conceived. But lest it seem new to you that we have said men give birth, we have already long since set forth how you ought to take the names of the members, that you may withdraw from bodily senses and grasp the understanding of the inner man. But if you wish that I satisfy you still further in this also from the Scriptures, hear the Apostle saying: "my little children, whom I again bring forth in travail, until Christ be formed in you." Perfect, therefore, and strong men are those who immediately, as soon as they conceive, give birth—that is, those who bring the conceived word of faith forth into works. But the soul which conceives and retains in the womb and does not give birth, this one is called a woman, just as the prophet also says: "the pains of childbirth have come upon her, and the power of giving birth is not in her." This soul, then, which now on account of its weakness is called a woman, when two men are quarreling with one another and in the contest bringing forth stumbling-blocks—which the contention of words is always wont to have—is struck and scandalized, so that it casts out and loses the word of faith which it had faintly conceived; and this is the quarrel and contention "unto the subversion of the hearers." If, therefore, the soul which has been scandalized casts out the word not yet formed, he who scandalized it is said to suffer loss. Do you wish to know that in some the word is formed, in some not yet formed? The word of the Apostle plainly teaches us, which we recalled above, when he says: "until Christ be formed in you"; but Christ is the Word of God. By this he shows that at the time when he was writing, the Word of God was not yet formed in them; if, therefore, it comes forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss. Concerning the losses of teachers the Apostle also teaches, when he says: "but if anyone's work burns, he shall suffer loss. But he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire." But the Lord too says in the Gospels: "for what does it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, but lose his own soul or suffer loss of it?" Whence it seems to be shown that certain sins pertain indeed to loss, yet not to destruction; because he who has suffered loss is nonetheless said to be saved—"he himself"—although "through fire." Whence, I believe, the Apostle John too in his epistle says that some sins are unto death, and some are not unto death. But what the kinds of sins unto death are, and what indeed "not unto death," but unto loss, I do not think can easily be discerned by any of men. For it is written: "who understands transgressions?" Nevertheless, from the things which are related in the Gospel through parables, we can in some part come to know of what sort those are which are named losses, since there we see certain things reckoned to gain which are said to have been acquired through trading. For example, when it is related that beyond five minas five others were acquired, or beyond two others two were acquired; or when a drachma or a denarius or a talent is set down and is named as a kind of money in the profit of works; but also when the householder is said to make a reckoning with his servants and there is offered to him one who owed ten thousand talents. Such, therefore, is a kind of reckoning of loss, so that, for example, one who was to receive ten minas for his wage receives not ten, but eight or six or even less; and he is said to be struck with this loss who has offered the occasion of stumbling to the weaker and womanly soul.

But he shall pay, it says, according to what "the woman's husband shall impose" or lay upon him, "and he shall pay with honor." The husband of the learning soul is its teacher; according, therefore, to what that husband shall impose—either Christ, who is the teacher of all, or he who in Christ's stead presides over the Church as teacher of souls—that man who "unto the subversion of the hearers" contends with words shall suffer loss for that soul which has cast out the "infant not yet formed." This can perhaps be taken of the scandal of a catechumen not yet formed. For it can come about that again the very one who caused the injury may instruct, repair, and restore to the soul the things which it lost, and may now do this "with honor," with modesty, with patience, as the Apostle says: "with meekness correcting those who resist"—not with quarreling, as before, when he brought in the scandal. "But if the infant be already formed, he shall give life for life." The "formed infant" can seem to be the word of God in the heart of that soul which has obtained the grace of baptism, or which has more plainly and more clearly conceived the word of faith. This soul, then, if, struck by the excessive contention of teachers, it casts out the word and is found to be of those of whom the Apostle spoke: "for already certain ones have turned back after Satan," "shall give life for life." Either it is to be understood as in the day of judgment before that judge "who is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna"; because elsewhere too the prophet says to Jerusalem: "I have given Egypt as your exchange, and Ethiopia and Syene for you." Or indeed perhaps this too can be fitted, that he who is conscious to himself of so great a scandal should lay down his own "life for the life" of that one whom he has scandalized, and should labor even unto death for how that one may return, may be repaired, may be restored to faith. Let him also lay down "eye for eye": if he has injured the eye of the soul, that is, has disturbed its understanding, let his own eye be taken from him by the one who presides over the Church, and let that turbulent and fierce understanding of his, which generates scandal, be cut away. But also if he has injured the tooth of the hearer, with which, receiving the food of the word, he was wont either to grind it small or to crush it with his molars, so as to transmit from these a refined sense to the belly of the soul—if he has vexed and torn out this tooth, so that by his contention the soul cannot subtly and spiritually receive the word of God, let the tooth be taken from him who does not rightly grind small and divide the foods of the Scriptures. For perhaps on this account it is said elsewhere too concerning the Lord: "you have shattered the teeth of sinners"; and elsewhere it is nonetheless written: "he who eats a sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge"; and elsewhere: "the Lord has broken the grinding teeth of lions." Thus, therefore, the soul is said to be injured and struck through its members. "Hand" too "for hand" and "foot for foot" is demanded. The hand of the soul is the power by which it can hold and grip something, as if we should say its action and strength; and the foot is that by which it walks toward good things or bad. Because, therefore, if the soul suffers scandal, it is cast down not only in faith but also in acts, which are signified by the hands and feet, there are taken from him who offered the stumbling-block the hands with which he does not work rightly, and the feet with which he does not walk rightly. He shall also receive back the "burn" with which he burned and handed the soul over to Gehenna. By each of these particulars this is shown, that this striker, cut off in all his members, is to be excised from the body of the Church, "that the rest," it says, "seeing, may have fear and may not do likewise." Therefore the Apostle too, when he describes the teacher of the Church, among other things commands "not a striker," lest, striking pregnant women, souls just beginning, he lay down "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth." Such also are those souls which the Lord too weeps over in the Gospels, when he says: "woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days," in which there shall be scandalized, "if it be possible, even the elect." Yet it should be known that it is not for the perfect to be scandalized, but either for women or for little ones, just as the Lord too says in the Gospel: "if anyone shall scandalize one of these least little ones." He, then, is little and least who can be scandalized: "but the spiritual man judges all things" and "tests all things and, what is good, holds fast, and abstains from every evil kind." These things, as far as they could occur to us, we have said in the present passage. But let us ask of the Lord that he himself may deign to reveal to us the things that are perfect, through Jesus Christ our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Celsus does not quote any passages from the law which are apparently in contradiction to what stands in the gospel, so that we might compare them. He says, "And to a man who has struck one once one should offer oneself to be struck again." But we will say that we are aware that "it was said to them of old time, 'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth,' " and that we have read also the words "But I say unto you, to him that strikes you on one cheek offer the other one also." However, I imagine that Celsus derived some of his vague notions from those who say that the God of the gospel is different from the God of the law and so made remarks like this. I would reply to his objection that the Old Testament also knows the doctrine that to him that strikes you on the right cheek you should offer the other one also. At any rate, it is written in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: "It is good for a man when he bears a yoke in his youth, he will sit alone and in silence when he has taken it on himself. He will give a cheek to the man who smites him and shall be filled with reproaches." The gospel then does not lay down laws in contradiction to the God of the law, not even if we interpret literally the saying about a blow on the jaw. And neither Moses nor Jesus "is wrong." Nor did the "Father forget when he sent Jesus the commands which he had given to Moses." Nor did he "condemn his own laws, and change his mind and send his messenger for the opposite purpose."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Watch therefore, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. Not giving "sleep to the eyes" of our soul nor "slumber to the eyelids," so that we may await either our own end or the end of the age, whether that we should depart from this life or that this world should be brought to its consummation for us.

But someone will ask how the Lord, established as present among the disciples, speaks thus, as though not present but about to come, saying to them: watch, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. And the one who is more simple will say that he spoke this discourse concerning the second coming, in which he was to come. But another will say that he was speaking of the intelligible coming of the Word, still to come into the understanding of the disciples, because it was not yet in their understanding in the way it was going to be: since (as he shows through this passage) in those who watch he works the day of his coming in the soul of those who are illumined by the true light of him who comes to their souls.

Now the householder is the understanding of the man, and his house is his soul; but the thief, who comes suddenly while the householder sleeps and breaks into the house, is, I think, the devil or every contrary word, according to what the evangelist John teaches us, saying in this manner: "amen amen I say to you, he who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold but climbs up another way, that man is a thief and a robber". As, therefore, he who "enters through the door into the sheepfold" is "the shepherd of the sheep", for whom "the doorkeeper opens", but "he who does not enter through the door but climbs up another way is a thief and a robber", so the lord of the house enters into it confidently "through the door" when he wills, rewarding the one who watches; but the thief, being a thief, does not enter into the house to the soul of the negligent by the natural entrance, but (as one who has already broken into it) first destroying certain natural buildings of his soul and natural understandings, in him who has not watched — the things which God the Word had built. And having entered through that very breach, the thief plunders it, disarming the understanding, when, despoiling the householder who does not watch, "he will distribute his spoils".

But sometimes someone catches the thief in the very act of breaking in, and seizing him as one having his own weapons, he strikes the thief, and, confuting the word that breaks in, he kills it, when, though killing, he is not reckoned a murderer, killing it without any delay. But if not in his own presence, yet in the presence of him who makes all hidden things manifest, someone catches him who has stolen his goods, and understands him and refutes him (that is, kills him), he has no pardon, the thief being dead and made manifest: for he too will die.

And see whether perhaps the law of Moses signifies some such thing, saying: "but if the thief is found in the very breaking in and, being struck, dies, there is no bloodguilt for him; but if the sun has risen over him, he is guilty: he shall die for it". For he who, before he does the evil, recognizes the evil and crushes it in himself, is the one who catches and kills it in himself, while it is being broken in upon by it. But he who, after he has done the evil, although he refutes it, is seen to have caught the evil outside himself and to have killed it outside his house — it profits him nothing, for he has been made guilty of death. For after any man has sinned and turned back into himself, the divine understanding which is in us illumines him like a light, so that we may understand that the evil we have committed was to our own condemnation, not to our salvation. Yet in the text of this Gospel of which we are speaking, the thief comes not by day, when the soul of the earnest man has been illumined by the sun of righteousness, but by night and in the time while malice still remains.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Some people give no thought to the question of demons, that is to say, to the fact that these demons, in order to be able to exist in the heavy atmosphere that encircles the earth, must have the nourishment of exhalations and consequently are always on the lookout for the savor of burnt sacrifices, blood and incense. Since they attach no importance to the matter of sacrifice, we would express ourselves also on this subject. If men who give sustenance to robbers, murderers and barbarian enemies of the great king are punished as criminals against the state, how much more will they be punished justly who through offering sacrifice proffer sustenance to the minions of evil and thus hold them in the atmosphere of the earth! And this holds true especially if knowing the text, "He that sacrifices to gods other than the Lord alone will be destroyed utterly," they nevertheless sacrifice to these authors of evil on earth. In my opinion, when there is question of crimes committed by these demons operating against men, they who sustain them by sacrificing to them will be held no less responsible than the demons themselves that do the crimes. For the demons and they that have kept them on earth, where they could not exist without the exhalations and nourishment considered vital to their bodies, work as one in doing evil to mankind.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In accordance with this we also note that saying: "The barren has borne seven, and she who was fruitful in children has grown weak." And as it is said among the blessings: "There shall not be among you one without children nor a barren woman." Therefore, if these things are so, just as there is said to be a certain carnal love, which the poets have also called Cupid, according to which he who loves sows in the flesh; so also there is a certain spiritual love, according to which that inner man who loves sows in the spirit. And to say it more plainly, if there is anyone who still bears the image of the earthly according to the outer man, he is driven by an earthly desire and love. But he who bears the image of the heavenly according to the inner man is driven by a heavenly desire and love.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
If anyone should worthily understand either the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt or the crossing of the Red Sea, and indeed this whole road that is traveled through the desert and each of the several encampments of the camp; if he should prove so capable of these things that he even receives the law of God "written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God"; if anyone, I say, should so come to these things through the order of the journeyings, that, fulfilling each one in the spirit, he attains also those increases of the virtues which are indicated in them, then he can consequently arrive also at the vision and understanding of the tabernacle. Concerning this tabernacle the divine Scriptures make mention indeed in many places and seem to indicate certain things which human hearing could scarcely be capable of; yet above all the Apostle Paul, concerning the understanding of the tabernacle, discloses to us certain tokens of a more exalted knowledge, but, in some way — perhaps regarding the frailty of his hearers — he in a manner closes up the very things that he opens. For he says, writing to the Hebrews: "For the first tabernacle was made, in which were the candlestick and the setting-forth of the loaves, which was called the holy of holies. But after the second veil the tabernacle, which is called holy, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the testament, and within it the two tables, and the manna and the rod of Aaron, which had put forth leaves". But to these things he added: "of which it is not now to be spoken one by one". Now that he says, "of which it is not now to be spoken", some refer to that time at which he was writing the epistle to the Hebrews; but to others it seems that, on account of the greatness of the mysteries, he denies that all the time of the present life is fit for explaining these things. Yet the Apostle does not leave us wholly sorrowful, but, as is his custom, he opens a few things out of many, so that it may indeed be closed to the negligent, but found by those who seek, and opened to those who knock. He resumes therefore again concerning the tabernacle and says: "For Jesus entered not into the holy places made by hand, the copies of the true, but into heaven itself, that he may now appear before the face of God through the veil, that is, through his own flesh". He therefore who interpreted the veil of the inner tabernacle as the flesh of Christ, and the holy places themselves as heaven or the heavens, and the Lord Christ indeed as the high priest, and says that he entered "once into the holy places, having found eternal redemption" — if from these few words anyone knows how to understand the sense of Paul, he can perceive how great a sea of understanding he has opened up to us. But those who love the letter of the law of Moses well enough, yet flee its spirit, hold the Apostle Paul under suspicion for bringing forth interpretations of this kind.

Let us therefore see whether some also of the ancient saints did not hold an opinion of the tabernacle far other than these men now reckon. For hear how magnificently David, that surpassing one among the prophets, thinks concerning the tabernacle: "While it is said" he says "to me every day: Where is thy God? these things have I remembered, and I have poured out my soul within me, for I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God". And again in the fourteenth Psalm he says: "Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle? or who shall rest in thy holy mountain? He that entereth without spot and worketh righteousness" and the rest. What then is this "place of the wonderful tabernacle", from which one comes "even unto the house of God", whereof, because he was made mindful, his soul was poured out within him and he was as it were dissolved by some intolerable longing? Is it then finally to be believed that this tabernacle, which was made up of skins and curtains and coverings of goats' hair and other materials of our use, the prophet, longing for it, was poured out in soul and collapsed with his whole mind? Or indeed how will it be true that it is said of this tabernacle that none dwells in it except the "innocent in hands and clean in heart, who hath not taken his soul in vain", when the history of the Kingdoms discloses that most wicked priests, "sons of pestilence", dwelt in the tabernacle of God, and that the very ark of the testament, captured by the Allophyli (Philistines), was held among the impious and profane? From all which it stands firm that the prophet thinks with a far other sense concerning this tabernacle, in which he says that none dwells except the "innocent in hands and clean in heart, and who hath not taken his soul in vain, nor done evil to his neighbor, and hath not received reproach against his neighbor". Such, then, must be the dweller of this tabernacle, which the Lord fixed and not man. But let us come also to the Gospels, if we find anything said in them concerning tabernacles, so that through the judgment of the Lord what we seek may be beyond doubt. We find, then, that the Savior himself, Jesus Christ, mentions not one tabernacle, but many, and not temporal, but eternal, when he says: "Make yourselves friends of the mammon, that, when it shall fail, they may receive you into the eternal tabernacles". Thou hast heard the Lord declaring the tabernacles to be eternal; hear now also the Apostle saying: "desiring to be clothed over with our tabernacle, which is from heaven". Is not the way now opened to thee from all these things, whereby, the earth being forsaken, following the prophetic and apostolic sense and — what is greatest of all — following the word of Christ with the whole mind and whole sense, thou mayest ascend to heaven and there seek the magnificence of the eternal tabernacle, whose figure is shadowed forth through Moses on the earth? Finally, thus also the Lord says to him: "See" he says "that thou make all things according to the figure which was shown thee in the mount". But the human mind, and ours especially — we who know ourselves to be least, or even nothing, in divine wisdom — could perhaps advance thus far, so as to perceive indeed that these things which are set forth in the divine volumes are spoken not of earthly, but of heavenly things, and are forms not of present, but of "good things to come", not of corporeal, but of spiritual things; but how the narration of these can be fitted to heavenly and eternal things is neither of our measure to say nor, as I suppose, of your capacity to hear. Yet a few things — if the Lord, while you pray, deign to enlighten us — which pertain to the edification of the Church, we shall attempt to open up.

The whole people therefore is commanded, each one contributing according to his powers, to make the tabernacle, so that in a manner all together may be one tabernacle. But the contribution itself is made not by necessity, but of free will. For God says to Moses that each one, "as it shall have seemed good to his heart", should offer gold, silver, precious stones, brass, and moreover fine linen, scarlet, hyacinth and purple, red skins of rams also and hyacinthine skins, but also incorruptible woods, the hairs of goats too, for the construction of the tabernacle. Women also wise in the art of weaving are required, and craftsmen who know how to fit gold or silver or brass, and stones also, and to form woods with gold. Then afterward the measures of the courts are handed down. These courts, spread out with tent-hangings, raised up with pillars, made stable with bars and stretched taut with cords, are made firm. There are made besides certain things marked off by veils, which are called holy, and others nonetheless separated by a second veil, which are called the holy of holies. Within is placed the ark of the testament, above which are set the Cherubim with wings extended and touching one another, and there of gold is placed for them as it were a certain base and seat, which is called the propitiatory, but also the golden altar of incense. Then besides, in the outer place, the candlestick of gold is set in the part of the south, that it may look toward the north. But in the part of the north the table is placed, and the setting-forth of loaves upon it. And also the altar of holocausts is placed beside the inner veil. But why do I go over these things one by one? Scarcely do we suffice merely to narrate these things, scarcely can the very form of the material things be brought before our eyes; and how shall anyone suffice to unfold the mysteries lying hidden in them? Nevertheless the cause for which the tabernacle ought to be made is found foretold in the passages above, the Lord saying to Moses: "Thou shalt make" he says "for me a sanctification, and thence I will be seen by you". God wills, then, that we make for him a sanctification. For he promises that, if we make for him a sanctification, he can be seen by us. Whence also the Apostle says to the Hebrews: "Follow peace and sanctification, without which no one shall see God". This, then, is the sanctification which the Lord commands to be made, which the Apostle also wills to be in virgins, "that they may be holy in body and in spirit", knowing without doubt that he who makes for the Lord a sanctification through the purity of his heart and body shall himself see God. Let us therefore, we also, make a sanctification for the Lord, and all one, and each one through the several ones make one. Perhaps we all make the sanctification the Church, which is holy, "having neither spot nor wrinkle", in this manner: if she have as pillars her teachers and ministers, of whom the Apostle says: "Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and to Barnabas". In this tabernacle, then, the pillars are joined by bars set between; in the Church the teachers are joined together by the right hands given to one another. But let these pillars be overlaid with silver, and their bases overlaid with silver. And let two bases be assigned to each single pillar: one, which is called the "head" and is placed on top, the other, which is truly called the "base" and is put under the pillar as for a foundation. Let the pillars therefore be overlaid with silver for this reason, that they who preach the word of God shall receive through the Spirit the "oracles of the Lord", which are "chaste oracles, silver tried by fire". But these men have as bases of their preaching the prophets; for "upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets" they establish the Church, using whose testimonies they confirm the faith of Christ. But the head of the pillars is he, I suppose, of whom the Apostle says that "the head of the man is Christ". And the bars of the pillars, the right hands of the apostolic fellowship given to one another, we have already spoken of above. The tent-hangings, which, sewn with small loops and hung by rings and knotted together with cords after the manner of curtains, are stretched out twenty-eight cubits in length and four in breadth — let these be held to be the remaining people of believers, which cleaves and hangs upon the cords of faith. For "a threefold cord is not broken", which is the faith of the Trinity, from which hangs and by which is sustained the whole Church. And as for the twenty-eight cubits by which it is stretched in length and four in breadth, the measure of one court, I think that the law inserted into the Gospels is designated. For the number seven is wont to signify the law, on account of the many sacraments of the seventh number. When this is joined to four, four times seven consequently make the number twenty-eight. But these courts are made ten, that they may hold the whole number of perfection and signify the decalogue of the law. Now indeed the kinds of scarlet and hyacinth and fine linen and purple set forth many and diverse works. Thence the tent-hangings, thence the veil outer and inner, thence the whole priestly and pontifical vestment is furnished with gold and gems adjoined. But lest we tarry too long over the several kinds of the virtues, we can briefly say that by these things are signified those with which the Church is adorned. Her faith can be compared to gold; the word of preaching to silver, the brass to patience; to the incorruptible woods, the knowledge which comes through the wood, or the incorruption of chastity, which never grows old; to the fine linen, virginity; to the scarlet, the glory of confession; to the purple, the splendor of charity; to the hyacinth, the hope of the kingdom of heaven. Let these for the present be the materials out of which the whole tabernacle is constructed, the priests are clothed, and the high priest also is adorned. And what their garments are, or of what sort, the prophet declares in another place and says: "Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness"; all these, then, are garments of righteousness. And again the Apostle Paul says: "Put on the bowels of mercy"; there are, then, also garments of mercy. But the same Apostle nonetheless designates other, nobler garments, when he says: "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh to fulfill its lusts". These, then, are the garments with which the Church is adorned.

But each one of us also can construct within his very self a tabernacle for God. For if, as certain who were before us have said, this tabernacle holds the figure of the whole world, but each single one can also have the image of the world, why can not each one also fulfill within his very self the form of the tabernacle? He, then, ought to fit for himself the pillars of the virtues, silver pillars, that is, reasonable patience. For there can be in a man something that seems patience, but which is not reasonable. For he too who does not feel an injury and therefore does not requite it seems patient, but this patience is not reasonable. This man, then, has pillars indeed, but they are not of silver; but he who suffers for the word of God and bears it bravely, this man is decorated and fortified with silver pillars. He can also stretch out courts within himself, when he has enlarged his heart according to the voice of the Apostle saying to the Corinthians: "Be ye also enlarged". He can also fortify himself with bars, when he has bound himself with the oneness of mind of love. He can stand upon silver bases, when he is set upon the stability of the word of God, the prophetic and apostolic word. He can have on the pillar a gilded head, if the faith of Christ be to him a golden head. "For the head of every man is Christ". And ten courts he can stretch out within his very self, when he is enlarged not in one word only of the law, nor in two or three, but can enlarge the breadth of the spiritual understanding in the whole decalogue of the law; or when he brings forth the fruit of the spirit — joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, modesty, faith, continence — with charity added, which is the greatest of all. Let that soul have besides within itself — the soul that has not given "sleep to its eyes" nor "slumber to its eyelids" nor "rest to its temples", "until it find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob" — let it have, I say, fixed within itself an altar also, on which it may offer to God the sacrifices of prayers and the victims of mercy, on which with the knife of continence it may immolate pride as it were a bull, slay wrath as it were a ram, offer as goats and kids luxury and all lust. Yet let it know how to separate for the priests from these sacrifices also the "right arm" and the "little breast" and the jaws, that is, good works and works of the right hand (for let it reserve nothing of the left); the little breast whole, which is the upright heart and the mind consecrated to God, and the jaws for speaking the word of God. Let it know that in the holy places also a candlestick of light must be set for it, that there may be to it "lamps" always "burning and the loins girded", and it itself "as a servant who waits for his lord to return from the marriage". For concerning these lamps the Lord also said: "The lamp of thy body is thine eye". But let it set this candlestick of lamps in the south, that it may look toward the north. For, the light being kindled, that is, with a watchful heart, it ought always to look toward the north and to observe "him who is from the north"; just as the prophet also says that he sees "a kindled cauldron, or pot, and its face from the face of the north"; for "from the north are kindled the evils of all the earth". Let it therefore, watchful and solicitous and burning, ever behold the cunning devices of the devil and ever look from what quarter temptation is about to come, from what quarter the enemy rushes in, from what quarter the foe creeps up. For the Apostle Peter also says that "your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour". Let the table of the setting-forth also, having twelve loaves, be set in the part of the north, looking toward the south. Let these loaves be to it the apostolic word, as much in number as in power, using which unceasingly — for it is commanded to set these "before the Lord" daily — let it again look toward the south, whence the Lord comes: "for the Lord shall come from Teman", as it is written, which is of the south. Let it have in the inmost recesses of its breast also the altar of incense, that it too may say: "for we are the good odor of Christ". Let it have also the ark of the testament, in which are the tables of the law, that it may "meditate in the law of God day and night", and its memory may be made an ark and a library of the books of God, because the prophet also calls those blessed who hold in memory his commandments, that they may do them. Let there be laid up within it also the urn of manna, the subtle and sweet understanding of the word of God; let there be also the rod of Aaron within it, the priestly doctrine and the flowering severity of discipline; but above all glory let there be to it the pontifical adornment. For that part can exercise the pontificate within itself which is in it more precious than all — which some call the principal part of the heart, others the reasonable sense or the intellectual substance, or by whatever manner it can be called in us, that portion of ours through which we can be capable of God. This part in us, then, let it be adorned as it were a certain high priest with garments and precious jewels, with a robe of fine linen. This kind of garment is one that is led down even to the feet, covering the whole body; in which it is designated that first of all it should be wholly clothed with chastity. Let it receive afterward also the jeweled shoulder-piece, in which is set the splendor of works, "that men seeing your works may glorify the Father who is in heaven". Let it receive also the logium, which can be called the rational, placed upon the breast, distinguished by a fourfold order of stones; but let there also shine on the forehead a golden plate, which is called the "petal", in both of which the "truth" and the "manifestation" are said to be set. I, in these things which are said to be placed on the breast, perceive the evangelical word, which in a fourfold order expounds to us the truth of the faith and the manifestation of the Trinity, referring all things to the head, namely to the nature of the one God. In these, then, is all truth and all manifestation of truth. Therefore, if thou wilt duly bear the pontificate to God, let the evangelical word and the faith of the Trinity always be held by thee in the breast. To which the apostolic word also is fitting, as much in power as in number, provided only that the name of God be always held in the head and all things be referred to the one God. Let the high priest have also in his inner parts his coverings, let him have his shameful parts covered, "that he may be holy in body and in spirit" and pure in thoughts and in works. Let him have also around the circuit of the garment little bells, that "entering" he says "into the holy places he may give a sound and not enter with silence". And these little bells, which ought always to sound, are placed at the extremity of the vestment, for this reason, I believe, that concerning the last times and the end of the world thou mayest never be silent, but thence always sound, thence dispute and speak according to him who said: "Be mindful of thy last things, and thou shalt not sin". In this manner, then, let our inner man be adorned as a high priest to God, that he may be able to enter not only into the holy places, but also into the holy of holies; that he may be able to approach the propitiatory, where are the Cherubim, and thence God may appear to him. The holy places can be those things which a holy manner of life can have in the present age. But the holy of holies, into which entrance is made once only, I think to be the passage to heaven, where is the propitiatory and the Cherubim, where also God shall be able to appear to the clean in heart, or because the Lord says: "behold, the kingdom of God is within you". Let these things, for the present, as far as in passing they could occur to our senses, and as far as we could moderate them to the ears of the hearers, be said concerning the tabernacle, so that each one of us also may be zealous to make within himself a tabernacle for God. For not in vain is it related of the fathers that they dwelt in tabernacles. I so understand that Abraham dwelt in tabernacles, and Isaac and Jacob. For these men constructed within themselves a tabernacle for God, who adorned themselves with so great and such splendors of the virtues. For there shone in them the royal ensign of purple, on account of which it was said to Abraham by the sons of Heth: "thou art among us a king from God". There shone also the scarlet; for he held a right hand ready to slay to God his only-begotten. There shone the hyacinth, when, ever gazing on heaven, he followed the Lord of heaven. But in the rest also he was similarly adorned. I so understand also the festal day of tabernacles, which is commanded in the law, that the people should go out on a certain day of the year and dwell in tabernacles, having branches of palms and boughs of willow and of the poplar and branches of a leafy tree. The palm is a sign of the victory of that war which the flesh and the spirit wage between themselves; and the poplar tree and the willow, as much in power as in name, are the shoots of chastity. Which if thou keep whole and entire, thou canst have also the branches of the wooded and leafy tree, which is the eternal and blessed life, when "the Lord shall have set thee in a green place upon the water of refreshment" through Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But when the passage about the equipment of the tabernacle is read, believing that the things described therein are types, some seek for ideas which they can attach to each detail that is mentioned in connection with the tabernacle. Now so far as concerns their belief that the tabernacle is a type of something they are not wrong. But in rightly attaching the word of Scripture to the particular idea of which the tabernacle is a type, here they sometimes fall into error.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But also the oracles of the Lord, "the chaste oracles," are called "silver tried by fire." And likewise in another place the tongue of the just man is spoken of as "kindled silver." But the cherubim are called golden, since indeed they are interpreted as "the fullness of the knowledge of God." But also the candlestick in the tabernacle of the testimony was commanded to be set up golden and solid; which seems to me to hold the form of the natural law, in which the law of knowledge is held. … that gold is to be referred to the sense and the mind, but silver is to be referred to the word and to oracles?
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 2

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Moreover it was said to Moses himself, "See that you make all things according to the form and likeness which was shown to you in the mount." It seems to me, therefore, that … in this earth the law was a kind of schoolmaster to those who by it were appointed to be led to Christ and to be instructed and trained in order that after their training in the law they might be able with greater facility to receive the more perfect precepts of Christ. So also that other earth, when it receives all the saints, first imbues and educates them in the precepts of the true and eternal law in order that they may with greater facility accept the precepts of heaven which are perfect and to which nothing can ever be added. And in heaven will truly exist what is called the "eternal gospel" and the Testament that is always new, which can never grow old.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Twofold is the house of the tabernacle of testimony or of the temple of the Lord. The first is that in which is the "altar of the whole burnt offerings", which is stirred up with perpetual fires, in which house it is lawful for the priests alone to stand and to celebrate the rites and ministries of the sacrifices, and to neither the Levites nor anyone else besides is access granted. But the second house is the interior one, separated from this only by a "veil". Within which veil are the "ark of the testament" and the "propitiatory", upon which the "two cherubim" are set, and the "altar of incense" is placed. Into this house "once in the year" whoever was first, the high priest, having first offered the victims of atonement of which we have expounded above, would enter, having both hands filled, one with the "censer of coals" and the other with the "incense of composition".… You have heard of two houses, one as it were visible and open to the priests, the other as it were invisible and inaccessible: except the one high priest alone, the rest are outside.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For do not suppose that almighty God commanded this and sanctioned it by law, that frankincense be brought to him from Arabia. But this is the frankincense which God seeks to be offered to him by men, from which he takes "an odor of sweetness": prayers from a pure heart and a good conscience, in which God truly receives the fragrance of sweetness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But on the "tenth day of the seventh month" is this solemnity of atonement. "On this" day alone the high priest is clothed with all the priestly garments, then he is clothed with "manifestation and truth", then he enters into those inaccessible places, whither it is permitted to approach only "once in the year", that is, into the "holy of holies". For "once in the year" the high priest, leaving the people, enters into that place where is the "propitiatory" and above the "propitiatory" the "cherubim", where is also the "ark of testimony" and the "altar of incense", whither it is lawful for no one to enter except the high priest alone. If therefore I consider my true "high priest" the Lord "Jesus" Christ, how, placed in the flesh, he was with the people throughout the whole year, that year of which he himself says: "he sent me to evangelize the poor and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of remission", I observe how "once in" that "year", on the day of atonement, he enters into the "holy of holies", that is, when, the dispensation being fulfilled, he "penetrates the heavens" and enters to the Father, that he may make him propitious to the human race and entreat for all who believe in him. This atonement of his, by which he makes the Father propitious to men, the Apostle John, knowing it, says: "these things I say, little children, that we may not sin. But even if we have sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he himself is the atonement for our sins". But Paul likewise makes mention of this atonement, when he says of Christ: "whom God set forth as a propitiatory in his own blood through faith". Therefore the Day of Atonement remains for us until the sun sets, that is, until the world receives its end.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore just as the people are God's when they do not sin but are no longer said to be his when they sin, so also the feats are the feats of sinners when they are hated by the Lord's soul, but when they are ordained by the Lord, they are called the Lord's.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.80

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet there are also those who go out well and are blessed because they go out. I will show this too from the Scriptures. In Exodus it is written: "All," it says, "who sought the name of the Lord went out forth to Moses outside the camp." These went out well "outside the camp," because they followed Moses, that is, the law of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Like to this also is that which is said by God through Moses: "Behold, I have set you in a hole of the rock, and you shall see My back parts." Therefore this rock, which is Christ, is not closed on every side, but has a hole. And the hole of the rock is that which reveals God and makes Him known to men. No one, then, sees the Father except the Son; no one, then, sees the last things of God — that is, the things which come to pass in the last times — except one placed in the hole of the rock, namely when he has learned those things by the revelation of Christ.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 4

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For it is well known that he, that is, the one who gave the oracles to Moses, says, "You shall not see my face but my back." Certainly these statements must be understood by the aid of that symbolism which is appropriate to the understanding of divine sayings, and those old wives' fables, which ignorant people invent on the subject of the front and back parts of God, must be utterly rejected and despised. Nor indeed must anyone suppose that we have entertained some impious thought in saying that the Father is not visible even to the Savior, but he must consider the exact meaning of the terms we use in controverting the heretics. For we have said that it is one thing to see and be seen, another to perceive and be perceived or to know and be known. To see and be seen is a property of bodies, which it would certainly not be right to apply either to the Father or to the Son or to the Holy Spirit in their relations one with another. For the Trinity by its nature transcends the limits of vision, although it grants to those who are in bodies, that is, to all other creatures, the property of being seen one by another. But incorporeal and above all intellectual nature is capable of nothing else but to know and be known, as the Savior himself declares when he says, "No one knows the Son save the Father, neither does any know the Father save the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him." It is clear then that he did not say, "No one sees the Father save the Son" but "No one knows the Father save the Son."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
A reading from Exodus has been recited to us, one that may either spur us on to the search for understanding or drive us back from it. It spurs on minds that are studious and free; it drives back those that are idle and preoccupied. For it is written: "Aaron and all the sons of Israel saw Moses, and his face was glorified and the color of his countenance, and they were afraid to approach him." And a little after: "Moses," it says, "placed a veil over his face. But when he entered into the sight of the Lord, to speak with him, he laid the veil aside." Now the Apostle, expounding these things with that magnificent understanding which he employs in the rest, of which he said: "but we have the mind of Christ," says: "for if the ministry of death, formed in letters upon stones, was in glory, so that the sons of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is done away: how shall not the ministry of the spirit be rather in glory?" And again a little later he says: "and not as Moses put a veil over his face, that the sons of Israel might not gaze upon the face of his countenance. For their perceptions were dulled; for until this present day, when Moses is read, the veil is placed over their heart." Who would not marvel at the greatness of the mysteries? Who would not be filled with dread at the mark of the dulled heart? The face of Moses was glorified, but the sons of Israel could not "gaze upon the face of his countenance," the people of the synagogue could not "gaze" upon it. But if anyone can have a manner of life and a way of living more eminent than the rest of the common crowd, he is able to behold the glory of his countenance. For even now, as the Apostle says, "a veil is placed over the reading of the Old Testament," and even now Moses speaks with glorified countenance, but we cannot behold the glory that is in his countenance. And the reason we cannot is that we are still the common people and have no more of zeal, no more of merit, than the rest of the multitude. But since the holy Apostle says: "yet the same veil remains over the reading of the Old Testament," the pronouncement of so great and such an Apostle would cut off from us every hope of understanding, had he not added: "but when anyone shall have turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away." Therefore he says that the cause of the veil's removal is our turning to the Lord. From which we ought to gather these indications: that so long as, when we read the divine Scriptures, the understanding lies hidden from us, so long as the things that are written are obscure and closed to us, we have not yet turned to the Lord. For if we had turned to the Lord, without doubt the veil would be taken away.

But let us see also what this very thing, "to turn to the Lord," may be. And that we may know more plainly what it is to be turned, we must first say what it is to be turned away. Everyone who, when the words of the law are recited, is occupied with common tales, is turned away. Everyone who, "when Moses is read," carries anxiety about the affairs of the world, about money, about profits, is turned away. Everyone who is bound tight by cares for possessions and stretched out by desire for riches, who is eager for the glory of the age and the honors of the world, is turned away. But even one who seems indeed a stranger to these things, yet stands by and hears the words of the law and is intent in face and eyes, yet wanders in heart and thoughts, is turned away. What then is it to be turned? If we turn our backs on all these things and, in zeal, in deeds, in mind, in solicitude, give our labor to the word of God, if we "meditate on his law day and night," if, setting all else aside, we are at leisure for God and exercise ourselves in his testimonies—this is to be turned to the Lord. If you wished your son to know the letters that men call liberal, to know the discipline of grammar or of rhetoric, would you not render him free and unoccupied from all else, would you not make him, setting the rest aside, devote his labor to this one study, would you not see that he lack nothing at all—tutors, teachers, books, expenses—until he carries off the perfected work of the study he has purposed? Which of us has so turned himself to the studies of the divine law, which of us has given such labor? Who seeks the divine letters with as much zeal and toil as he has sought the human? And what do we complain of, if we are ignorant of what we do not learn? Some of you, as soon as they have heard the things that are read recited, straightway depart. There is no inquiry among yourselves about the things that were read, no comparing together, nowhere a remembering of that commandment by which the divine law admonishes you: "ask your fathers and they will tell you, your elders and they will declare to you." Others do not even patiently wait for this very thing, until the readings are recited in the church. And others, even if they are recited, do not attend to them, but in the more remote places of the Lord's house are occupied with secular tales. Of whom I have made bold to say that, "when Moses is read," there is now no longer "a veil over their heart," but a kind of partition and wall has been set up. For if he who is present, who hears and is intent and reconsiders and examines what he hears, and questions and learns what he cannot attain—if he can scarcely reach the freedom of knowledge, then he who hides away his ears, that he may not hear, and turns his back upon the face of the reader, how is he to be said to have a veil laid over his heart, to whom not even the very veil of the letter—by which the sense is veiled, which is the sound of the voice—has come near? It is therefore an evident figure, of how the face of Moses is made glorious; for the things he speaks have glory, but this is covered and hidden, and all his glory is within.

Consider also of what sort this is: that in the law the face of Moses is indeed reported as glorified, though it be covered with a veil; but his hand, put "within his bosom," is recorded as "made leprous like snow." In which there seems to me to be most fully depicted the form of the whole law; for in his face is designated the word of the law, in his hand its works. Since, therefore, "by the works of the law no one was to be justified," nor could the law bring anyone "to perfection," for that reason the hand of Moses is made "leprous" and is hidden away "in his bosom," as though destined to have no perfect work; but his face is glorified, yet is covered with a veil, because his word has the glory of knowledge, but hidden. Whence also the prophet says: "unless you hear in secret, your soul shall weep," and David says: "the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made manifest to me." In the law, therefore, Moses has his face alone glorified, and his hands have no glory, nay rather even disgrace; but neither do his feet.
