In short, he is commanded to loose his sandal; thus there was no glory in his feet—though this too came about not without the form of some mystery; for the feet are the last part of a man. It was shown, therefore, that in the last times Moses would loose his sandal, so that another might receive the bride, and that she would be called "the house of the unshod" "unto this present day." Moses, therefore, has nothing else glorious in the law except his face alone; but in the Gospels he is wholly glorified, entirely. For hear what it says in the Gospels: "when Jesus had ascended into a high mountain, taking with him Peter and James and John, and was transfigured there before them; and behold," it says, "there appeared Moses and Elijah in glory, speaking with him." Here it is not reported that his face was glorified, but that he wholly "appeared in glory," speaking with Jesus; and there is fulfilled for him that promise which he received on Mount Sinai, when it was said to him: "you shall see my hinder parts." He saw, therefore, his hinder parts. For he saw the things that were done in the latter and last days, and he rejoiced. For just as Abraham longed to see the day of the Lord "and saw it and rejoiced," so also Moses longed to see the day of the Lord "and saw it and rejoiced"; and necessarily "he rejoiced," because now he descended from the mountain glorified not in face alone, but ascended from the mountain wholly glorified. "Moses rejoiced," without doubt, because he now beheld present, and confirming his own words, the one of whom he had said: "the Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like myself; him you shall hear in all things." And that he might not hesitate in anything, he hears the Father's voice saying: "this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him." Moses long ago said: "him you shall hear": now the Father says: "this is my Son, hear him," and points out present the one of whom he speaks. Moses seems to me also to rejoice for this reason: that he too now in a certain manner lays aside "the veil, being turned to the Lord," when the things he foretold are evidently fulfilled, or when the time comes that the things he had covered over might, through the Spirit, be revealed.

Yet the holy Apostle's meaning must be reconsidered, and it must be pondered what he had in view when, having said: "but if anyone shall have turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away," he added: "now the Lord is the Spirit," by which he seems as it were to interpret what the Lord is. For who does not know that "the Lord is the Spirit"? But surely in this place it was not the Lord's nature or substance that was being treated, that he should say "the Lord is the Spirit"? Let us see, then, whether not only "when Moses is read," but also when Paul is read, "a veil" may be "placed over" our "heart." And plainly, if we hear negligently, if we bring no zeal to erudition and understanding, not only the Scripture of the law and the prophets, but even that of the Apostles and the Gospels is covered from us with a great veil. But I fear lest, through excessive negligence and dullness of heart, the divine volumes be for us not only veiled but even sealed, so that, "if a book to be read is given into the hands of a man who does not know letters, he says: I do not know letters; if it is given into the hands of a man who knows letters, he says: it is sealed." Whence it is shown that we must not only apply zeal to learning the sacred letters, but must also entreat the Lord and "day and night" beseech him, that the Lamb "from the tribe of Judah" may come and himself, taking the "sealed book," may deign to open it. For he it is who, "opening the Scriptures," kindled the hearts of the disciples, so that they said: "was not our heart burning within us, when he opened to us the Scriptures?" May he, therefore, even now deign to open to us what it is that he inspired his Apostle to say: "now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." I indeed, so far as I can perceive according to the smallness of my understanding, think that the Word of God, according to what concerns the hearers—as we have often already said—is named now "the way," now "the truth," now "the life," now "the resurrection," now also "flesh," but now "spirit." For although he truly received the substance of flesh from a virgin, in which he both endured the cross and inaugurated the resurrection, yet there is a place where the Apostle says: "even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer." Since, therefore, even now his word summons the hearers to a subtler and spiritual understanding, and wishes them to perceive nothing carnal in the law, he says that whoever wishes "the veil to be taken away" from his heart "let him turn to the Lord"—not as to a Lord according to the flesh—for there is this too, since "the Word was made flesh"—but as to a Lord according to the spirit. For if he turns as to a Lord according to the spirit, he will come from carnal things to spiritual, and will pass from servitude to liberty: for "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." And that what is said may become still more evident, let us make use also of other meanings of the Apostle. To certain ones, whom he had perceived to be incapable, he says: "I judged myself to know nothing else among you save Christ Jesus, and him crucified." To such ones as these he did not say that "the Lord is the Spirit," nor did he say to them that Christ is the "wisdom" of God. For "they could not recognize Christ according to that which is wisdom," but according to that which is "crucified." But those to whom he said: "we speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this age nor of the princes of this world, who are brought to nothing, but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery," did not need to receive the Word of God according to that which "was made flesh," but according to that which is "wisdom hidden in a mystery." So, therefore, in this place also, to those who are summoned from the carnal to the spiritual understanding, it is said: "now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." And that he might show that he himself has now arrived at the liberty of knowledge and has been stripped of the servitude of the veil, he adds to these words and says: "but we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord." If, therefore, we too beseech the Lord that he may deign to take the veil from our heart, we can grasp the spiritual understanding—provided, however, that we turn to the Lord and seek the liberty of knowledge. But how can we find liberty, we who serve the age, who serve money, who serve the desires of the flesh? I rebuke my own self, I judge my own self; I convict my own faults; let those who hear look to what they think of themselves. I meanwhile say that, so long as I am in bondage to any one of these things, I am not turned to the Lord, nor have I attained liberty, so long as such affairs and solicitudes bind me tight. Of that affair and solicitude by which I am bound tight, I am the servant; for I know it is written that "each one is delivered as a servant to that by which he is overcome." Even if the love of money does not overcome me, even if care for possessions and riches does not bind me, yet I am greedy of praise and pursue human glory, if I hang upon the faces and words of men—what this man thinks of me, how that man regards me, that I may not displease him, that I may please him. So long as I seek these things, I am their servant. But I would wish at least by this to be sufficiently in earnest, if I might become free, if I might be released from the yoke of this foul servitude and arrive at liberty according to the Apostle's admonition, who says: "you were called unto liberty, do not become the servants of men." But who will grant me this manumission? Who will free me from this most shameful servitude, save he who said: "if the Son shall free you, you shall be truly free"? But indeed I know that a servant cannot be granted liberty unless he serves faithfully, unless he loves his Lord. And therefore let us too serve faithfully and "with our whole heart and with our whole soul and with our whole strength love the Lord our God," that we may be worthy to be granted liberty by Christ Jesus his Son our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For so long as a man does not attend to the spiritual meaning "a veil lies upon his heart," in consequence of which veil, in other words his duller understanding, the Scripture itself is said or thought to be veiled. This is the explanation of the veil which is said to have covered the face of Moses when he was speaking to the people, that is, when the law is read in public. But if we turn to the Lord, where also the Word of God is and where the Holy Spirit reveals spiritual knowledge, the veil will be taken away, and we shall then with unveiled face behold in the holy Scriptures the glory of the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We had indeed already spoken before about the tabernacle, to the best of our ability; but since the description itself is often repeated in the book of Exodus — for it is set forth both when God commanded Moses how it ought to be made, and again when Moses commanded the people to offer materials for the work to be constructed, as this reading contains, which has just now been recited to us; but also afterwards the individual items are enumerated, when they are fashioned by Bezalel and the other wise men, and again when they are brought into the sight of Moses, and once more when they are dedicated by the Lord's command. Moreover, a mention of these things is made also in other books or places, and it is frequently repeated, inasmuch as it is necessarily brought to mind. Now, then, that discourse has been recited to us where it says: "and Moses said to all the synagogue of the sons of Israel, saying: this is the word which the Lord commanded, saying: take from among your own selves a redemption for the Lord. Everyone who has conceived it in his heart, let him bring the first offerings to the Lord: gold, silver, bronze, hyacinth, purple, doubled scarlet, and twisted fine linen, goats' hair, and rams' skins dyed red and hyacinthine skins, imperishable woods, and sardius stones and stones for carving on the shoulder-piece and on the full-length robe; and let everyone wise in heart among you come and work all the things which the Lord has commanded". When I consider myself first and examine myself, I am loath to set my hand to opening these things. For I fear that perhaps, even if the Lord should deign to reveal them, if indeed He deigns to reveal them to anyone — for concerning myself I have not dared to say it — I fear, I say, and I greatly doubt, whether he will find hearers; and since this is so, lest perhaps it be required of him who shall attempt to explain, where or how or before whom the Lord's pearls are cast. But since you greatly expect that some of the things which have been read should be discussed, and since my Lord has commanded me, saying: "you ought to have put my money at the table, and I, when I came, would surely have exacted it with interest", I will ask Him that He deign to make my word His own money, so that I may lend to you not my money, not my gold, but His own; that I may speak to you by His word and by His "understanding", and bring these things to the table of your hearing. See you now to it, as you receive the Lord's money, how you may prepare its interest for the Lord when He comes. Now the interest of the word of God is to have in the practice of life and of deeds those things which the word of God has commanded. If therefore, hearing the word, you make use of it and act according to the things you hear, and live according to these things, you are preparing interest for the Lord; and it can come to pass that each one of you may make from "five talents" ten, and may hear from the Lord: "well done, good and faithful servant, you shall be having power over ten cities". Only see to this, that none of you either gather up the money he has received "in a napkin" or bury it "in the earth", for you well know what the outcome of such a man is at the coming of the Lord. We shall therefore attempt a few things out of many, indeed even fewer out of the few, seeing that both our discourse must be weighed and your hearing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: First of all, then, let us see what it is that Moses says to the sons of Israel: "take from among your own selves a redemption for the Lord; everyone who has conceived it in his heart, let him offer the first offerings to the Lord". Moses does not wish you to offer to God something that is outside you: "from your own selves", he says, "take, and bring the first offerings to the Lord, according as each one has conceived it in his heart". Gold and silver are commanded to be brought, bronze and the other materials; how can I bring this from my own self? Surely gold is not born within me, or silver and the other things that are commanded? Does not each one bring these forth from his storerooms and from his chests? What is it, then, that Moses says: "bring from your own selves, and each one according as he has conceived it in his heart"? That gold indeed and silver and the other materials, from which the tabernacle was constructed, are agreed to have been brought forth from the chests and storerooms of each one; but the spiritual law requires gold for the tabernacle which is within us, and silver which is within us, and demands all those remaining materials which we both can have within us and bring forth from ourselves. For the Scripture says that: "the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart; for, if you confess the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you shall be saved". If therefore "you have believed in your heart", your heart and your understanding is gold; you have therefore offered gold to the tabernacle, the faith of your heart; but if you have also "confessed" with speech, you have offered the word of confession, silver. For this reason, then, Moses, who is the spiritual law, says: "take from your own selves". These things you take from your own self, these are within you, these, even if you are naked, you can have. But also what he added: "each one according as he has conceived it in his heart", looks to this. For you will not be able to offer anything to God from your understanding or from your word, unless first you have conceived in your heart the things that are written; unless you have been attentive and have listened diligently, your gold cannot be genuine, nor your silver; for it is required that it be "tested". Hear the Scripture saying: "the words of the Lord, chaste words, silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold". If therefore you have conceived in your heart the things that are written, your gold, that is, your understanding, will be genuine, and your silver, which is your word, genuine. What, too, shall we say about bronze? Bronze is also needed for the construction of the tabernacle. Bronze indeed seems able to be taken for strength and to be set in place of fortitude and constancy; but lest anyone say: this is to divine rather than to explain, where what is said is not fortified by the authority of the Scriptures, I think, then, that bronze can be taken for the voice. For speech is one thing, the voice another. Speech is called an utterance grounded upon reason; but the voice is, for example, whether one speaks in Latin, whether in Greek, whether more loftily, whether more subdued. But you demand that we prove these things too from the Scriptures, as is necessary. Hear what the Apostle says: "if", he says, "I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am one thing, as sounding bronze or a tinkling cymbal". So then, to speak with tongues and to translate from one language into another is an offering of bronze. For the tabernacle of the Lord must have all things, and nothing must be lacking in the house of God. There is, therefore, as we said, an offering of bronze, the voice. Now the voice is that which turns the meaning of another into another language; but speech is that which brings forth one's own meaning. Let all these things, therefore, be offered to God; let the understanding be offered to God, and the speech, and the voice.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What shall we say about the rest? For they are many, and to discuss each one is a huge task. But what will it profit, that they be spoken with our own huge labor, yet be spurned and perish, spurned by preoccupied hearers who attend upon the word of God for scarcely the point of a single hour? For "unless the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it". Nevertheless we, as has already been said above, deliver the Lord's money to the table; let each one of the hearers see how he receives the things that are delivered. "Let each one", he says, "according as he has conceived it in his heart, bring the first offerings to the Lord". As for what he called "first offerings", I ask what are the first offerings of gold, or what the first-fruits of silver? And how do first-fruits seem to be contributed from scarlet and purple and fine linen? Or how does one offer "according as he has conceived it in his heart"? This now strikes each one of us; let us see at the same time also how we have conceived in our heart, as many of us as are here present just now, and the word of God is being expounded. There are those who conceive in their heart the things that are read; there are those who do not at all conceive the things that are said, but their mind and heart is either in business or in the affairs of the world or in the reckonings of gain; and especially the women — how, do you think, do they conceive in their heart, who chatter so much, who make such an uproar with their tales that they do not permit there to be silence? Now what shall I discuss concerning their mind, what concerning their heart, if they are thinking either of their infants or of wool or of the necessities of the house? I truly fear that they may follow those women of whom the Apostle says: "who learn to go about the houses, not only talkative, but also curious, speaking the things that are not fitting". How, then, do such women as these conceive in their heart? One does not conceive in his heart unless he is empty in heart, unless he is free in mind and wholly attentive; unless he keeps watch in his heart, he cannot conceive in his heart and offer gifts to God. And even if we have neglected this hitherto, from this time at least let us be more attentive and diligently intent, that we may be able to conceive with the mind. For it is just that each one be found to have his own portion in the tabernacle of the Lord. For it does not escape the Lord what each one offers. How glorious it is for you, if it be said in the tabernacle of the Lord: that gold, for example, with which the ark of the covenant is overlaid, is his; the silver, from which the bases and columns are, is his; the bronze, from which the rings and the basin and some of the bases of the columns were made, is his; but also those stones of the shoulder-piece and of the oracle are his; the purple with which the high priest is adorned is his, and the scarlet is his, and each of the rest, one by one. And again, how unseemly, how wretched it will be, if the Lord, coming to inspect the building of the tabernacle, should find in it nothing of your gift, should recognize nothing offered by you. Have you lived so undevout, so unfaithful, that you have longed for nothing of your memorial to be in the tabernacle of God? For just as "the prince of this world" comes to each one of us and seeks whether he may find in us anything of his own deeds, and, if indeed he finds it, claims us for himself; so also, on the contrary, if the Lord, coming, should find anything of yours in His tabernacle, He defends you for Himself and calls you His own. Lord Jesus, grant me that I may deserve to have some memorial in Your tabernacle. I would wish, if it could be, that there be something of mine in that gold from which the mercy-seat is fashioned, or from which the ark is overlaid, or from which the lampstand of light and the lamps are made. Or if I have no gold, that I may at least be found to offer something of silver, that may serve for the columns or for their bases; surely at least that I may deserve to have something of bronze in the tabernacle, from which the rings are made and the rest that the word of God describes. And would that it were possible for me to be one of the princes and to offer gems for the adornment of the high priest's shoulder-piece and oracle. But since these things are above me, at least may I deserve to have goats' hair in the tabernacle of God, only that I be not found empty and unfruitful in all things. "Each one", therefore, "according as he has conceived it in his heart". See whether you are conceiving, see whether you are holding fast, lest perhaps the things that are said flow away and perish. I wish to admonish you by the examples of religion; you who are accustomed to take part in the divine mysteries know how, when you receive the body of the Lord, you guard it with all caution and reverence, lest any small part of it fall down, lest anything of the consecrated gift slip away. For you believe yourselves guilty, and rightly do you believe it, if anything of it should fall down through negligence. But if you employ such caution in preserving His body — and rightly do you employ it — how do you think it is of less guilt to have neglected the word of God than His body? First offerings, therefore, are commanded to be offered, that is, first-fruits. He who offers what is first, necessarily has himself what remains. See how much we ought to abound in gold, how much in silver and in all the rest that are commanded to be offered, that we may both offer to the Lord and have a surplus for ourselves. For first of all, my understanding ought to understand God and offer to Him the first-fruits of its understanding, so that, when it has understood God well, it may consequently recognize the rest. Let the speech do this too, let all things that are in us do this. But let us see the rest as well. "Hyacinth and purple and doubled scarlet and twisted fine linen". These are four things, from which are made either the vestments of the high priest or the rest that are prepared for the sacred adornment. Concerning these certain men before us have also spoken, and just as it is not fitting to steal what belongs to another, so I think it fitting to make use of another's good sayings while acknowledging it. These four things, then, as it seemed also to our predecessors, hold the figure of the four elements from which both the world and the human body are composed, that is, of air, fire, water, and earth. Hyacinth, therefore, is referred to air — for its very color indicates this — as scarlet is to fire. Purple holds the figure of water, as one that takes its dye from the waters; fine linen, of earth, because it arises from the earth. We therefore also have all these things in us, and because we are commanded to offer the first-fruits of these to the Lord, therefore he says: "take from your own selves, and you shall offer the first-fruits to the Lord".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But I think this must be considered, that, whereas Moses spoke of the rest simply, he added to scarlet alone "doubled", and to fine linen "twisted". It is asked, therefore, why the other materials, by which the remaining elements are indicated, he named simply, but scarlet, by which fire is designated, he alone set down as "doubled". These things are difficult to understand and much more difficult to expound. Nevertheless, as the Lord shall grant, we shall attempt to explain. For some things must be spoken and some things kept in reserve. Let us see, then, for what reason he called "scarlet doubled". This color, as we said, indicates the element of fire. Now fire has a twofold power, one by which it illuminates, another by which it burns. This is the reasoning of the literal sense; let us come also to the intellectual meanings. Even in these matters fire is twofold; there is a certain fire in this age, and there is one in the age to come. The Lord Jesus says: "I have come to send fire upon the earth": this fire illuminates. The same Lord again says in the age to come to the "workers of iniquity": "go into the eternal fire, which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels": that fire burns. Nevertheless this fire, which Jesus came to send, indeed "illuminates every man coming into this world", yet it has also something that burns, as those confess who say: "was not our heart burning within us, when He opened the scriptures to us?" At the same time, therefore, it both burned and illuminated in "opening the scriptures". But I do not know whether that fire also in the age to come, which burns, has anything too that illuminates. There is, therefore, as we have shown, a twofold nature of fire, and for this reason "doubled scarlet" is commanded to be offered. Let us see, then, how we can offer this doubled fire for the building of the tabernacle. If you are a teacher, you build the tabernacle by constructing the church of God; God therefore says also to you what He said to Jeremiah: "behold, I have given my words in your mouth as fire". If therefore, teaching and building the church of God, you only rebuke and censure and chastise and reproach the sins of the people, but bring forth no consolation from the divine scriptures, explain nothing obscure, touch nothing of deeper knowledge nor open anything of more sacred understanding, you have indeed offered scarlet, but not doubled. For your fire only burns and does not illuminate. And again, if, teaching, you open the mysteries of the law, discuss the secrets of hidden things, but do not reprove the sinner, do not correct the negligent, do not maintain the severity of discipline, you have indeed offered scarlet, but not doubled. For your fire only illuminates, it does not kindle. He therefore who "offers rightly" and "divides rightly" offers doubled scarlet, so that with the light of knowledge he mingles a little fire of severity.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now let us see what "twisted fine linen" too means. For here also he gave something of addition beyond the other elements. We said that fine linen holds the form of earth, which is our flesh. He does not wish, therefore, the flesh to be offered to God floating in luxury and loosened by delights, but he commands it to be twisted and constrained. Who, then, is he who twists his flesh? Assuredly he who said: "I mortify my body and subject it to servitude, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself become reprobate". Thus, then, is it to offer twisted fine linen also, to wear down the flesh by abstinence, by vigils and by the labor of meditations. Goats' hair also is offered. This kind of beast in the law is commanded to be offered for sin; but hair is a species that is dead, bloodless, lifeless. He who offers this shows that in himself the sense of sin is already dead, and that sin no longer lives or reigns in his members.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Rams' skins also are offered. Certain men before us have also set the ram for fury. And because the skin is a token of a dead animal, he who offers rams' skins to the Lord shows fury dead in himself.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things: "and the men", he says, "took from their women, all to whom it seemed good in their understanding, and brought gems and earrings and rings and hair-clasps and armlets". You see here too how those bring gifts to God who see with the heart, who conceive understanding in the heart, who have the mind intent and devoted to the word of God. These, then, bring gifts, and they bring them even from their women: "earrings", he says, "and gems and armlets". We have already often said that, according to the allegorical interpretation, the woman is taken as the flesh and the man as the rational sense. Good, therefore, are these women who obey their husbands; good is the flesh which no longer fights against the spirit, but complies and consents, and therefore "if two or three of you agree, concerning whatever thing you shall ask, it shall be done for you", the Lord said. They offer, therefore, "earrings from their women". You see how the hearing is offered to the Lord. But armlets too are offered to the Lord: right works and good works, which are performed through the flesh. These the rational sense offers to the Lord. But hair-clasps also are offered. He offers hair-clasps who knows well to discern what is to be done, what is to be avoided, what pleases God, or what displeases, what is just, what is unjust. These are the hair-clasps that are offered to the Lord. Here, then, the women offer earrings to the Lord, because they are wise women. For there came, he says, wise women, and made whatever things were necessary for the vestments of the high priest. But those women who offered their earrings that the calf might be made were foolish, women who "turned away their hearing indeed from the truth, but turned it to fables and impiety"; and therefore they offered their earrings that the head of a calf might be made. But in the book of Judges too we find likewise another idol made from women's earrings. These, then, are blessed women, blessed is that flesh, which offers to the Lord its earrings and its armlets and its rings and all the works of its hands which it performs in the commandments of the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It is added after these things that "he too with whom imperishable woods were found", brought them to the Lord. If anyone "loves Christ the Lord in incorruption", he offers imperishable wood to God. Blessed, therefore, is he with whom is found either an incorrupt understanding or an incorrupt body, and offers this to God. Hence too he said very well: "with whom imperishable woods were found". For "imperishable woods" are not found with everyone. Of gold he did not say, nor of silver, with whom it was found; for understanding and speech can be found with everyone. But neither did he say this of the four colors; for it belongs to all to consist, according to the body, of four elements. But "imperishable woods", that is, the grace of incorruption and virginity, can be found with only a rare one, as the Lord too says: "not all receive this word, but those to whom it is given".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But also the "princes", he says, "offered" their gifts. What are these gifts which the princes offer? "Gems", he says, "they offered, emerald stones and stones of filling and stones for the shoulder-piece". Stones of filling are called those which are placed in the oracle, that is, which are set on the breast of the high priest, inscribed with the names of the tribes of Israel. This which is called the oracle, that is, the rational, which is set on the breast of the high priest, has the form of the rational sense which is in us. In this are said to be placed the "stones of filling", which yet cling and are connected to the shoulder stones and are held bound together by these. The adornment of the shoulder-piece is a token of good deeds. Deeds, therefore, are joined with reason and reason with deeds, so that there may be a harmony in both: "for he who shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven". Let there be in us, therefore, speech depending upon deeds, and let deeds adorn the speech; for this refers to the adornment of the high priest. But to accomplish these things princes are required; this adornment belongs to those who have advanced so far that they deserve to preside over peoples.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The princes also offer oil, to serve for a twofold use, for the lamps and for the anointing. For the lamp of those who preside over peoples ought not to be hidden or "put under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house". But the princes also offer "the composition of incense", which is to be compounded by Moses "for a sweet odor to the Lord", so that they too may say that "we are a good odor of Christ".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And after the people had offered, "Moses", he says, "called every wise man" for the fashioning, and the architect, that they might put together and fashion each of the things that are written. "But also the women", he says, "the wise women he called", that they might make the things which were suitable in the tabernacle of the Lord. You see, then, that all the things which are made are made by wise persons; both women are called wise and men are called wise. For "all the works of the Lord" are made "in wisdom". Each one, therefore, comes "wise in understanding" and makes the works of the Lord. It does not suffice for us if we only offer, but there is need that we also work with wisdom those things that are in us, that we may know how to mingle gold with fine linen and to double scarlet or to mingle it with purple. For what does it profit you, if you have these things and know not how to use them, nor recognize how you ought to fit and bring forth each thing in its own time and in its own place? And therefore we must give effort to being wise and being able to bring forth these things which we hear from the holy scriptures in their time and to fit and to compose them, and from these to adorn "the tabernacle for the God of Jacob", through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom is "glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".

author: Pacian of Barcelona
quote: What does this mean? The vision that is said to have appeared to Moses in the desert is sometimes called an angel, sometimes the Lord. It means this: he is called angel when he served by speaking externally, and Lord, because he ruled within and produced the conditions needed for speaking. For when the speaker is ruled from within, he is called both angel because of his service and Lord because of his inspiration. Exposition of the Old and New Testament, Exodus

author: Pacian of Barcelona
quote: In Moses and Aaron the law and the prophets are prefigured. A sick soul often murmurs to itself against the sacred words. After it has begun to hear and follow the heavenly words, the opposition of the Egyptian king—that is, the temptation of an evil spirit—rises up. So the physician should carefully make known to the soul that is making progress which temptations will attack it, so that it can carefully prepare itself for the snares of an evil spirit. Exposition of the Old and New Testament, Exodus

author: Pacian of Barcelona
quote: The Egyptians disdained the eating of sheep. But what the Egyptians abhor, the Israelites offer to God. The unjust despise a clean conscience as weak and abject, but the just turn it into a sacrifice to God of virtue. The righteous, as they worship God, offer their purity and gentleness to him. The reprobate despise these virtues and consider them foolishness. Exposition of the Old and New Testament, Exodus

author: Pacian of Barcelona
quote: To make an altar of earth for the Lord is to place our hope in the incarnation of the Mediator. Our gift is accepted by God when, on this altar, our humility rests whatever it does upon faith in the Lord's incarnation. We place the gift we offer on an altar made of earth if we base all our actions on faith in the Lord's incarnation. Exposition of the Old and New Testament, Exodus

author: Pacian of Barcelona
quote: What can the silver bases of the frames signify, except the order of prophets? They were the first to speak openly of the Lord's incarnation. They were like bases, and we see them rising from the foundations and sustaining the weight of the structure built on them. So when the Lord bade Moses build the frames of the tabernacle, Moses had the builders set them on their silver bases. What do the frames mean, except the apostles, who were spread out into the world by their preaching? What do the silver bases mean, except the prophets? They are firm, cast metal, and sustain the frames placed on them. The apostles' lives are guided by their proclamation and strengthened by their authority. So two bases are joined and placed under each frame. For when the holy prophets agree in what they say about the incarnation of the Mediator, they undoubtedly build up the preachers in the church who follow them. They do not disagree among themselves, and they make the preachers stronger. God rightly commands that the bases, which signify the prophets, should be cast in silver. The gleam of silver is maintained by use; when it is not used, it turns black. The prophets spoke before the Mediator came. Since their words were not joined into one spiritual understanding and could not be seen clearly because of the darkness, they remained, as it were, black. But afterwards, the Mediator came and cleansed our eyes with the hand of his incarnation. Whatever light was concealed in our eyes he made clear. He made the intentions of the ancient fathers useful, because he confirmed their words with his deeds. Exposition of the Old and New Testament, Exodus

author: Pacian of Barcelona
quote: The tabernacle is a type of the church. So God says to Moses that the bases of the four pillars placed within it should be silver. What does silver mean except the clarity of the divine Word? Scripture says, "The words of the Lord are chaste words, silver tried by fire, cleansed from earth." The bases are overlaid with silver and hold up the four pillars of the tabernacle, just as the preachers of the church are adorned with divine eloquence. They provide an example in every way; they have the words of the four Evangelists on their lips and in their deeds. Exposition of the Old and New Testament, Exodus

author: Pacian of Barcelona
quote: The place is the church, the rock is the Lord, Moses is the multitude of the people of Israel, who did not believe in the Lord when he preached on the earth. So that multitude stood on the rock and beheld the back parts of the Lord as he passed by. After the Lord's passion and ascension they were led into the church and merited to receive faith in Christ. They did not recognize him face to face on earth but later acknowledged him "from behind." Exposition of the Old and New Testament, Exodus

author: Paterius
quote: What does this mean? The vision that is said to have appeared to Moses in the desert is sometimes called an angel, sometimes the Lord. For when the speaker is ruled from within, he is called both angel because of his service and Lord because of his inspiration.

author: Paterius
quote: What does it mean that the Lord now says through Moses, "You visit the iniquity of fathers on their sons and grandsons"? In these two passages a different sense is found, but the mind of the hearer is taught to inquire subtly along the path of discernment. We inherit original sin from our parents, and unless we are washed by the grace of baptism, we bear even our parents' sins, because up to that point we are one with them. So God will visit the iniquity of the fathers upon their sons, for, through original sin, the soul of the offspring is stained by the guilt of the parent. But then God does not visit the iniquity of fathers on their sons, because, when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we no longer have our parents' guilt but only the guilt for sins we ourselves committed. This passage can also be understood in another way, because when each one imitates the iniquity of his sinful parent, he is rendered guilty through his parent's fault. But whoever does not imitate the iniquity of his parent is not burdened with his sin. Thus it happens that the sinful son of a sinful father pays the penalty not only for his own sins, which he committed, but also for his father's sins. For he does not fear to add his own malice to his father's vices, even though he knows that the Lord is angered by them. It is just that a man who does not fear to imitate the ways of his wicked father before a busy judge is forced in this present life to pay the penalty for the faults of his wicked father. So Scripture says, "The soul of my father is mine; … the soul that sins, that one will die." For in the flesh sons sometimes perish for their father's sin. But when the original sin that comes from the parents' iniquity is forgiven, it is no longer kept in the soul. What does it mean that small children are often snatched away by demons, unless the son's flesh suffers to punish the father? For the wicked father is struck at in his very self and refuses to sense the force of the blow. Generally he is struck in his sons, so that he burns painfully, and the father's sorrow is visited on the son's flesh, insofar as the father's evil heart is punished by the son's suffering. But when the sons who are punished for their fathers' guilt are not little children but already grown, what else should we understand except that they are suffering the punishments of those people whose deeds they imitated? Thus Scripture says rightly, "To the third and fourth generation." For the sons can see the lives of the parents they imitate up to the third and fourth generation. Punishment extends up to them, for they saw what they would imitate sinfully.
source_title: EXPOSITION OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT, EXODUS 60

author: Paulinus of Nola
quote: We find that arms have always needed faith, but faith has never needed arms. The rod of faith parted the sea which submerged the army bereft of faith together with its wicked leader.

author: Paulinus of Nola
quote: Note how the teachers of the Old and New Testaments differ in their deeds but are paired in glory, for the one Wisdom issued twin laws in the two Testaments, so equal distinction gives the same weight to differing powers. Peter did not divide the sea with a rod, but then Moses did not walk on the waters. However, both have the same bright glory, for the one Creator inspired both the cleavage of the waters with a rod and the treading of the waves underfoot.

author: Paulus Orosius
quote: The Hebrews proceeded safely over the dry passage, and the masses of stationary water collapsed behind them. The entire Egyptian multitude with their king was overwhelmed and killed, and the entire province, which had previously been tortured by plagues, became empty by this last slaughter. Even today there exists most reliable evidence of these events. For the tracks of chariots and the ruts made by the wheels are visible not only on the shore but also in the deep, as far as sight can reach. And if perchance for the moment they are disturbed either accidentally or purposely, they are immediately restored through divine providence by winds and waves to their original appearances, so that whoever is not taught to fear God by the study of revealed religion may be terrified by his anger through this example of his accomplished vengeance.
source_title: SEVEN BOOKS OF HISTORY AGAINST THE PAGANS 1.10

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: This is why he summons Moses by his fatherly voice, addresses him with paternal love and invites him to be the liberator of his people. Why should I say more? He makes him a god; he sets him up as a god before Pharaoh. He makes him a god, fortifies him with signs, arms him with virtues, wins wars through mere commands, grants to him as a soldier victory gained by a mere word. By his orders he concedes him a triumph and leads him through all the crowns of virtues to his own friendship, gives him an opportunity to share in his heavenly kingdom and allows him to be a legislator. However, Moses received all this that he might love—that at length he might be so inflamed with the love of God that he would burn with it himself and encourage others to have it too.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: Hence it is that through the influence of these three things Moses is made a god: for the sake of his military triumphs he brings all the elements under his control. He bids the sea to withdraw, its waves to solidify, its bottom to become dry and the sky to drop its rain. He supplies food, compels the winds to scatter meats, illumines the night with the splendor of the sun, tempers the sun by the veil of the cloud. He strikes the rock to make it yield from its fresh wound cool streams of water for those who thirst. He first gives to the earth heaven's law, writes down the norms of living, sets the terms of disciplinary control.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: At one time he appears all aglow in a bush. For you are cold with the perfidy of infidelity, and he wants to enkindle you with the heat of faith. At another time he glows like fire in a pillar extending toward heaven, that the darkness of your ignorance may be removed and that you can follow the way of saving knowledge through the wilderness of this world. At yet another time he is changed for you into a pillar of cloud, in order to restrain the burning ebullience of your passions.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: This name is related to prophecy and salutary to those reborn. It is the badge of virginity, the glory of purity, the indication of chastity, the sacrificial gift of God, the height of hospitality, the sum total of sanctity. Rightly therefore is this motherly name that of the mother of Christ.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: The rain of manna fed the Jewish people for forty years in the desert. It did not by its customary service cause an increase of sprouts from the earth but streamed on the earth like harvested grains. It took away all the toil of human labor and by its pleasant dew offered and spread out heavenly produce for the hungry.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: Moses himself was so purified and freed from his body by a fast of forty days that his whole self took on a glorious appearance of divinity. Still in the darkness of our body, he gleamed with the full radiance of divinity. The eyes of mortals could not gaze upon him who, long nourished by the substance of God, had forgotten all about the aids provided by mortals' food. From this he learned that the sustenance of life does not fail those who live in God's sight and with him.

author: Peter Chrysologus
quote: This is why love which longs to see God, even if it lacks judgment, does have the spirit of devotion. This is why Moses dares to say, "If I have found favor in your sight, show me your face." This is why another man says, "Show us your face." Finally, this is why the Gentiles fashioned idols. In their errors they wanted to see with their eyes what they were worshiping.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: But fear thou not, neither be thou afraid, for instead of Moses, Jesus is with thee, for like as Moses clave to the congregation, even so also doth Christ cleave to thy soul, and He saith unto thy tortured and afflicted mind that which was said by Moses to the Jews, "The Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace." Therefore thou shalt not be in fear as were the people, but thou shalt rouse up, and watch like Moses, and cry out to the Lord even as he cried out. Therefore do thou in thy thoughts repeat the words of Moses, "The Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace"; and as the Hebrews passed over with Moses, even so shall all thy triumphs pass over with thee.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Moses prayed the whole night with much crying out and suffering, and at the morning watch the Lord said to him, "Why criest thou before Me? Incline thy hand over the sea, and divide it, and the Hebrews shall pass over it, but the Egyptians shall be drowned therein." Now all the things which happened at that time are a type of those which shall be done unto thee. And enemies, that is, evil devils, shall gather together and crowd against thy soul, even as the Egyptians who pursued after the Jews were gathered together and crowded upon them; but as Moses forsook the fear of the Egyptians and turned himself unto prayer and unto crying out to God, do thou also forsake the anxieties and thoughts which devilish enemies make to rise up in thee. And stand thou up in earnest prayer, and cry out with deep feeling from the heart, and from the depth of the thoughts of the soul let the voice of thy cry rise up, and straightway that answer which was returned unto Moses shall also be spoken unto thee, "Why dost thou cry out before Me? Incline thy hand over the sea, and divide it"; and straightway thy afflictions will give way, and the covering which was set before thy face will be rolled up, and the terrible depths of affliction will give way, and the things which thou didst think could not be crossed over with the foot, thou shalt tread upon, and thou shalt pass over the depth thereof. And difficult things shall become easy for thee, and that wall, which is built in such a manner that thou didst think it could not be broken through, shall be immediately swept away from before thee, and thy prayer shall rend and pass over the abyss of all the wickedness which is gathered together and laid before thee.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 9 -- Second Discourse on Poverty

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: The Jews ate flesh in the wilderness, and it is written concerning them that, "While the flesh was yet between their teeth the anger of God had dominion over them," not because they had eaten flesh, but because with lust they had asked to eat it. And in the place where they required flesh it is written that, "The people said to Moses, It was better for us when we were in Egypt, for we sat by the flesh pots, and did eat, and were filled with everything that our soul lusted for." Behold then, according to the word of Moses unto the Jews, every one that eateth in lust, rejecteth the Lord Who is in him, and he resteth upon his lust's desire.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And thou must in another way understand that it is lust which is reprehensible, for every day, morning after morning, the people gathered the manna which came down, and so long as they gathered it according to the command they were not reprehended or condemned; but when they lusted to gather it in too great a quantity, it swarmed with worms and stank, to the shame of the lust which gathered it.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And moreover when they ate it formerly, its taste was changed into that of all kinds of meats in their mouth, and it is well known that it also took the place of flesh unto them, for it is written, "It was like honey comb, and its taste was as if it had been kneaded in oil." And although it was changed into all these varieties of food the eaters thereof were not condemned thereby, for it was a gift of Grace, and not that which their lust had demanded.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And God also gave the law by the hand of Moses, which was filled with many and divers commandments, and to all the commandments He linked fear, for without fear the commandments would not be kept. "Thou shalt do no murder", and "whosoever slayeth shall be slain;" for the sickness He ordained the medicine of fear, that it might not increase and grow strong in iniquity.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 6 -- First Discourse on the Fear of God

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: "Thou shalt not commit adultery", and "whosoever committed adultery shall be slain;" and fear keepeth [this] commandment from being held in contempt. For by fear He checked them from doing wickedness to one another, and because He saw that they loved wickedness, He restrained them from their [evil] deed by the fear of the judgment. Where there is no love, it is fear that keepeth the commandments.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 6 -- First Discourse on the Fear of God

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And like this holy man the blessed Moses also was twice deemed worthy to go unto the thick darkness and to receive the law upon the tablets; and he was made pure by fasting like unto this, and then he was deemed worthy of the terrible sight.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Now this is the first lust which conquered the world, and because of it the first transgression of the law took place. It destroyed the people in the wilderness by penalties of all kinds; from the table of lust they rose up and worshipped a dead calf. Incited thereby they were ungrateful for all the acts of grace which had been shewn unto them.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And together with the testimony of the Word we may also see from the fact itself how they came to offer praises before the calf in the wilderness, "The people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play;" until food had entered in blasphemies did not go forth, and until wine had been poured into them they were not clothed with the fornication which is against God.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: Now this is the first lust which conquered the world, and because of it the first transgression of the law took place. It destroyed the people in the wilderness by penalties of all kinds; from the table of lust they rose up and worshipped a dead calf. Incited thereby they were ungrateful for all the acts of grace which had been shewn unto them.

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And that He might increase in them this fear, immediately, by the mouth of offence, the rod of His chastisement was revealed, and after the offence the Chastiser gave them no respite, because their servitude was not worthy of His longsuffering. Above their head the rod of justice hung continually, and immediately they committed sin they were chastened, and at the time of their offence they were beaten, and at the entrance of the path of their sins they forthwith received rebuke; for longsuffering teacheth the foolish servant contempt, and in order that that stupid nation, which in the manner of an evil-doing servant, sat in the house of God, might not [learn] contempt, the Chastiser took away longsuffering, especially when they went forth from Egypt. And we must also understand the object of that swift punishment in another way, and that there was not longsuffering as regardeth the correction of their sins; for God the Teacher took the people, like a child, from Egypt their nurse, that He might deliver unto them the doctrine of His knowledge, and might teach them the instruction of His wisdom. But the people, in their ignorance, when instruction had been delivered unto them, forgot it, and they never kept in remembrance the meditation of the commandments of God, and they were frequently punished with severity, so that, if it were only through fear of chastisement, they might lay hold upon the remembrance of instruction. The man who gathered sticks on the Sabbath day was stoned by all the congregation; and the earth opened and swallowed up others who were called by Moses, and who scorned him and came not; and fire went forth suddenly, and burnt up the bodies of others who thought lightly of his priestly office, and who sought honour for themselves; and others, who in the guise of paying honour, brought strange fire out of season, were burnt up by a tongue of fire which went forth from the tabernacle, and they perished; and others, because they asked for flesh and rejected the bread of angels, were tortured by the indigestion which came upon them; and others who went astray as concerning the calf, were pierced through by the swords of the Levites; and others, who were the cause of the revolt at the waters of trial were set apart for destruction; and others who murmured against the Lord perished by fiendish snakes; and likewise they all, because they strove against going into the land of promise, came to an end and were destroyed in the wilderness. To these offences, then, these punishments were united, and together with each act of wickedness a punishment straightway sprang up by its side, so that evil deeds might be suppressed by stripes, and sins by vengeance, and so that the people might be like a child who feareth the teacher who giveth him instruction, and that it might tremble before the Judge who would beat them like a wrongdoing slave.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: "But the young man Joshua departed not from the tent, but was there continually in the service of Moses;" and he that was free from going out and coming in among the multitude was especially nigh unto simplicity. If cunning and wickedness are gathered together from conversation with the multitude, it is evident that simplicity and integrity can be acquired from being brought up to lead a life of silent contemplation, and the more a man increaseth his life of contemplation, the more his possession of simplicity groweth.
source_title: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

author: Philoxenus of Mabbug
quote: And like this holy man the blessed Moses also was twice deemed worthy to go unto the thick darkness and to receive the law upon the tablets; and he was made pure by fasting like unto this, and then he was deemed worthy of the terrible sight.

author: Prudentius
quote:
Thus Moses in a former age
Escaped proud Pharaoh's foolish law,
And as the savior of his race
Prefigured Christ who was to come.
A cruel edict had been passed
Forbidding Hebrew mothers all,
When sons were born to them, to rear
These virile pledges of their love.
Devoutly scornful of the king,
A zealous midwife found a way
To hide her charge and keep him safe
For future glory and renown.

author: Prudentius
quote:
It was the Word, breathed from the Father's mouth,
Who of the Virgin took a mortal frame.
The human form that not yet in the flesh
Appeared to Moses wore a brow like ours,
Since God, who would by power of the Word
Assume a body, made the face the same.
Flames rose and seemed to burn the thorny bush.
God moved amid the branches set with spines,
And tresses of the flames swayed harmlessly,
That he might shadow forth his Son's descent
Into our thorny members sin infests
With teeming briers and fills with bitter woes.
For tainted at its root that noxious shrub
Had sprouted from its baneful sap a crop
Of evil shoots beset with many thorns.
The sterile branches suddenly grew bright
As God enkindled with his mighty power
The leafy boughs, nor harmed the tangled briers.
He touched the scarlet berries, blood-red fruits,
And grazed the twigs that grew from deadly wood,
Shed by the tortured bush with cruel pangs.

author: Pseudo-Macarius
quote: After having inflicted the Egyptians with many plagues, he led them out of Egypt in the month of flowers, when the most pleasant spring appears and the sadness of winter passes away.

author: Pseudo-Macarius
quote: This, I say, is the first month of the year. This brings joy to every creature. It clothes the naked trees. It opens the earth. This produces joy in all animals. It brings mirth to all. This is for Christians Xanthicus, the first month, the time of the resurrection in which their bodies will be glorified by means of the light which even now is in them hidden. This is the power of the Spirit who will then be their clothing, food, drink, exultation, gladness, peace, adornment and eternal life.

author: Pseudo-Macarius
quote: But if man groans and cries out to God, he sends him the spiritual Moses, who redeems him from the slavery of the Egyptians. But man first cries out and groans and then he receives the beginning of deliverance. And he is delivered in the month of new flowers, in the springtime when the ground of the soul is able to shoot forth the beautiful and flowering branches of justification. The bitter winter storms of the ignorance of darkness have passed, as well as the great blindness that was born of sordid deeds and sins.

author: Salvian the Presbyter
quote: Thus is it written: "The Lord therefore struck the people for their guilt on the occasion of the calf which Aaron had made." What greater and more manifest judgment could God have made regarding sinners than that punishment immediately follow their sins? Yet, since all were guilty, why was not condemnation visited on all? Because the good Lord struck some with the swords of his sentence in order to correct others by example and to prove to all at the same time, his judgment by correcting, his love by pardoning. When he punished, he judged; when he pardoned, he loved. His judgment and love were unequal: his love was more evident than was his severity.

author: Tertullian
quote: … Jesus Christ was to introduce the second people (which is composed of us nations, lingering deserted in the world previously) into the land of promise, "flowing with milk and honey" (that is, into the possession of eternal life, than which nothing is sweeter). This had to come about not through Moses (that is, not through the law's discipline) but through Joshua (that is, through the new law's grace), after our circumcision with "a knife of rock" (that is, with Christ's precepts, for Christ is in many ways and figures predicted as a rock). Therefore the man who was being prepared to act as an image of this sacrament was inaugurated under the figure of the Lord's name, even so as to be named Jesus.

author: Tertullian
quote: The Egyptians put in a claim on the Hebrews for these gold and silver vessels. The Hebrews assert a counterclaim, alleging that by the bond of their respective fathers, attested by the written engagement of both parties, there were due to them the arrears of that laborious slavery of theirs for the bricks they had so painfully made and the cities and palaces which they had built.

author: Tertullian
quote: But we know that prophecy expressed itself by things no less than by words. By words and also by deeds is the resurrection foretold. When Moses puts his hand into his bosom and then draws it out again dead, and again puts his hand into his bosom and plucks it out living, does not this apply as an anticipation of the resurrection to all humankind?—inasmuch as those three signs denoted the threefold power of God: when it shall, first, in the appointed order, subdue to man the old serpent, the devil, however formidable; then, second, draw forth the flesh from the bosom of death; and then, at last, shall pursue all blood [shed] in judgment.
source_title: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 28.1-2

author: Tertullian
quote: For who is really holy but the Son of God? Who properly opened the womb but he who opened a closed one? But it is marriage which opens the womb in all cases. The Virgin's womb, therefore, was especially opened, because it was especially closed.

author: Tertullian
quote: Again, water is restored from its defect to its native grace of "sweetness" by the tree of Moses. That tree was Christ, restoring of himself the veins of what had been envenomed and bitter nature into the all-salutary waters of baptism.

author: Tertullian
quote: But, to come now to Moses, why, I wonder, did he merely at the time when Joshua was battling against Amalek, pray sitting with hands expanded, when, in circumstances so critical, he ought rather, surely, to have commended his prayer by knees bent, and hands beating his breast, and a face prostrate on the ground; except it was that there, where the name of the Lord Jesus was the theme of speech—destined as he was to enter the lists one day singly against the devil—the figure of the cross was also necessary, [that figure] through which Jesus was to win the victory?

author: Tertullian
quote: But what parts of the law can I defend as good with a greater confidence than those which heresy has shown such a longing for—as the statute of retaliation, requiring eye for eye, tooth for tooth and stripe for stripe? Now there is not here any smack of permission to mutual injury. There is rather, on the whole, a provision for restraining violence. To a people which was very obdurate and wanting in faith toward God, it might seem tedious and even incredible to expect from God that vengeance which was subsequently to be declared by the prophet: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord." Therefore, in the meanwhile, the commission of wrong was to be checked by the fear of retribution immediately to happen. So the permission of this retribution was to be the prohibition of provocation. In this way a stop might thus be put to all hot-blooded injury. By the permission of the second the first is prevented by fear. By this deterring of the first the second act of wrong fails to be committed.

author: Tertullian
quote: For Joshua was to introduce the people into the land of promise, not Moses. Now he called him an angel on account of the magnitude of the mighty deeds which he was to achieve (which mighty deeds Joshua the son of Nun did, as you can yourselves read) and on account of his office of prophet announcing the divine will. Similarly the Spirit, speaking in the person of the Father, calls the forerunner of Christ, John, a future angel, through the prophet: "Behold, I send my angel before your"—that is, Christ's—"face, who shall prepare your way before you."

author: Tertullian
quote: He called him an angel indeed, because of the greatness of the powers which he was to exercise and because of his prophetic office, while announcing the will of God. He is called Joshua (also Jesus), because it was a type of his own future name.

author: Tertullian
quote: But why was it that [Christ] chose twelve apostles, and not some other number? In truth, I might from this very point conclude of my Christ that he was foretold not only by the words of prophets but by the embodied language of facts. For of this number I find figurative hints up and down the Creator's dispensation in the twelve springs of Elim; in the twelve gems of Aaron's priestly vestment; and in the twelve stones appointed by Joshua to be taken out of the Jordan and set up for the ark of the covenant.

author: Theodoret of Cyrus
quote: Why did God command Moses to erect the tabernacle on the first day of the first month? Because at that time he created the world. The sprouting of the trees attests to this fact. For Scripture says, "Let the earth sprout forth grass for fodder, and sow seed according to its kind and its likeness, and fruit-bearing trees that produce fruit, with its seed within it in its likeness, according to its kind upon the earth." When spring begins, the meadows bloom, the fields grow like waves, and the trees germinate their fruit. So too in this very season God set Israel free from slavery under the Egyptians and the archangel Gabriel brought the holy virgin the good news of her mysterious childbearing. In this same season the Lord Christ underwent his saving passion. Most fittingly, the Lord God of all ordered the tabernacle to be erected on the first day of the first month because it was the image of the entire world, and also so that the people would prepare for the feast of Passover, which the law commanded the Jews to celebrate as the first feast. At that time, they were going to celebrate this feast for the first time in the desert, for this was the second year after their deliverance from slavery.

author: Victorinus of Pettau
quote: Moses, foreseeing the hardness of that people, on the Sabbath raised up his hands, therefore, and thus figuratively fastened himself to a cross. And in the battle they were sought for by the foreigners on the Sabbath-day, that they might be taken captive, and, as if by the very strictness of the law, might be fashioned to the avoidance of its teaching.
source_title: On the Creation of the World
